title: Introduction to RF Signal Generators and Signal Modulators
text:
1.1 INTRODUCTION

R adio signal transmission and reception originate from the process of carrier signal generation and signal modulation              to radiation of radio frequency (RF) signal in form of electromagnetic wave. Except the RF signal radiation which occurs outside radio transmitter, the carrier signal generation and signal modulation occur inside the transmitter. Carrier signals are generated by oscillators while the signal modulation is done by signal modulators. Oscillators are classified in two ways according to nature of signal frequency generated. These are audio frequency oscillators and radiofrequency oscillators. Audio frequency oscillators are generally used for generating low frequency signal of audio range. Good examples include Wein bridge oscillator, phase shift oscillators. The radio frequency oscillators are normally used for generating carrier (very high frequency) signals. By function, carrier oscillators (generators) and modulators are separate circuits inside radio transmitter, but combination of the two as a single unit circuit form a signal generator. Signal generator, like an oscillator, is a source of sinusoidal signals, but the signal generator has the capability to modulate its sinusoidal output signals with other (modulating) signal. This is the main difference between the two. In this chapter, our focus shall be on the RF oscillators and the signal modulators.

1.2 RADIO FREQUENCY OSCILLATORS

RF oscillators are oscillator circuits that are capable of generating carrier wave form in the range of Medium Frequency (MF), Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF)by converting energy of d. c form to a. c. The wave form can be of any type but occurs at some regular frequency. The oscillators within this class are LC oscillators and crystal-controlled oscillator. Generally, oscillators have basically three parts or elements. The elements are the oscillatory circuit, amplifier and feedback network. The oscillatory circuit is the section of the oscillator from where the signal is generated. The amplifier, usually a transistor or operational amplifier (OP-Amp) supplies the energy that sustains the generated signals and prevents it from damping. It produces this energy by converting d. c power supply into a. c for supply to the oscillatory circuit. Because of the amplifying properties of the amplifier, we get increased output of these oscillations. The feedback network supplies a part of output power to the oscillatory circuit in correct phase to aid the oscillations. In other words, the feedback circuit provides positive feedback. The block diagram of an oscillator is illustrated in figure 1.1
[Figure 1.1: General block diagram of Oscillators]

1.2.1 LC OSCILLATORS

An LC oscillator is an oscillator build from an LC tank circuit which a (positive) feed- back amplifier is connected to so that it will generate a continuous wave. The commonly used amplifiers that are connected to the oscillator are BJT and FET. In the mathematical analysis of the frequency of the signal generated by the oscillators, the parameters of the amplifier (BJT or FET) used are usually considered. However, in our discussion here, we shall treat the frequency of the oscillators in view of frequency of tank circuit, neglecting the resistances and conductance of the BJT or FET, in use, though we may include them in the drawing of the oscillators. The LC oscillators that are popularly used for the radio signal generation are Colpitt’s oscillator, Hartley oscillator and Clapp’s oscillator. Nevertheless the name and construction, each of the mentioned oscillators produces a continuous wave at a resonant frequency predicted by the formula, fo = 2𝜋√Lc                                                      …1.2.1

1.2.1.1 Colpitt’s Oscillator

The Colpitt’s oscillator circuit is a superb circuit and it is widely used in commercial signal generators up to 100 MHz. The basic circuit of a Colpitt’s oscillator is as shown in Figure 1.2. It basically consists of a single stage amplifier and an L-C phase shift network, as obvious in the diagram as shown. The two series capacitors C1 and C2 form potential divider used for providing the feedback voltage - the voltage developed across capacitor C2 provides the regenerative feedback required for sustained oscillations. Parallel combination of RE and CE along with resistors R1 and R2 provides the stabilized self-bias. The collector supply voltage Vcc is applied to the collector through a radio frequency choke (RFC) which permits an easy flow of direct current but at the same time it offers very high impedance to the high frequency currents. The presence of output of coupling capacitor Cc in the output circuit does not permit the dc current to go the tank circuit (the flow of dc current in a tank circuit reduces its quality factor Q.). The through the capacitor Cc. the output of the of the phase-shift L- C network is coupled from the junction of L and C2 to the amplifier input at the base through coupling capacitor Cc, which blocks d. c but provides path to a. c. Transistor itself produces a phase shift of 180◦ and another phase shift of 180◦ is provided by the capacitive feedback. Thus, a total phase shift of 360◦ is obtained which is an essential
condition for developing oscillations. The output voltage is derived from a secondary winding L′ coupled to the inductance L. the frequency is determined by the tank radio frequency energy developed across RFC is coupled to the tank circuit circuit and is varied by gang-tuning the two capacitors C1 and C2. It is to be noted that capacitors C1 and C2 are ganged. As the tuning is varied, values of both capacitors vary simultaneously, the ratio of the two capacitances remaining the same. When the collector supply voltage Vcc is switched on, the capacitors C1 and C2 are charged through the coil L, setting up oscillations of frequency given by the formula fo =                                                                   …1.2.2 2𝜋√[C1 C2 ⁄(C1 +C2 )]L1
The oscillations across capacitor C2 are applied to the base–emitter junction and appear in the amplified form in the collector circuit. Of course, the, the amplified output in the collector circuit is of the same frequency as that of the oscillatory circuit. This amplified output in the collector circuit is supplied to the tank circuit in order to meet the losses. Thus, the tank circuit is getting energy continuously from the circuit to make up for the losses occurring in it and, therefore, ensures undamped oscillations.
[Figure 1.2: Basic circuit for Colpitt’s Oscillator]

1.2.1.2 Hartley Oscillator

The Hartley oscillator is as popular as Colpitt’s oscillator and is widely in use as local oscillator in radio receivers. The circuit arrangement is as shown in figure 1.3. Hartley
oscillator circuit is similar to Colpitt’s oscillator circuit, except that phase-shift network consists of two inductors L1 and L2 and a capacitor C instead of two capacitors and one inductor. The output of the amplifier is applied across inductor L1 and the voltage across inductor L2 forms the feedback voltage. The coil L1 is inductively coupled coil L2, the combination functions as an auto-transformer. The operation of the circuit is similar to that of the Colpitt’s oscillator circuit. The oscillation frequency produced by the oscillator is given as fo =                                                                …1.2.3 2𝜋√(L1 +L2 )C
[Figure 1.3: Basic circuit for Hartley Oscillator]

1.2.1.3 Clapp’s Oscillator

The Clapp oscillator is a refinement of the Colpitt’s oscillator. It is illustrated in figure 1.4. The single inductor found in the Colpitt’s oscillator is replaced by a series L-C combination. Addition of C3 in series with L improves the frequency stability and eliminates the effect of transistor parameters on the operation of the circuit. The operation of the circuit is the same as that of the Colpitt’s oscillator. The equivalent capacitance of the capacitors is approximately equal to C3, and the frequency of the oscillation is given as
fo =                                               …1.2.4 2𝜋√LC3
The Clapp oscillator is preferable to Colpitt’s oscillator because of the advantages it offers against the Colpitt’s oscillator. In the Colpitt’s oscillator, the resonant frequency is affected by the transistor and stray capacitances because the capacitors C1 and C2 are shunted by the transistor and stray capacitances and so their values are altered. But in a Clapp oscillator, the transistor and stray capacitances have no effect on capacitor C3, so the oscillation frequency is more stable and accurate. High frequency stability can further be obtained by enclosing the entire circuit in a constant temperature chamber and by maintaining the supply voltage constant with the help of a zener diode.
[Figure 1.4: Basic circuit for Clapp’s Oscillator]

1.2.2 CRYSTAL CONTROLLED OSCILLATIOR

The crystal control oscillator is used to produce a very high carrier signal of high stability. The oscillator functions depend heavily on the piezo-electric effect of crystal. Crystal oscillator is of very strategic importance for use as a carrier signal generator in radio transmitter system. Radio channels operate within a specific frequency band and on predefined frequencies or channels. Deviating from the assigned frequency by
even a small amount can cause channel interference with signals on adjacent channels. In other to avoid this, the oscillator being the transmitter carrier generator must be very exact, operating on the particular assigned frequency within very close tolerances of less than 0.1%. Again, the transmitter must remain on the assigned frequency. It must not drift from its assigned value irrespective of the many operating conditions such as temperature changes and variations in power supply voltage that affects the frequency. The conditions mentioned above usually and greatly affect RF L-C oscillators. The only oscillator capable of withstanding variations and drifting due to the operational changes (temperature and voltage changes) is the crystal oscillator. A crystal oscillator is constructed with a piece of quartz that is cut and ground into a thin flat wafer and mounted between two metal plates. Its working principle depends on piezoelectric effect. 1.2.2.1 Working Principle of the Crystal Oscillator The quartz crystal has piezoelectric properties; ability to vibrate at the frequency of an applied a. cvoltage or when mechanically strained, it vibrates and produces a. c voltage. However, if the frequency of the applied voltage is made equal to the natural frequency of the crystal, resonance takes place and the crystal vibrates at a maximum value. 1.2.2.2 Frequency of Crystal Oscillator The crystal oscillator has its frequency of vibration when excited and as well its natural frequency. The natural frequency,f of vibration is determined primarily by the thickness, t, of the crystal and the cut of the crystal (the place and angle of the cut), k. The frequency, the thickness and the cut, are related by the formula;
F= k⁄t                                                             …1.2.5 F = Frequency of the crystal k= The cut of the crystal t = Thickness of the crystal. From the equation 1.2.5, it is clear that the frequency of the quartz crystal is inversely proportional to the thickness. Nevertheless, extremely thin crystal may break because of the vibrations. As the crystal vibrates or oscillates, it maintains a very constant frequency. Once a crystal has been cut or ground to a particular frequency, it will not
change to any extent even with wide voltage or temperature variations. This is what gives it the greater advantage of been used as carrier generator in AM transmitters. Even, greater stability can be achieved by mounting the crystal in sealed temperature- controlled chambers known as crystal ovens. The ovens maintain an absolute constant temperature ensuring a stable output frequency. The crystal may be used to replace an entire LC tank circuit and stand on its own to form an oscillator, or it may be used to replace one of the reactance in a tank circuit of an LC oscillator. 1.2.2.3 Equivalent Circuit of the Crystal Oscillator Equivalent circuit of the crystal oscillator describes how the natural properties of the crystal behave as electrical elements if it were to be translated into electrical circuit. Figure 1.5 (a) shows the crystal connected in series with a. c voltage source and figure 1.5 (b) shows the equivalent circuit of the crystal.
Figure1.5:(a) Crystal connected in series with a. c voltage source. (b) Diagram of the equivalent circuit
The crystal has electromechanical resonance properties. Notwithstanding, it can be represented by an equivalent electrical circuit. The equivalent electrical circuit of the crystal oscillator is an R-L-C circuit. Two conditions can be interpreted from the equivalent circuit of the crystal in line with its natural behaviour in a particular state or condition. These conditions are non-vibrating state and vibrating state.
Crystal in non-vibrating state When the crystal is in non-vibrating state, it is equivalent to a static capacitance represented in the equivalent circuit of figure 1.6 by Cm. This capacitance is known as mounting capacitance.
Crystal in vibrating state When the crystal is in vibration state, its action is equivalent to R-L-C series circuit, therefore, the equivalent circuit of the vibrating crystal is R-L-C series circuit shunted by the mounting capacitance, Cm as shown in figure 1.6
[Figure 1.6: Crystal is R-L-C series circuit shunted by the mounting capacitance]
The two major properties of R-L-C circuit are the frequency, f and the quality factor, Q. The quality factor is given as: 1       L Q= √                                                                         …1.2.6 R       C
And the frequency is given as: f=                                                                           …1.2.7 2𝜋 √LC
Where R = Equivalent resistance of the crystal L = Equivalent inductance of the crystal C =Equivalent capacitance of the crystal.
1.2.2.4 Frequency Response of the Crystal When the crystal is vibrating, its equivalent electrical behaviour is as shown in figure 1.6. The capacitance values of C and Cm are relatively low, at the range of pico-Farad (pF). However, the value of C is usually much lower than that of Cm.
In the vibration state, there are four possible different conditions in the frequency response which the crystal can assume by its equivalent circuit. These are Low frequency, Series- resonance frequency, Parallel- resonance frequency, andShort circuit.
Low frequency At low frequency, the impedance of the crystal is controlled by extremely high values of capacitive reactance of the mounting capacitance, Xcm and the capacitive reactance of the equivalent capacitance, Xc (the extremely large value of the capacitive reactance is due to the extremely small values of Cm and C). In other words, at low frequencies, the impedance of the network is high. Series- resonance frequency As the frequency of the crystal increases, the R-L-C branch approaches its resonant frequency. At some definite frequency, the inductive reactance, XL will equal the capacitive reactance Xc. The crystal at this point acts as a series resonant circuit. At this condition, the impedance of the crystal is very low; being equals to the resistance R. The frequency at which this occurs in the crystal is referred to as its series- resonance frequency. The frequency can be represented as: fs =                                                               …1.2.8 2𝜋√LC
Parallel-resonance frequency At a slightly higher frequency, the reactance of branch R-L-C becomes inductive and equal to the reactive capacitance of the mounting capacitance. The crystal at this point acts as a parallel-resonance circuit. At this condition, the crystal offers very high impedance. The frequency at which this vibrating crystal behaves as a parallel- resonance circuit is called parallel-resonance frequency. The frequency can be represented as: fP =                                                               …1.2.9 2𝜋√LCT
CT is the total series capacitance of the circuit, given as CxCm CT =                                                                …1.2.10 C+Cm
Short circuit At frequencies greater than the parallel-resonance frequency, the value of the Xcm drops and eventually the crystal acts as short circuit. 1.2.2.5 Precision or Stability of a Crystal Oscillator The precision or stability of a crystal is the measure of the range at which an expected frequency varies from the actual value. It is expressed in part per million (ppm). For example, to say that a crystal with frequency of 1 MHz has a precision of 100 ppm means that the frequency of the crystal is within the range 1 MHz±100Hz. This means that it has the value range of 999,900 Hz to 1000, 100Hz. The precision as well can be expressed in percentage.

1.2.3 PIERCE CRYSTAL OSCILLATOR

The pierce crystal oscillator is basically a Colpitts oscillator in which the inductor is replaced by the crystal. The circuit is shown in figure 1.7 (a), with an equivalent circuit in figure 1.7 (b)in which the crystal has been replaced by its equivalent circuit. The resonant frequency of the circuit is determined by the series resonance of the circuit made up of C1 , C2 , Cs and Ls . C1 and C2 are both very much larger than Cs , so the resonant frequency is almost entirely dependent on the value of Cs with little dependence on the input capacity of the amplifier, C1 and C2 .The resonant value is almost the series value of the crystal itself.

1.3 SIGNAL MODULATORS

Signal modulators can be described as electronic circuits that are used to produce an output that modifies any of the basic properties of the carrier signal generated by a carrier oscillator when a modulating signal is introduced in it. The modulating signal varies the parameter(s) of the modulator and this varied parameter(s) is added to the carrier signal to introduce a change in the amplitude, frequency or phase of the carrier signal resulting in a modulated signal. Based on the three properties of the carrier signal that that be modified, modulators are broadly classified as amplitude modulator, frequency modulator and phase modulator.

1.3.1 AM MODULATORS

AM modulators are the types of signal modulator which are used for modifying the amplitude of carrier signals. The common types are BJT collector modulator, and square-law diode modulator. 1.3.1.1 BJT Collector Modulator Amplitude modulation may be achieved in a number of ways, the most common method being the use of BJT collector modulator. The basic circuit for a BJT modulator is shown in figure 1.8. Here, the transistor is normally operated in the class-C amplifier mode in which it is biased well beyond cutoff. The carrier input to the base must be sufficient to drive the transistor into conduction over part of the RF cycle, during which the collector current flows. The tuned circuit in the collector is tuned to resonate at the fundamental component giving a sinusoidal RF voltage at the collector.
When a modulating voltage vm (t), is applied, the steady collector voltage changes to a slowly varying voltage (slow compared to the RF cycle) given by VC = VCC + vm (t). The modulating voltage is applied in series with VCC through the low-frequency transformer. The RF bypass capacitor provides a low-impedance path for the RF to ground so that negligible RF voltage is developed across the LF transformer secondary. Through this mean, the circuit gives an output that is an amplitude modulated signal.
[Figure 1.8: The basic circuit of a BJT modulator]

1.3.1.2 Square-law Diode Modulator

Square-law diode modulator circuit makes use of non-linear current-voltage characteristic of diode for AM signal modulation. This method is suited at low-voltage levels because of the fact that current-voltage characteristic of a diode is highly non-linear particularly in the low-voltage region. Figure 1.9 shows the square-law diode modulator circuit. In the circuit, carrier and modulating signals are applied across the diode. A d. c battery Vcc is connected across the diode to get a fixed operating point on the V-I characteristics of diode.
[Figure 1.9: Square-law diode modulator circuit]
1.3.2 FM MODULATORS The FM modulators produce change in a carrier signal by the variation of its own parameter(s) when a modulating signal is applied to them. The common types of frequency modulators include varactor diode modulator, FET reactance modulator, BJT reactance modulator and voltage-control-oscillators.

1.3.2.1 Varactor Diode Modulator

Varactor diodes are employed frequently to produce frequency modulation of carrier signals. It is a semiconductor diode whose junction capacitance changes with d. c bias voltage. In the FM signal generation arrangement using varactor diode, the capacitor of the oscillator is made much smaller than the varactor diode capacitance Cd, so that the radio frequency (RF) voltage from the oscillator across the diode is small as compared to reverse bias d. c voltage across the varactor diode. In addition to this, the reactance of the capacitor C, at the highest modulating frequency is made large enough compare to resistor R, so that the shunting of the modulating signal through the turned circuit may be checked. This arrangement is shown in figure 1.10. The figure shows that the diode is reverse-biased to provide the junction capacitance effect. This bias voltage is varied by the modulating voltage which is in series with it and varies the junction capacitance accordingly.
[Figure 1.10: Varactor diode modulator]
The varactor diode modulator operation depends on the principle of reverse bias property of diode. Reverse bias diode has P-N junction (depletion region) capacitance which varies in proportion to the applied reverse biased voltage. The simple illustration is that the P- and N- type materials act as the two plates of the capacitor, and the depletion region acts as the dielectric. The arrangement is shown in figure 1.11.
[Figure 1.11: Depletion region of reverse bias diode with P-N junction]
From the figure, the width of the depletion layer determines the width of the dielectric and, therefore the amount of capacitance. If the reverse bias voltage is high, the depletion region will be wide and the dielectric will cause the plates of the capacitor to be widely spaced, producing a low capacitance. Decreasing the amount of reverse bias narrows the depletion region; the plates of the capacitor are effectively closer together, producing a higher capacitance. The above principle of function of diode is utilized in producing the varactor diode to bring this effect in a regular and systematic manner so that the capacitance variations of the diode are wide and linear as possible. (b) 1.3.2.2 FET Reactance Modulator
FET reactance modulator is chiefly constructed using junction field effect transistor. This modulator has two different categories which are capacitive FET modulator and inductive FET modulator. These categories will later be discussed in detail in chapter 2. Figure 1.13 is the basic circuit of FET reactance modulator, which behaves as a reactance that may be connected across the tuned circuit of the oscillator to produce frequency modulation.
[Figure 1.13: Circuit diagram of FET reactance modulator]
The primary intention of the circuit operation is to determine the impedance of the FET as seen at the input terminals A-A′ of the figure. This impedance must behave as a reactance, that is, it is almost entirely reactance. The reactance from the above circuit is capacitive but can be made inductive by simply interchanging the positions of C and R. The value of this reactance is proportional to the transconductance, gm of the FET, which can be made to depend on the gate bias voltage of the FET and its variations. In order to determine the impedance, Z of the FET, a voltage, V is applied to the terminals A-A′ between which the impedance is measured, and the resulting current Ii is calculated. The applied voltage is divided by this current, given the impedance seen when looking into the terminals.

1.3.2.3 Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) Reactance Modulator

The BJT reactance modulator is similar to FET reactance modulator and the connections are equally similar. The differences are that in this case, BJT is used instead of FET and voltage dividers are resistors R1 and R2 instead of capacitance, C and resistor R or inductor L and resistor R. The BJT reactance modulator is efficient and provides a large deviation. It is popular and used often in FM transmitters. Figure 1.14 is the circuit diagram of the BJT reactance modulator.
[Figure 1.14: Circuit diagram of the BJT reactance modulator]

1.3.2.4 Voltage – Controlled-Oscillators

This is the class or type of oscillators whose frequency is controlled by an external input voltage. They produce an output frequency that is directly proportional to the controlled voltage level. They are represented by the short form, VCO. The VCOs are used in FM transmitter for as modulators. Presently they are available in IC form, which make FM generation very simple. The circuit is as shown in figure 1.15.
[Figure 1.15: Block diagram of Voltage Controlled Oscillator]

1.3.3 PM MODULATORS

PM modulation is an indirect method of producing an FM signal. PM modulators are used for this purpose. The modulators cause the phase of the carrier signal to be changed, producing a phase modulated signal. Types of the PM modulators include
varactor phase modulator, transistor phase modulator, FET phase modulator and tuned-circuit phase modulator. 1.3.3.1 Varactor Phase Modulators
This modulator is formed by replacing the capacitor of a phase-shift circuit with a varactor diode with a (junction) capacitance Cd. The circuit is shown in figure 1.16 In this circuit, the modulating signal through an inverting amplifier A, causes the capacitance, Cd , of the varactor to change. If the modulating signal’s amplitude at the output of the amplifier A becomes more positive, it adds to the varactor reverse bias from R1 and R2 causing the capacitance to decrease. This causes the reactance to increase, thus the circuit produces less phase-shift and less deviation. A more negative modulating signal from A subtracts from the reverse bias on the varactor diode, increasing the capacitance or decreasing the capacitive reactance. This increases the amount of phase shift and the deviation.
[Figure 1.16: A varactor phase modulator]

1.3.3.2 Transistor Phase Modulators

Figure 1.17 shows a transistor used as a variable resistor to create a phase modulator. The circuit is simply a standard common emitter class A amplifier biased into the linear region by resistors R1 and R2 .
[Figure 1.17: Transistor Phase Modulators]

1.3.3.3 FET Phase Modulator

The FET phase modulator is shown in figure 1.18. It uses a phase shifter made up of a capacitor and the variable resistance of a field-effect transistor Q1 . The carrier signal from a crystal (control) oscillator is applied directly to the output through C1 and C2 and appears across the FET from source to drain. The carrier signal is also applied to the gate of the FET through C1 . The series capacitance of C1 and C2 and the FET source-to-drain resistance produce a leading phase shift of current in the FET and a leading voltage at the output.
[Figure 1.18: An FET phase modulator]

1.3.3.4 Tuned-Circuit Phase Modulators

This is a phase modulator circuit designed based on the principle of circuit resonance of tuned LC circuit. The circuit is shown in figure 1.19(a). Figure 1.19(b) shows the circuit response. In this type of circuit, the parallel tuned circuit is usually part of the output circuit of an RF amplifier driven by the carrier oscillator. A varactor diode D1
is connected in parallel with the tuned circuit, thereby providing a capacitance change with the modulating signal. The modulating signal is first passed through a low-pass network, made up of R3 and C3 , which provides the amplitude compensation necessary to produce FM.
[Figure 1.19: Tuned-Circuit Phase Modulators]
All the modulators briefly discussed in this chapter will be treated in detail in chapter 2

title: Generating Modulated Radio Signal
text:
M odulated radio signals are                Using Frequency Modulators generated in one of the            2.5    Indirect Method of FM signal sections in a radio transmitter           generation called modulation section. This section is where modulation of radio signals takes place. Radio                               signal modulation involves two signals, one is the carrier signal or RF signal and the second is the modulating signal. The modulating signal is also called other names which are used interchangeably. These other names include intelligence signal, audio frequency signal or baseband signal. There are two broad classifications of modulated signals. These are amplitude modulated (AM) signal and frequency modulated (FM)signal. AM signal is produced when the amplitude of carrier signal generated by carrier oscillator is modulated by modulating signal(s). On the other hand, FM signal is generated when the modulating signal modifies the frequency of the carrier signal. Each of these modulated signals reaches a transmitting antenna via the transmitter and is released into the space in form of (electromagnetic) radio wave.

2.2 GENERATION OF AMPLITUDE MODULATION (AM) SIGNAL

The generation of AM signal basically applies crystal oscillators or crystal controlled oscillators together with amplitude modulators. Crystal oscillators are used as carrier signal generators. The suitability of crystal oscillator is due to the need for high frequency stability required for AM signal. The amplitude modulators are used to vary the amplitude of the generated carrier signal in accordance with variation in modulating signal. Good and popular examples of the amplitude modulators are square-law diode modulators, and BJT collector modulator. In the process of AM
signal generation, there are broadly classified two methods that are used; Low-level Amplitude Modulation, and High-level Amplitude Modulation.

2.2.1 LOW-LEVEL AMPLITUDE MODULATION

Figure 2.1 shows the block diagram of a low-level AM modulation system. In a low- level amplitude modulation system, the modulation is done at low power level. At low power levels, a very small power is associated with the carrier signal and the modulating signal. Because of this, the output power of modulation is low. Therefore, the power amplifiers are required to boost the amplitude-modulated signals up to the desired output level. From the block diagram in figure 2.1, it is clear that modulation is done at low power level. After this, the amplitude-modulated signal (i.e. a signal containing a carrier and two sidebands) is applied to a wide-band power amplifier. A wideband power amplifier is used just to preserve the sidebands of the modulated signal. This method of amplitude modulation is employed in low-level amplitude modulation transmitters. One good example of this modulation method is square-law diode modulation.
[Figure 2.1: Block diagram of a low-level AM modulation]

2.2.1.1 Square-Law Diode Modulation

Square-law diode modulation makes use of square-law modulator circuit. This circuit makes use of non-linear current-voltage characteristic of diode. This method is suited at low-voltage levels because of the fact that current-voltage characteristic of a diode is highly non-linear particularly in the low-voltage region as shown in figure 2.2. Figure 2.3 shows the square-law diode modulator circuit.
[Figure 2.2: Current-voltage characteristic of a diode Figure 2.3: Square-law diode modulator circuit]
Operating principle It may be observed from the figure 2.3 that carrier and modulating signals are applied across the diode. A d. c battery Vcc is connected across the diode to get a fixed operating point on the V-I characteristics of diode. The working of this circuit may be explained by considering the fact that when two different frequencies are passed through a non-linear device, the process of amplitude modulation takes place. Hence when carrier and modulating frequencies are applied at the input of the diode, then different frequency terms appear at the output of diode. These different frequency terms are applied across a tuned circuit which is tuned to the carrier frequency and has a narrow bandwidth just to pass two sidebands along with the carrier and reject other frequencies. Hence at the output of tuned circuit, amplitude modulated signals are produced, that is, carrier signals and two sidebands are obtained. Let the modulating voltage be expressed as vm(t) = Vm cos 2𝜋fm t                                                      …2.2.2

2.2.2 HIGH-LEVEL AMPLITUDE MODULATION

Figure 2.4 shows the block diagram of a high level AM modulation system. In high- level amplitude modulation systems, the modulation is done at high power level. Therefore, to produce amplitude-modulation at these high power levels, the modulating signal and the carrier signal must be at high power levels. In block diagram of figure 2.4 the modulating signal and carrier signal are first power amplified and then applied to AM high-level modulator. For modulating signal, the wide-band power amplifier is required just to preserve all the frequency components present in modulating signal. On the other hand, for carrier signal, the narrow-band power amplifier is required because it is a fixed-frequency signal. The BJT collector modulation method is the example of high-level modulation.

2.2.2.1 The BJT collector modulation method

In Collector modulation method, a BJT collector modulator is employed to produce AM modulated signal. This method is a very popular method. Figure 2.5 illustrates the circuit diagram. Here the transistor T1 makes a radio frequency (RF) class-C amplifier. At the base of T1, the carrier signal is applied. Vcc makes the collector supply used for biasing purpose. Also, the transistor T2 makes a class B amplifier which is used to amplify the modulating signal. The modulating signal appears across the modulation transformer after amplification. This amplified modulating signal appears in series with the collector supply Vcc . The function of the capacitor C is to offer low impedance path for the high-frequency signal and hence the carrier signal is prevented from flowing through the modulation transformer.

2.3 GENERATION OF FREQUENCY MODULATED (FM) SIGNAL GENERATION
The basic process of generating FM signal is to modulate the frequency of carrier (RF) signal generated by a signal generator, in accordance with the modulating signal. In this process, two (circuits) devices are connected to form a larger circuit which is then FM signal generator. The two circuits that are connected in this process are oscillator circuit and frequency modulator circuit. The oscillator circuit generates the RF signal which its frequency is modulated. The oscillators that are commonly used for this process are LC oscillators. The frequency of the RF signal generated by the oscillator is fixed and it is determined by the components (inductor and capacitor) values of the oscillator tuned circuit. The parameter (inductance or capacitance), usually the capacitance, of the frequency modulator circuit is changed correspondingly with amplitude voltage signal of the modulating wave thereby introducing change in the frequency of the RF signal by affecting (increasing or decreasing) the capacitance or inductance of the local oscillator tank circuit. The whole process and arrangement eventually leads frequency modulated signal. There are basically two different approaches that are used in generating FM signal. These approaches are direct method and indirect method. In direct method, the FM signal is generated from a carrier source and directly modulated into the FM signal in the modulator before being transmitted. The direct FM signal is transmitted using direct FM transmitter. The indirect method of generating FM signal involves generating the RF signals firstly and modulates it into a PM signal. This in turn is
modified into FM signal. The indirect FM signal is transmitted using indirect FM transmitter.
2.3.1 DIRECT METHOD OF FM SIGNAL GENERATION The direct method of generating FM signal is also referred to as parameter variation method. In this approach, one major technique is to vary either the capacitance or the inductance of the local oscillator by the change in capacitance or inductance value of the frequency modulator which is brought about by a modulating signal, hence the name, parameter variation method. In this case, the FM signal is achieved if the change in any of the parameters of the local oscillator originally under resonant frequency condition, been the original (unmodulated) frequency of the carrier signal generated, is made to change in direct proportion to the amplitude of the modulating signal voltage. The original (unmodulated signal) frequency of the carrier signal generated in the tuned circuit when no external influences have played a role is the resonant frequency of the oscillator circuit. It is expressed by the formula; fosc = 2𝜋√LC                                                              …2.3.1

The resulting (new) frequency is the modulated frequency, fm , and the signal that results is the frequency modulated (FM) signal. The new frequency is achieved by either a minimum or maximum change in the capacitance (C ± ∆c) or inductance (L ± ∆l) of the oscillator introduced by the change in the modulator’s circuit variable. 2.4.1.1 Processes of FM Generation in Varactor Diode Modulator Circuit The figure 2.10 on page 40 shows a schematic varactor diode modulator circuit. With no modulating signal (i.e. audio frequency signal) applied, the parallel combination of Ci and Li and the varactor diode’s capacitance, Cd forms resonant carrier frequency. The varactor diode is effectively in parallel with Li and Ci because –Vcc supply appears as a short circuit to the a. c signal. The coupling capacitor, Cc isolates the Vm (t) levels and modulating signal while looking like a short circuit to the high
frequency carrier. When the modulating signals, Vm (t) is applied to the diode, its reverse bias is varied, which causes the diode’s junction capacitance to vary in steps with theVm (t). The oscillator frequency is subsequently varied as required for frequency modulation, and the FM signal is available at Q1’s collector. In a more detailed circuit, there is the presence of potentiometer which serves as d. c bias (keeping the varactor at a steady or desired centre frequency and allows it to be adjusted over a narrow range) and oscillator feedback circuit. While at a particular centre frequency, the input modulating signal (from microphone) is amplified and fed to the modulator. As the signal varies, it adds to and subtract from the fixed biased voltage (provided by the potentiometer). Thus, the effective voltage applied to the diode causes its capacitance to vary. This in- turn, produces the desired deviation of the carrier frequency. A positive going-signal adds to the reverse bias, decreasing the capacitance and increasing the carrier frequency. A negative going-signal subtract from the bias, increasing the capacitance and decreasing the carrier frequency.

2.4.2 FM GENERATION USING FET REACTANCE MODULATOR

[Figure 2.12: FET reactance modulator circuit]
Figure 2.12 is the basic circuit of FET reactance modulator. The primary intention of the circuit operation is to determine the impedance of the FET as seen at the input terminals A-A′ of the figure. This impedance must behave as a reactance, that is, it is almost entirely reactance. The reactance from the above circuit is capacitive but can be made inductive by simply interchanging the positions of C and R. The value of this reactance is proportional to the transconductance, gm of the FET, which can be made to depend on the gate bias voltage of the FET and its variations. In order to determine the impedance, Z of the FET, a voltage, V is applied to the terminals A-A’ between which the impedance is measured, and the resulting current Ii is calculated. The applied voltage is divided by this current, given the impedance seen when looking into the terminals. To achieve the desired reactive capacitance (as the impedance in the circuit), the following conditions must apply: 1. The bias gate current must be negligible compare to the drain current Id . 2. The drain-to-gate impedance (i.e. capacitive reactance of the circuit Xc) must be greater than the gate-to-source impedance ( i.e resistance R) of the circuit at least by 5:1.

The typical reactance modulator circuit is shown in figure 2.13 below. The circuit is formed by connecting the reactance modulator circuit in parallel with Colpitts oscillator (tank circuit).
[Figure 2.13: Diagram of FET reactance modulator circuit]
In the circuit of figure 2.13 above, the transconductance gm, of FET is varied by the modulating AF input signal voltage. The variable capacitive reactance of the FET
reactance modulator is connected in parallel with the tank circuit formed by C, C1, C2 and C3 of the Colpitt’s oscillator. In the absence of modulation, the oscillator frequency is set to the desired carrier frequency by adjusting the capacitance C3. The radio frequency chokes RFC are used to prevent short-circuiting of RF or a. c output through power supply to ground.

2.4.2.6 Configurations of FET Reactance Modulators

There are two categories of FET modulators. These categories are based on the electric circuit elements, capacitor C and resistor R or inductor L and resistor R, used in FET modulator circuit and their positioning in relation to the three terminals of the FET, and the ratio of the drain-to-gate impedance to the gate-to-source impedance. These two categories are capacitive FET modulators and inductive FET modulators. Each of the categories has two types. The two types of capacitive FET modulators are RC capacitive FET modulator and RL capacitive FET modulator. Also, for the inductive FET modulators, the two types are RC inductive and RL capacitive FET modulator. Whether a FET modulator will be inductive or capacitive depends on its value of drain-to-gate impedance to the gate-to-source impedance ratio. If the ratio is far less than a unit, the FET is capacitive; otherwise the FET is an inductive. Each is the circuit can be defined by the following parameters; •   Gate-to-drain impedance. •   Gate-to-source impedance. •   The size of the reactance compared to the resistance. •   The impedance ratio. •   The time constant of the circuit. •   The reactance equation.
RC capacitive In the RC capacitive FET modulator, the following conditions are obtainable; i. The gate-to-drain impedance is capacitive (C). ii. The gate-to-source impedance is resistive (R). iii. The capacitive reactance is far larger than the resistance ( Xc≫ R). iv. The impedance ratio is less than a unit (𝜔𝜏 ≪1) v. The time constant of the circuit is 𝜏 = CR
vi. The (equivalent) reactance formula is Ceq = gmCR. (Ceq = gm𝜏 )

2.4.3 FM GENERATION USING BJT REACTANCE MODULATOR

The figure below illustrates a typical BJT reactance modulator circuit. Refer to it regularly as we discuss the circuit and its operation.
[Figure 2.18: Circuit diagram of BJT reactance modulator circuit]
The circuit consists of the BJT reactance circuit and the master oscillator. The reactance circuit operates on the master oscillator to cause its resonant frequency to shift up or shift down depending on the modulating signal being applied. The reactance circuit appears capacitive to the master oscillator. In this case, the reactance seems like a variable capacitor in the oscillator’s tank circuit. Transistor Qa makes up the reactance modulator circuit. Resistor Rb and Rc establishes a voltage divider network that biases Qa. Resistor Rd furnishes emitter feed-back to thermally stabilize Qa . Capacitor Ccis a bypass component that prevents a. c input
signal degeneration. Capacitor Ca interacts with transistor Qa’s inter electrode capacitance to cause a varying capacitive reactance directly influenced by the input modulating signal. The master oscillator is a Colpitts oscillator built around transistor Qb. Coil La, capacitor Ce and capacitor Cf make up the resonant tank circuit. Capacitor Cg provides required regenerative feedback to cause the circuit to oscillate. Qa and Qb are impedance coupled and capacitor Cb effectively couples the changes at Qa’s collector to the tank circuit of transistor Qb while blocking d. cvoltages. When a modulated signal is applied to the base of transistor, Qa through resistor Ra, the reactance of the transistor changes in relation to that signal. If the modulating voltage goes up, the capacitance of Qa goes down, and if the modulating voltage goes down, the reactance of Qa goes up. This change in reactance is felt on Qa’s collector and also at the tank circuit of the Colpitt’s oscillator transistor, Qb. As capacitance reactance at Qa goes up, the resonant frequency of the master oscillator, Qb decreases. Conversely, if Qa’s capacitance reactance goes down, the master oscillator resonant frequency increases.

2.4.4 FM GENERATION USING VOLTAGE – CONTROLLED-OSCILLATORS

Figure 2.19 is the circuit diagram of a voltage-control oscillator. In the circuit, the capacitor C, repeatedly charges and discharges under the control of current source. The amount of the current supplied by this module is determined by Vin and by the resistor R. since the amount of current determines the rate of capacitor charging, the resistor effectively controls the period of the output. The capacitance also controls the rate of charging. The capacitor voltage is the input to the Schmitt trigger, which changes the mode of the current source when a certain threshold is reached. The capacitor voltage then heads in the opposite direction, generating a triangular wave. The output of the Schmitt trigger provides the square wave output. These signals can be low-pass filtered to provide a sinusoidal FM signal. The major limitation of the VCO is that it can only work for a frequency up to 1MHz
[Figure 2.19: Circuit diagram of a voltage-control oscillator]

2.5 INDIRECT METHOD OF FM GENERATION

One of the difficulties encountered in FM transmitter which depends upon the direct method of FM generation is that because of the variable nature of the tuning of the tank circuit, crystal controlled oscillators cannot be used and therefore the stability inherent in such crystal-controlled is not available. An alternative technique for generation of the frequency modulated (FM) signals, which allows for the use of crystal oscillators is the indirect FM method. In this method, the crystal oscillator and a phase modulator are used. The output of the crystal oscillator is fed to a phase modulator which produces a phase shift to the signal and varies it in accordance with the modulating signal. Since the phase variations produce frequency variations, with some minor processing, the PM signal is passed off as an indirect FM signal. This indirect method of FM signal generation is usually referred to as Armstrong FM signal generation.

2.5.1 PHASE MODULATORS

The phase shifters are part of the phase modulator circuit. There are some basic types of phase modulators, namely; varactor phase modulators, transistor phase modulators, FET phase modulators and tuned-circuit phase modulators. 2.5.1.1 Varactor Phase Modulators
A simple phase-shift circuit can be used as a phase modulator if the resistance or capacitance can be made to vary with the modulating signal. One way to do this is to replace the capacitor shown in the circuit of figure 2.21 with a varactor. The resulting phase-shit circuit is shown in figure 2.22. In this circuit, the modulating signal causes the capacitance of the varactor to change. If the modulating signal amplitude at the output of the amplifier A becomes more positive, it adds to the varactor reverse bias from R1 and R2 causing the capacitance to decrease. This causes the reactance to increase, thus the circuit produces less phase- shift and less deviation. A more negative modulating signal from A subtracts from the reverse bias on the varactor diode, increasing the capacitance or decreasing the capacitive reactance. This increases the amount of phase shift and the deviation.
[Figure 2.22: A varactor phase modulator]
With this arrangement, there is an inverse relationship between the modulating signal’s polarity and the direction of the frequency deviation. This is the opposite of the desired variation. To correct this condition, an inverting amplifier A can be inserted between the modulating signal source and the input to the modulator. Then, when the modulating signal goes positive, the inverter output and modulator input go negative and the deviation increases. C1 and C2 in figure 2.22 are d. c blocking capacitors and have very low reactance at the carrier frequency. The phase shift produced is lagging, and as in any phase modulator, the output amplitude and phase vary with a change in the modulating signal amplitude.

2.5.1.3 FET Phase Modulator

The improved phase modulator shown in figure 2.24 uses a phase shifter made up of a capacitor and the variable resistance of a field-effect transistor Q1 . The carrier signal from a crystal (control) oscillator is applied directly to the output through C1 and C2 and appears across the FET from source to drain. The carrier signal is also applied to the gate of the FET through C1 . The series capacitance of C1 and C2 and the FET source-to-drain resistance produce a leading phase shift of current in the FET and a leading voltage at the output. The carrier signal applied to the gate of the FET also varies the FET current. C1 and R1 produce a leading phase shift of less than 90°. The leading voltage across R1 also controls the drain current in Q1 . When two signals control the FET drain current, the result is a phasor sum of the two currents
[Figure 2.24: An improved phase modulator]
The modulating signal is applied to the gate of the FET. RFC1 keeps the carrier RF out of the audio circuits. The audio signal now also controls the FET current. This changes the amplitude relationships of the other two controlling inputs, producing a phase shift that is directly proportional to the amplitude. The signal is then usually passed on to a class C amplifier or frequency multiplier that removes the amplitude variations but preserves the phase and frequency variations. 2.5.1.4 Tuned-Circuit Phase Modulators
Most phase modulators are capable of producing only a small amount of phase shift- the total being essentially limited to ±20° because of the narrow range of linearity of the transistor or varactor. The limited phase shift produces, in turn, a limited frequency shift. One technique for solving this problem is to use a parallel tuned circuit to produce phase shift. At resonance, a parallel resonant circuit acts like a very high- value resistor. Off resonance, the circuit acts inductively or capacitively and, as a result, produces a phase shift between its current and applied voltage. Figure 2.25 shows the impedance response curve and the phase variation of a parallel resonant circuit. At the resonant frequencyfo , the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal and their effects cancel one another. The result is extremely high resistive impedance atfo . The circuit acts resistively at this point, and the phase angle between the current and the applied voltage is therefore zero.
[Figure 2.25: Impedance and phase shift versus frequency of a parallel resonant circuit]
At frequencies below resonance, XL decreases and XC increases. This causes the circuit to act like an inductor, and the current lags the applied voltage. Above resonance, XL increases and XC decreases. This causes the circuit to act like a capacitor, and current leads the applied voltage. If the Q of the resonant circuit is relatively high, the phase shift will be quite pronounced, as shown in figure 2.25. The same effect is achieved if the frequency is constant and either L or C is varied. A relatively small change in L or C can produce a significant phase shift. The idea, then, is to cause the inductance or capacitance to vary with the modulating voltage, producing a phase shift. One of the varieties of circuits that have been developed based on this technique is illustrated in figure 2.26. In this type of circuit, the parallel tuned circuit is usually part of the output circuit of an RF amplifier driven by the carrier oscillator. A varactor diode D1 is connected in parallel with the tuned circuit, thereby providing a capacitance change with the modulating signal. The voltage divider, made up of R1 and R2 , sets the reverse bias on D1 . C2 acts as a d. cblocking capacitor, preventing bias from being applied to the tuned circuit. Its value is very large, so it is essentially, an a. c short circuit at the carrier frequency, and the capacitance of D1 controls the resonant frequency. The modulating signal is first passed through a low-pass network, made up of R3 and C3 , which provides the amplitude compensation necessary to produce FM. The modulating signal appears across potentiometer R4 , allowing the desired amount of modulating signal to be tapped off and applied to the phase-shift circuit.
[Figure 2.26: Phase modulator that uses tuned-circuit principle]
Potentiometer R4 acts as a deviation control. The higher the modulating voltage, the greater the frequency deviation. The modulating signal is applied to the varactor diode through capacitor C4 . With zero modulation voltage, the value of the capacitance of D1 , along with capacitor C1 and inductor L, sets the resonant frequency of the tuned circuit. C2 is ad. cblocking capacitor with a near-zero impedance at the carrier frequency. The indirect FM output across L is inductively coupled to the output. When the modulating signal goes negative, it subtracts from the reverse bias of D1 . This increases the capacitance of the circuit and lowers the reactance, making the circuit appear capacitive. Thus a leading phase shift is produced. The parallel LC circuit looks like a capacitor to the output resistance of the carrier amplifier, so the output lags the inputs. A positive-going modulating voltage decreases the capacitance; the tuned circuit then becomes inductive, producing a lagging phase shift. The LC circuit looks like an inductor to the output resistance of the carrier amplifier, so the output leads the input. The result at the output is a relatively wide phase shift, which, in turn, produces excellent linear frequency deviation.

2.5.1.5 Limitations of Phase Modulators

Phase modulators are relatively easy to implement, but they have two main disadvantages. 1. The amount of phase shift they produce and the resulting frequency deviation are relatively low. For that reason, the carrier is usually generated at a lower frequency, and frequency multipliers are used to increase the carrier frequency and the amount of deviation. 2. All the phase shift circuits described above, produce amplitude variations as well as phase changes. When the value of one of the components is changed, the phase shifts but the output amplitude changes as well.
The above limitations of the phase modulators are solved by feeding the output of the phase modulator to class C amplifiers used as frequency multipliers. These amplifiers eliminate amplitude variations at the same time they increase the carrier frequency and deviation to the desired final values.

2.5.2 MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLE OF THE INDIRECT FM SIGNAL GENERATION

Having discussed the phase modulators, the processes of the FM signal generation in the modulators can be analytically represented in a mathematical process. The modulated carrier is given by: vc(t) = Vc sin ( 𝜔c t + ∅c )                                    …2.5.10
Where vc(t) = instantaneous carrier signal
Vc = carrier amplitude 𝜔c =carrier frequency ∅c = carrier phase angle. When the carrier signal is phase modulated, ∅c in equation 2.5.10 is replaced by ∅(t) : The instantaneous value of the phase angle.
∅(t) = ∅c + KVm sin𝜔m t                                         …2.5.11 KVm = mp                                                        …2.5.12 Where K = phase deviation constant. Vm = modulating voltage mp = the phase modulation index. The equation 2.5.12 suggests that the modulating signal (the second terms of the R.H.S) is superimposed or is added to the original phase angle of the carrier signal (∅c ) to bring the necessary phase modulation. Since ∅c is replaced by ∅(t) in the state or process of modulation, Putting equation 2.5.12 into 2.5.10, we therefore get V = Vc sin (𝜔c t + ∅c + KVm sin𝜔m t)                            … 2.5.13 ∅c can be dropped from equation 2.5.13 since it is a constant that does not affect the modulation and we also put equation 2.5.12 into 2.5.13, we have
V = Vc sin (𝜔c t + mp sin𝜔m t)                                               … 2.5.14
Where V = the modulated signal voltage and (𝜔c t + mp sin𝜔m t) represents the instantaneous phase angle of the modulated wave. Therefore: 𝜃(t) = (𝜔c t + mp sin𝜔m t)                                                   …2.5.15
In the process of the modulation, the instantaneous change in 𝜃(t) brings about frequency change. We should also recall that the instantaneous angular frequency and instantaneous phase angle are related by the formula: d𝜃 (t) 𝜔i =                                                                         …2.5.16 dt
So, if we substitute equation 2.5.15 into 2.5.16, we get d(𝜔c t+mp sin𝜔m t) 𝜔i =                                                                          …2.5.17 dt
Differentiating the R.H.S of equation 2.5.17 with respect to time w. r. t time we, 𝜔i = 𝜔c + mp 𝜔m cos𝜔m t                                                       …2.5.18
So far, our focus has been on how to modify or modulate the phase angle of the carrier signal to achieve Phase Modulation and this is what equations 2.5.11– 2.5.18 has shown. However, our intention is to achieve the Frequency Modulation through the Phase modulation. In view of this, we need to recall the relation which frequency has with the equation 2.5.18. Remember, 𝜔=2𝜋f. Therefore, 𝜔i = 2𝜋fi ; 𝜔c = 2𝜋fc and 𝜔m = 2𝜋fm Replacing each of them in equation 2.5.18, gives us 2𝜋fi = 2𝜋fc + mp 2𝜋fm cos2𝜋fm t                                              …2.5.19 Dividing equation 2.5.19 by 2𝜋, we arrive at: fi = fc + mp fm cos2𝜋fm t                                                     …2.5.20
The second term on the R.H.S of equation 2.5.20, that is mp fm cos2𝜋fm t, represents frequency deviation. Then, the maximum equivalent frequency deviation is ±∆f= mp fm . This occurs when the term cos2𝜋fm t=±1. Where fm = modulating frequency
mp = maximum angular shift of carrier.
For the constant mp , the output of the transmitter is proportional to modulating frequency fm . Thus, frequency modulation is indirectly produced when a carrier is phase modulated. The noticeable difference between this method and direct method is that in direct method, the output of oscillator is directly modulated while in indirect method, the frequency of oscillator is produced beyond oscillator.
