text:
3.2 The basic processes involve in the function of a Radio Transmitter

3.3 AM Radio Transmitter


3.1 INTRODUCTION                                    3.4 Types of AM Transmitter


3.4 FM Transmitter

R adio transmitter is an                3.5 Impedance matching of Transmitter to electronic system or device           Antenna that is used for radio 3.6 Transmitter tests and measurements transmission which is capable of producing radio frequency waves, which                                                    is applied to the antenna for transmission. It takes                                       the information to be communicated from an appropriate                        transducer   and converts it into a modulated signal (in the radio frequency range) which is compatible with the communication medium. The in-coming message signals may be in a non-electrical form, for instance, a speech signal, which an acoustic pressure variation. The message signal is then converted into electrical signal using a suitable transducer. The radio transmitter operates further on this electrical signal. The signal is then fed through coaxial cable, wire or wave- guide to an antenna that launches it into the free space. Radio transmitters have various types and classifications based on the type of modulator used and the type of modulated signal generated. In this chapter, we shall concentrate majorly on the type broad types of transmitter; Amplitude modulated wave transmitter and frequency modulated wave transmitter.
[Figure 3.1: Simple block diagram of a radio transmitter.]
Figure 3.1 is a simple block diagram of a transmitter. From the block diagram, generally, every transmitter has five fundamental blocks. These are power supply, oscillator, modulator, amplifier and output.
3.2 THE BASIC PROCESSES INVOLVE IN THE FUNCTION OF A RADIO TRANSMITTER
There are four fundamental processes involve in the general functions of a transmitter. These are 1. Carrier generation 2. Signal modulation 3. Power amplification 4. Signal radiation

3.2.1 CARRIER GENERATION

The transmitter generates high frequency (carrier) signals, which is essential for carrying out modulation operation. A stable oscillator, usually a crystal oscillator, does the generation of carrier. 3.2.2 SIGNAL MODULATION
The low frequency signal (message signal) which is the information to be transmitted is superimposed on the carrier generated by the stable oscillator to modify any of its three parameters, namely; amplitude, frequency and phase angle.
Hence, the modulation that can take place in the transmitter may be amplitude modulation, frequency modulation or phase modulation. This modulation is done so that the fundamental limitation of the message signal which is its inability to travel a very long distance can be eliminated and to equally make it suitable for the transmission medium. 3.2.3 POWER AMPLIFICATION
The amplification process essentially involves amplifying the signal amplitude values and adding the required power levels. The transmitter must provide sufficient power amplification to ensure that the signal level is high enough to be carried to the desired distance. 3.2.4 SIGNAL RADIATION
After the amplification of the modulated signal by the transmitter, it is fed to the antenna by a suitable coupling network. The antenna in-turn serves as a transducer that radiates the signal into the atmosphere for propagation.

3.3 AM RADIO TRANSMITTER

AM radio transmitter is the radio transmitter that generates and transmits an AM radio wave. There are two types of AM transmitter based on the device used; low-level AM transmitter and high-level AM transmitter. The low-level AM transmitter is a laboratory AM generator. Here AM wave is produced at such a low power level that simplicity is a more important requirement than efficiency. The high-level AM transmitter generates such high power that its prime requirement is efficiency. In this case, quite complex means of AM generation may be used. However, the methods of generating AM described here relate to both applications, we shall shift our emphasis on high-level AM transmitter. In the AM transmitter, there are about six sections, namely; 1. Input section 2. Oscillator section 3. RF amplifier section
4. AF amplifier section 5. Modulator section 6. Output section
[Figure 3.2: Block diagram of AM transmitter]

3.3.1 INPUT SECTION

The input section of the AM transmitter comprises of transducer usually, a microphone which serves as the audio frequency (modulating signal) source or intelligence signal source, and audio signal processing and filtering units. The transducer converts the input audio signal, otherwise refers to as intelligence signals to equivalent electrical signals and feeds it to audio signal processor and filter circuit. This circuit ensures that only voice frequencies in certain range are passed, which helps to minimize the bandwidth occupied by the signals. It equally functions in an automatic manner to hold the amplitude of the signals to a certain maximum level. In doing this, it compresses the higher- amplitude signals (signals above required level) and amplifies the lower-amplitude signals more. The result is that over modulation is prevented, yet the transmitter operates as close to 100 percent modulation as possible. This process reduces the possibility of signal distortion and harmonics, which is capable of producing wider sidebands that can cause adjacent channel interference.
3.3.2 OSCILLATOR SECTION This is the starting point for all transmitters. The carrier or RF signals are generated at this stage. Once the carrier is generated at this point, it can be modulated, processed in various ways, amplified and finally transmitted. There are various types of oscillators that are used at this stage which include LC and RC oscillators, but in modern AM transmitters, the source of most carriers (RF signals) is a crystal oscillator.

3.3.3 RF AMPLIFIER SECTION

The RF amplifiers in AM the transmitter are associated with the amplification of the carrier signals at various stages before the signal is finally modulated. The RF amplifiers stage has three sections; RF buffer amplifier, RF driver amplifier and RF power amplifier. 3.3.3.1 RF Buffer Amplifier
When the oscillator generates the carrier signal, it feeds it to the buffer amplifier which is the first amplifier connected immediately after the oscillator. The buffer amplifier is a class A amplifier whose primary purpose in the transmitter is to isolate the oscillator from the remaining power amplifier stages. In the transmitter, the buffer operates to provide a modest increase in power output and simply prevent load changes from causing frequency variation in the oscillator by providing high impedance load for the oscillator to minimize drift. It also provides enough gain to drive the modulated amplifier sufficiently. 3.3.3.2 RF Driver Amplifier
The signal from the buffer amplifier is applied to a driver amplifier to ‘drive’ the RF signal. To drive the RF means that the amplifier is designed to provide an intermediate level of power amplification of the signal. Another purpose of this circuit is to generate enough output power to drive the last power amplifier stage. 3.3.3.3 Power Amplifier
The RF power amplifier is the final power amplifier stage and it operates at class C level at very high power. It amplifies the RF signal to a sufficient level suitable for modulation.

3.3.4 AF AMPLIFIER SECTION

The AF amplifiers are the amplifiers that process and amplify the intelligence or modulating signals to be transmitted. Referring to the block diagram of the AM transmitter, the audio amplifier stage receives its signal from the input transducer (often a microphone) and contains whatever stages of intelligence amplification that is required. This amplifier section also has three different units; AF pre-amplifier, AF driver amplifier and AF power amplifier. 3.3.4.1AF pre-amplifier
This is a linear voltage amplifier with high input impedance. It raises the original amplitude of the audio signal to a usable level with minimum non-linear distortion and as little thermal noise as possible. ````3.3.4.2 AF driver amplifier
This is a class B linear amplifier that further amplifies the audio signal from the pre- amplifier to a sufficient level that will adequately drive the high power modulator (modulation amplifier) 3.3.4.3 AF power amplifier
This amplifier is used to add more power to the audio signal suitable for modulation.

3.3.5 MODULATOR SECTION

The modulator stage is the last process in the generation of AM wave in the AM transmitter before the modulated signals are finally transmitted to the atmosphere. At the modulator stage, RF signals from the power amplifier and the signals from AF power amplifier are both mixed together to bring about the AM modulated signals. This modulator stage has a circuit (modulator circuit) which has three primary functions; It provides the circuitry necessary to bring the modulation. It contains the final power amplifier which drives the modulated signals.
It translates low-frequency information signals to radio-frequency signal that can be efficiently radiated from antenna.

3.3.6 OUTPUT SECTION

This section serves as the channel through which the modulated signal generated in the transmitter transmits and radiates into space. It is made up of impedance-matching or coupling network and antenna. The impedance-matching network ensures maximum power transfer between the output of the transmitter and antenna. The antenna serves as the transducer which collects the modulated signal and radiates it into space in form of electromagnetic wave.

3.4 TYPES OF AM TRANSMITTER

The AM transmitter is classified as low-level transmitter and high-level transmitter. This classification is based on the type of power amplifier used in the transmitter and the point in the transmitter at which the signal modulation takes place.

3.4.1 LOW-LEVEL AM TRANSMITTER

Low-level AM transmitter is more of a laboratory AM generator. Here AM waves are produced at such a low power level that simplicity is a more important requirement than efficiency. This is shown in figure 3.4
[Figure 3.4:Low-level AM transmitter]

3.4.2 HIGH-LEVEL AM TRANSMITTER

High-level AM transmitter generates such high power that its prime requirement is efficiency. In this case, quite complex means of AM generation is used. Figure 3.5 shows the block diagram of a high-level AM transmitter.
[Figure 3.5: High-level AM transmitter]
3.4.3 COMPARISON          BETWEEN        LOW-LEVEL        AND       HIGH-LEVEL             AM TRANSMITTERS
Figure 3.4 shows low-level AM transmitter and figure 3.5 shows high-level AM transmitter. Comparing both figures, it will be observed that the RF crystal oscillator (RF source) which provides the carrier frequency, buffer amplifiers, and subsequent RF power amplifiers are common to transmitters. The buffer amplifiers are usually class A amplifier whereas power amplifiers are class C amplifiers. In both, audio and power audio frequency (AF) amplifiers are present. In fact, the only difference is the point at which the modulation takes place. In the case of low-level AM transmitter, modulation takes place at low power level, that is, before the final output amplifier while in high-level, the modulation takes place at high power level. Again, in low-level AM transmitter, amplifier efficiency and bandwidth preservation are important factors since audio signal is having low power. But for high-level AM transmitter, other than efficiency of amplifier power handling capability, distortion, and capability of handling amplitude variations are important parameters. However, the outputs are the same in both. The output of final amplifier is passed through an impedance-matching or coupling network that includes the tank circuit of
the final amplifier. For tank circuits, the quality factor, Q, is kept low enough to pass all sideband signals without amplitude and frequency distortion, but at the same time provides sufficient attenuation at the second harmonic of the carrier frequency. In the terms of application, low-level AM transmitters are suitable for two-way communication device such as walkie-talkies. On the other hand, high-level AM transmitter is used in high power AM transmission like broadcast stations, and amateur high power transmission that operate in AM mode only.

3.4.4 AM BROADCAST TRANSMITTER

Most of the AM broadcast transmitters use an audio baseband range of 5 KHz. Figure 3.6 shows a typical AM transmitter.
[Figure 3.6: AM broadcast transmitter]
Here, a temperature-controlled crystal oscillator is used to generate stabilized RF signal. The crystal oscillator is followed by buffer amplifier and then by tuned class C amplifiers that provide the necessary power gain to drive the final power amplifier. For high power output, vacuum tubes would be used. The modulator system used here is known as triple equilibrium system. In this modulator system, the main part of the modulation is performed by plate-modulating the final class C power amplifier. Secondary modulation of both the final grid and the plate of the driver stage is also
provided to compensate for bias shift in the final amplifier that results from the non- linear characteristics of the amplifier. The final output amplifier is a push-pull parallel stage in which each side of the push- pull stage is composed of several vacuum tubes operating in parallel, to obtain power required. The greater advantage which this system offers is that, due to the parallel connection of the vacuum tubes, in the case where one or more tubes in system fails, the remaining tubes will provide partial output until repairs are made, thus making a more secure system. The output of the final amplifier is fed to antenna through matching network. The modulator amplifier is an audio-frequency push-pull parallel amplifier, which is transformer coupled to the modulator. The audio pre-amplifier stage provides a difference amplifier and an envelope detector that demodulates a sample of the transmitter output and uses the signal to provide negative feedback through the feedback circuitry. The basic function of the feedback system is to linearize the class C amplifier, thereby linearizing the modulation characteristics of the system, by reducing distortion in it.

3.4.4.1 Requirement of AM Broadcast Transmitter System

The main requirements of AM broadcast transmitters are; 1. They must produce output within the limits of the 5 KHz audio bandwidth. 2. They should have highest possible fidelity. 3. The modulator circuits in the transmitter must produce a linear modulation function. 4. Tuned class C amplifier must provide adequate power gain to drive the final power amplifier. 5. Antenna systems for the transmitter must be located at some point distant from the studio operation.
3.5 FM TRANSMITTER FM Transmitter generates and transmits FM signals. It also works along the same line as that of AM transmitter earlier described. For the generation and modulation of the FM signals, there two different methods that can be used; Direct method and Indirect method. In direct method, the FM signal is generated from a carrier source and directly modulated into the FM signal in the modulator before being transmitted. The direct
FM signal that is generated by this method is transmitted using direct FM transmitter. The most popular type of direct FM transmitter is the Crosby FM transmitter. The indirect method of generating FM involves generating the RF signals firstly and modulates it into a phase modulation which in turn is being modified into frequency modulation. The indirect FM is transmitted using indirect FM transmitter. The most fundamental and popular type of indirect FM transmitter is Armstrong FM transmitter.

3.5.1 FREQUENCY MULTIPLIERS AND MIXER IN FM TRANSMITTER SYSTEM

The combination of Frequency multiplier and mixer are used in FM transmitter system to obtain a desired high output RF frequency and a specified wideband frequency deviation by multiplication and heterodyning processes. Both devices may sometimes present confusions to the reader about their specific function, therefore, the distinction between the frequency multiplier and mixer is important in FM systems. Figure 3.7 shows how a combination of frequency multiplier and mixer may be used to increase deviation without increasing the nominal FM oscillator frequency.
[Figure 3.7: The action of frequency multiplier and mixer]

3.5.1.1 Frequency Multipliers

Frequency multipliers are (class C) amplifiers designed so that the output signal’s frequency is an integer multiple (harmonics) of the input frequency. The principle of its working is that when a frequency rich in harmonic distortion (from class C amplifier) is fed into an LC tank circuit (oscillator tank) tuned to two or three times
the input frequency, frequency multiplication occurs. The frequency multiplication is normally obtained in steps of x2 or x3. The frequency multiplier that multiplies a frequency by 2 is called doubler a while the frequency multiplier circuit that multiplies an input frequency by 3 is called a trippler. Frequency multiplier can also be cascaded. The frequency multiplier multiplies the instantaneous frequency (frequency supplied in the system). For example, if the instantaneous frequency of an FM oscillator is f(t) = fosc1 + ∆f , when passed through a frequency multiplier becomes nf(t) = nfosc1 + n∆f. n is usually 2 or 3 (doubler or trippler). If nf(t) is the total output of the RF signal, it means that n is total multiplying factor of the multipliers’ circuit. 3.5.1.2 Mixers
A mixer, otherwise called heterodyning circuit, is a circuit that does the heterodyning (mixing) of the multiplied frequency at a stage in the transmitter system by supplying certain frequency from an oscillator connected to it. The heterodyning process in the mixer does not affect the frequency deviation of the instantaneous frequency. Its action is only on the oscillator’s carrier frequency. It converts it to an IF signal. For example, if a signal with instantaneous frequency f(t) = fosc1 + ∆f is passed through a mixer, which is also fed by a local oscillatorfosc2 , the output circuit can be tuned to the difference frequency, f(t) - fosc2 The supplied frequency from the local oscillator heterodynes with only the carrier frequency of the FM oscillator and produces a frequency difference, without affecting the frequency deviation. The resulting signal becomes fosc1 + ∆f − fosc2 = IF +∆f. That means, fosc1 −fosc2 is the frequency difference (IF). The stages involved in this process will further be outlined later in this section. 3.5.1.2 The difference between frequency multiplication and mixing
The distinction between frequency multiplication and mixing is important in FM systems. With frequency multiplication, the oscillator frequency and the frequency deviation are both multiplied. For example, the instantaneous frequency after the multiplication is nf(t) = nfosc1 +n∆f, where n is the multiplying factor.
On the contrary, in frequency mixing, the frequency deviation is not affected. When the instantaneous frequency (nf(t) ) resulting from the multiplication stage is passed through a mixer, which is also fed by a local oscillator, the output of the circuit which is a difference frequency results but the deviation will passed through the circuit unaltered. This process only affects the multiplied carrier oscillator’s frequency by combining it with the frequency of the second oscillator fed to the mixer. The new
output after the mixing process is f(i) = IF +n∆f where n is still the original multiplying factor before the mixing.

3.5.2 AUTOMATIC FREQUENCY CONTROL SYSTEM

When the main oscillator of the transmitter is an LC (or RC) oscillator and it is directly frequency modulated to produce relatively large deviation, the circuit may not be capable of keeping the stability of the oscillator’s carrier frequency. So, to keep the carrier frequency stable, an Automatic Frequency Control (AFC) system is used. An AFC can be explained as a negative feed-back system used in a directly frequency modulated transmitter for the purpose of achieving high frequency stability of the carrier. Figure 3.8 shows the block diagram of a typical AFC system. From the circuit, a sample of the output signal taken from the final driver stage, is mixed with a signal from a stable crystal oscillator. The difference frequency (IF) output from the mixer is fed into the discriminator circuit where it is demodulated. The demodulated output consists of the original modulating signal plus any variations caused by drifting of the original frequency of the LC oscillator. The discriminator reacts on to the drifting of the original frequency of the carrier frequency but not the frequency deviations in the carrier (since it is too fast). Since the discriminator is tuned to the correct frequency difference which should exist between the LC oscillator and crystal oscillator, and its input frequency is now somewhat higher, it will develop a positive d. c voltage. This voltage is applied to the reactance modulator whose transconductance is increased by positive voltage developed by the discriminator. This increases the equivalent capacitance of the reactance modulator thereby decreasing the oscillator frequency. The frequency increase in the carrier frequency is thus lowered and brought to the correct value. The correcting dc voltage developed by the discriminator may be fed to a varactor diode connected across the tank circuit of the oscillator (not shown in the diagram) and be used for the AFC purposes.
[Figure 3.8: The block diagram of a typical AFC circuit]
3.5.3 DIRECT FMTRANSMITTER Direct FM transmitter generates and transmits FM signal directly. Figure 3.9 is a block diagram of typical directly modulated FM transmitter.
[Figure 3.9: Block diagram of typical directly modulated FM transmitter]
As we have known, in Frequency modulation, the major objective is to vary to appreciable level the frequency of the carrier. A system that generates very stable carrier frequency may not be very suitable as the deviation in the frequency may be inadequate. This fact makes it discouraging to use crystal oscillator since it offers high frequency stability in FM transmitter. For instance, if a crystal oscillator is used to provide the carrier signal or the reference frequency, the frequency cannot be varied sufficiently to meet up with the desired or recommended frequency deviation needed in wide band FM transmission. For instance, if a crystal oscillator is modulated to a deviation of ±50Hz and a 5MHz centre frequency and both are multiplied by 100 (frequency multiplier), a narrow band system with a 500 MHz carrier ±50 KHz deviation results. Though, it can be used in Narrow Band Frequency Wave (NBFW). On the other hand, LC or RC oscillator drifts a lot due to change in circuit conditions such as temperature change and voltage change which will make the generated carrier frequency or reference frequency to be unstable. To minimize this challenge and get a wide but flexible carrier frequency that can easily be modulated to achieve wide band system, a means of providing an Automatic Frequency Control has to be adopted. This is done by using an Automatic Frequency Control circuit. When this system is incorporated to a direct FM transmitter, we have a type of FM transmitter called Crosby direct FM transmitter. The transmitter uses LC or RC oscillators as carrier generator together with Automatic Frequency Control (AFC) circuit which is a negative feedback control system, to achieve high-frequency stability of the carrier. The essence of AFC circuit is to keep the carrier frequency generated by LC and RC oscillator from drifting while they still produce a desired frequency.

3.5.4 CROSBY FM TRANSMITTER

[Figure 3.10: Block diagram of Crosby FM transmitter]
Crosby FM transmitter is a direct FM transmitter that utilizes direct FM generation with AFC circuit. It transmits at 90 MHz broadcasting. The transmitter is shown in figure 3.10. From the figure, the reactance modulator starts at initial centre frequency of 5 MHz and has a maximum deviation of ± 4.17 KHz. This is a typical situation because reactance modulators cannot provide deviation exceeding about ± 5 KHz and still offers a high degree of linearity. As a result, frequency multipliers are utilized to provide x18 multiplication up to a carrier frequency of 90 MHz (18 x 5MHz) with a ± 75 KHz (18 x 4.17) deviation. Notice that both the carrier and frequency deviation are multiplied by the frequency multiplier. After the multiplication process (x18 multiplication), the process of the generation of frequency modulated signal by exciter is completed. Exciter is often used to denote the circuitry that generates the modulated signal. The excited output (modulated signal) goes to the power amplifiers for transmission and to the frequency stabilization system. The main function of the stabilizing system is to provide a control voltage to
the reactance modulator where it drifts from its desired 5 MHz value. The control (AFC) voltage then varies the reactance of the primary 5 MHz oscillator slightly to bring it back on frequency. The mixer has 90 MHz and 88 MHz crystal oscillator signal as inputs. The mixer output accepts only the difference components of 2 MHz, which is fed to the discriminator. The discriminator provides a dc level output based on the frequency inputs. The discriminator output will be zero if it has an input of exactly 2 MHz, which occurs where the transmitter is at precisely 90 MHz Any carrier drifts up or down causes the discriminator output to go positive or negative, resulting in the appropriate primary oscillator readjustment. 3.5.5 INDIRECT FM TRANSMITTER
In this type of FM transmitter, stable frequency of the crystal oscillator is firstly modulated to phase modulation (PM) signal which then in turn is modulated to FM signal. In this type of Frequency modulation transmitter, crystal oscillator or crystal – controlled frequency synthesizers can be used to set the carrier frequency accurately and maintain solid stability. The principle of the working is that the output of the crystal oscillator is fed to a phase modulator where the phase shift is made on the signal input to vary it in accordance with the modulating signals and since phase variations produce frequency variations, indirect FM is the result. The process is shown in the block diagram of figure 3.11. A type of an indirect FM transmitter uses the Armstrong FM generating method. This transmitter is called Armstrong FM transmitter.
[Figure 3.11: Indirect FM transmitter]

3.5.6 ARMSTRONG FM TRANSMITTER

The Armstrong transmitter is the type of indirect transmitter, which uses Armstrong method of indirect FM generation. This transmitter permits modulation of a signal of stable crystal oscillator without the need for the cumbersome of AFC circuitry and creates Wide Band Frequency Modulation (WBFM). In this transmitter, the modulating signal first amplitude modulates a carrier signal obtained from crystal oscillator and inputs it into a balanced modulator together with the output signal of audio amplifier (amplified audio signal). Figure 3.12 shows a block diagram of a simple Armstrong FM transmitter. From the diagram, as shown in figure 3.12 the output of the crystal oscillator and that of audio amplifier are the two inputs to the balanced modulator, in which amplitude modulation takes place. At the output of the balanced modulator, two sidebands are obtained with the carrier suppressed (AM-DSBCS). At the modulator output, only sidebands appear. The sidebands are then shifted in phase by 90° and combined with the unmodulated carrier present at the output of the buffer amplifier. The final result is a phase-modulated signal, and indirectly, also frequency-modulated. This method will produce the desired phase and frequency modulation only when the resulting signal has a maximum of 30° or less. If the phase shift exceeds 30°, then along with the phase modulation, we have amplitude modulation. This represents distortion. But, by keeping the phase shift within limits (not more than 30°), pure phase modulation is obtained.
[Figure 3.12: Block diagram of an Armstrong FM transmitter]
The block diagram in figure 3.12 is a complete block diagram of an Armstrong FM transmitter system providing a 75 KHz deviation. It uses a balanced modulator that firstly modulates the generated signal to AM signal, the 90° phase shifter to modulate phase-modulate a crystal oscillator’s frequency and the combination of frequency multipliers and mixers which produces the needed deviation. Pre-emphasis and Frequency Correcting Circuit In FM transmitter, the audio signal is first passed through a pre-emphasis circuit that first distorts the signal by amplifying high frequencies more than low frequencies before modulation. That is, the high frequencies are ‘emphasized’ before modulation. Through this process, the circuit alters the relationship between the incoming high frequency intelligence components and the noise. While the noise remains the same, the desired signal strength is increased. Therefore, the main reason for the pre- emphasis network in the FM transmitter is to prevent the high-frequency components of the transmitted intelligence being degraded by noise that would otherwise have more effect on the higher than on the lower intelligence frequencies. The major component of the circuit that does pre-emphasis function is an RC network as shown in figure 3.13 below.
[Figure 3.13: Diagram of pre-emphasis network]
Audio amplifier The output of the pre-emphasis circuit is then feed into the audio amplifier. The amplifier raises the strength of the signal.
Balanced modulator This is a suppressed carrier amplitude modulator, which carries out the amplitude modulation being the first stage of modulation during the process of FM modulation. Its output is a double sideband suppressed carrier AM signal. It receives the input of the crystal oscillator (carrier signal) and the (amplified) audio signal and then carries out the AM modulation of the two. 90° phase shifter This circuit shits the phase of the resulting DSBSC-AM which is output of balanced modulator by 90°. Crystal oscillator The oscillator generates the carrier signal which the audio signal modulates. This oscillator is connected into two channels; one channel goes to the balanced modulator for the first process in the modulation which is amplitude while the other channel goes to the buffer amplifier. Buffer amplifier It maintains the stability of the carrier signal by avoiding its drifting. The unmodulated carrier present at the output of the buffer amplifier combines with the 90° phase shited signal. 1stRF amplifier The resultant (modulated signal) of the combined carrier (from the buffer) and output of the phase shifter is fed into this amplifier. It then boosts the signal strength. First stage of frequency multiplier This multiplier stage raises to the value of the reference frequency and the frequency deviation of the RF signal. Mixer This circuit serves as a heterodyning circuit. It mixes the output of the first frequency multiplier and the output of the second crystal oscillator to provide the difference in the frequency (being the result of the heterodyning) without affecting the frequency deviation. This process is important because, the first stage of the frequency multiplier could raise both the carrier frequency and deviation to such level that if both are allowed to pass through the second stage of frequency multiplier which is necessary to achieve the desired deviation for FM transmission, the carrier value will rise to such
an outrageous value, far above the required value for FM transmission or value for a particular transmitter. Second crystal oscillator This generates and supplies the signal that is used to heterodyne the RF FM output. The generated frequency of this crystal oscillator must not be equal to the RF frequency, otherwise zero signals occurs. 2ndRF amplifier This amplifies the RF signals that results from the heterodyne process before it undergoes the second stage of the frequency multiplication. Second frequency multiplier At this multiplier stage, the output from the mixer, that is, the heterodyned frequency, together with the frequency deviation are further increased. RF power amplifier This amplifier is at the last stage of the system. It boosts the power of the last output signal before the signal is radiated in form of electromagnetic wave through the antenna.

3.5.6.1 Obtaining Wideband Deviation and Heterodyning in Armstrong Transmitter

For the Armstrong FM transmitter shown above, assuming that the carrier frequency of the transmitter is 90 MHz with a maximum deviation of 75 KHz, we can work out how these values can be obtained from the transmitter from a 200 KHz crystal oscillator and 50 Hz audio frequency using the frequency multiplier and mixer. Without these devices, the indirectly created FM is not capable of adequate frequency deviation. A typical deviation is 50 Hz out of 1 MHz. Since the maximum phase shift permissible in this method as earlier mentioned, is 30° (0.524 radian), amplitude of all audio frequency in the range will be adjusted to produce not more than 30° phase shift of the carrier. The equivalent frequency deviation, corresponding to maximum amplitude of AF signal is, ∆f= ±mp fm = 0.524 x 50= 26. 2 Hz. Where
∆f= frequency deviation mp = maximum phase shift fm =modulating (audio) frequency Audio frequency higher than 50 Hz will be attenuated in amplitude by the frequency correcting circuit to limit the phase shift to 30°. Usually, the phase modulation is carried out on a lower carrier frequency generated by the first crystal oscillator. Let us take the carrier frequency generated by the crystal oscillator in this case to be 200 KHz. Now the question is how to increase the 200 KHz ±26.2 Hz to 90 MHz ± 75 KHz. In order to deal with a round figure, let us approximate 26.2 Hz to 26 Hz. To raise 26 Hz to 75 KHz, we need to determine the frequency multiplication that is needed. This is gotten from 75 KHz/ 26 Hz = 2884. The figure can be approximated up to 2900. Although it may be very difficult to have exactly a 2900 increase using doublers and triplers, we can get something little above but very close to 2900, say 2916. The signal is passed through successive stages until the total multiplication of 2916 is obtained. However, we cannot have all the frequency multiplier together in one stage, otherwise we shall get outrageous carrier frequency, but with normal 75 KHz deviation. Therefore, we divide the frequency multiplication stages into two with mixer in-between. Let us refer back to the block diagram under discussion. 3.5.7PHASE- LOCKED-LOOP FM TRANSMITER
[Figure 3.17: PLL FM transmitter block diagram]
The block diagram shown in figure 3.17 is the block diagram of a PLL transmitter. It provides a very practical way to fabricate an FM transmitter. From what the diagram depicts, the amplified audio signal is used to frequency-modulate a crystal oscillator. The crystal frequency is pulled slightly by the variable capacitance exhibited by the varactor diode. The approximate ±200-Hz deviation possible in this fashion is adequate for narrowband systems. The FM output from the crystal oscillator is then divided by 2 and applied as one of the inputs to the phase detector of a phase-locked- loop (PLL) system. As indicated in the figure, the other output to the phase detector is the same, and its output is therefore (in this case) the original audio signal. The input control signal to the VCO is therefore the same audio signal, and its output will be its free-running value of 125 MHz ±5kHz, which is set up to be exactly 50 times the 2.5MHz value of the divided-by-2 crystal frequency of 5MHz.
The FM output signal from the VCO is given power amplification and then driven into the transmitting antenna. This output is also sampled by a ÷50 network, which provides the other FM signal input to the phase detector. The PLL system effectively provides the required x50 multiplication but, more important, provides the transmitter’s required frequency stability. Any drift in the VCO center frequency causes an input to the phase detector that is slightly different from the exact 2.5-MHz crystal reference value. The phase detector output therefore develops an error signal that corrects the VCO center frequency output back to exactly 125MHz. This dynamic action of the phase detector/VCO and feedback path is the basis of a PLL.
3.6 IMPEDANCE MATCHING OF TRANSMITTER TO ANTENNA Impedance matching of the transmitter to antenna occurs when the characteristics impedance of the transmission line (feed-line) matches the output impedance of the transmitter and the impedance of the antenna itself. At this condition, the Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) will be 1:1 and maximum power transfer will take place. The impedance matching is one of the most critical aspects of transmitter system that ensures maximum power transfer from the transmitter to the antenna. Transmitters are connected to antenna through guided media, usually wires which include twisted cable, co-axial cables, optic fibre etc. These wires are called feed- lines. Feed lines transfer energy from the transmitter to the antenna. To obtain the maximum power transfer to the antenna, the transmitter output impedance is properly matched to the antenna’s input impedance. This is achieved using coupling networks or couplers. The function of coupling networks is to achieve efficient energy transfer and in some cases, they are required to perform some signal filtering action (to eliminate some unwanted frequency components). Therefore, the essence of matching the transmitter to the antenna is to greatly minimize power loss due to reflection of signal wave. Under ideal impedance matching, maximum power transfer is achieved. This entails that the total power delivered by the transmitter is ‘totally’ absorbed by the antenna, though practically, this is not so. 3.6.2 TRANSMITTER’S IMPEDANCE-MATCHING NETWORKS

Impedance matching networks are circuits which are used for matching transmitters to antenna through a feed line(s) in other to achieve maximum power transfer. The network is composed of reactance and transformer either lumped or distributed depending on the operating frequency. In addition to providing maximum power transfer, coupling networks provide signal filtering (suppression of higher harmonics) and selectivity. The process of using coupling networks to match a transmitter to match antenna is described as coupling. 3.6.3 TYPES OF IMPEDANCE-MATCHING NETWORKS
There are various devices which are used for impedance matching. Some of the devices include matching stub, balun, torodial transformer, and antenna tuners.

3.6.3.1 Matching Stub

The matching stub or otherwise called Q-section is a quarter wavelength of coaxial or balanced transmission line of a specific impedance that is connected between a transmitter or receiver (as the source) and the antenna (as the load) for the purpose of matching impedance. A matching stub can be used for impedance matching according to the mathematical relationship:
ZQ =√ZO ZL
Where
ZQ = Characteristics impedance of the matching stub
ZO = Characteristic impedance of the transmitter or transmission line
ZL = Characteristics impedance of the antenna feed-point
[Figure 3.19: Quarter wavelength matching stub]

3.6.3.2 Balun

Balun is type of transformer use for impedance matching. This transformer transforms impedance from balance line to unbalance line and vice-versa. It is from this process of transformation from balance to unbalance that the name ‘balun transformer’ is derived. Baluns have a very wide bandwidth and, therefore, are essentially independent of frequency. Balun can be created for producing impedance matching ratios of 4:1, 9:1, and 16:1. A special type of balun has the ratio 1:1 impedance ratio. The major function of this type is to convert between balance and unbalance condition with no phase reversal. A typical Balun transformer is shown below in figure 3.20.
[Figure 3.20: Balun transformer]

3.6.3.3 Antenna Tuners

Antenna tuner is a variable inductor, one or more variable capacitors, or a combination of these components connected in various configurations. In the tuner, inductor and capacitor values are adjusted until the standing wave ratio indicates that the impedances match. The various configuration of the antenna tuner that are widely in use and which also determine the name of various types of the antenna tuner are L- configuration, T-configuration and π-configuration. The names of the configurations are determined by how capacitor(s) and inductor(s) are arranged and the letter-shapes they form in the tuner network. Each of the configurations has different placements of the inductors and capacitor according to application. For simplicity, we choose one sample each of the basic configurations; L-network, T-network and π-network. The diagram for each of the tuner network is shown in figure 3.21
(a) L-network                        (b) T-network                      (c)pi-network
[Figure 3.21: Antenna tuners]

3.6.4 GENERAL REQUIREMENTS OF TRANSMITTER’S COUPLING NETWORKS

Impedance matching networks should be able to fulfill the following requirements; • Tuning of reactive components of antenna impedance. • Adjusting correct value of load resistance. • Prevention of unnecessary radiation of spurious frequencies.

3.6.5 EFFECTS OF MISMATCHING TRANSMITTER TO ANTENNA

When antenna is not properly matched to a feed-line, it may result to a high voltage standing wave ratio (VSWR), high radiation loss due low radiation resistance for the antenna, and heat dissipation in the cable. All these factors reduce the efficiency of the system. The high standing wave ratio causes wave reflection. The occurrence of the reflection causes the voltage maximums along the feed-line to exceed the cable’s dielectric strength, causing a breakdown of the cable. In addition, the presence of this reflected wave means greater power loss (I2R) which can be a severe problem when a feed-line is physically long. In addition, a high VSWR also tends to accentuate noise problems and causes ‘ghost’ to be transmitted with video or data signals from the transmitter. In summary the effects of not matching the transmitter to the antenna perfectly are as follows: • The full generator power does not reach the load. • The feed-line (cable) dielectric may break down as a result of high-value standing waves of voltage (voltage node). • The existence of reflection and re-reflection increases the power loss in the form of I2R heating, especially at the high-value standing waves of current (current node). • Increase in noise problems. • Creation and presence of ‘ghost’ signal.

3.7 TRANSMITTER TESTS AND MEASUREMENTS

Tests and measurements are carried out on transmitter for several reasons;
1. Transmitter as equipment that radiates a radio signal is governed by Federal Communication Commission (FCC) rules and regulations. For a transmitter to
2. meet its intended purpose, the FCC specifies frequency, power, and other measurements to which the equipment must comply. Therefore, the measurements and tests are taken to make sure the transmitter is in line with the rules. 3. The tests on transmitter are normally made when it is first installed to be sure that everything is working correctly. 4. Tests on transmitter may be made for troubleshooting. If the transmitter is not working properly, these tests are some of first that should be made to help identify the trouble.

3.7.1 EQUIPMENTS FOR TRANSMITTER TESTS AND MEASUREMENTS

There are numerous test equipment use for transmitter measurement and test but we shall discuss a few essential ones in this section 3.7.1.1 Oscilloscope
The oscilloscope use in RF measurement of transmitter is of two basic types; the analog oscilloscopes and the digital storage oscilloscopes (DSOs). Analog oscilloscopes amplify the signal to be measured and display it on the face of a CRT at a speed rate. They are available for displaying and measuring RF voltage to about 5 MHz. figures 3.22 is an analog oscilloscope. The digital storage oscilloscopes, also known as sampling oscilloscope use high speed sampling or analog-to-digital (A/D) converter techniques to convert the signal to be measured into series of digital words that are stored in an internal memory. The sampling rates vary from approximately 20 million samples per second to more than 8 billion samples per second depending upon the oscilloscope. Each measurement sample is usually converted into an 8-or10- bit parallel binary number that is stored in an internal memory. These types of oscilloscopes are very popular for high frequency measurement because they provide the means to display signals with frequencies up to about 30 MHz. This means that complex modulated microwaves signals can be readily viewed, measured, and analyzed.
[Figure 3.22: Analog oscilloscope]

3.7.1.2 Spectrum Analyzers

A spectrum analyzer is an electronic device that visually displays, on its CRT, the amplitude of the components of a wave as a function of frequency. It is, in effect, an automatic frequency-selective volt-meter that provides both frequency and voltage on its CRT display. As well, it can be thought of as a radio receiver with broad frequency- range coverage and sharp sweep tuning, narrow-bandwidth circuit. The more sophisticated units are calibrated to read signals in dB. Most recent spectrum analyzers utilize microprocessor principles (software programming) for ease of operation. In the course of evaluating transmitter’s performance, such as the harmonics and spurious signal measurement, the spectrum analyzer is obviously very handy tool for use. Figure 3.23 shows a typical spectrum analyzer. The display of spectrum analyzer can be contrasted with an oscilloscope display, which shows the amplitude of the total wave (all components) versus time. Thus, an oscilloscope shows us the time domain while the spectrum analyzer shows the frequency domain.
[Figure 3.23: Spectrum analyzer]

3.7.1.3 Power Meter

Power meter is one of the most commonly use RF test instruments for transmitters. Power meters come in variety of sizes and configurations. One of the most popular is a small in-line power meter designed to be inserted into the coaxial cable between a transmitter and an antenna. The meter is used to measure the transmitters’ output supply to the antenna. A short coaxial cable connects to the transmitters’ output to the power meter, and the output of the power meter is connected to the antenna or dummy load. Power meters may have either an analog readout meter or a digital display.

3.7.1.4 Deviation Meters

Deviation meters are designed to measure the amount of carrier deviation of an FM/PM transmitter. It is usually an FM demodulator that has been calibrated to provide an output indication of the amount of deviation on a meter scale or on a digital readout. The readout may be indicated in percentage of total deviation or in frequency deviation from Hertz to kilohertz. Although, separate deviation meters are made, they are usually built into another piece of equipment containing signal generators, power meters, and other instruments which together form a complete transmitter test set.

3.7.1.5 Frequency Counters

One of the most widely used communication test instruments for transmitter test is frequency counter. This instrument measures the frequency output of transmitter. It displays the frequency of a signal on a decimal readout.

3.7.1.6 RF Voltmeters

An RF voltmeter is a special piece of test equipment designed to measure sine-wave voltage of high frequency signals with readout given in root-means-square. Some of these RF voltmeters can measure voltage from microvolts to hundreds of volts at frequencies up to 2 GHz. The RF voltmeters are of analog and digital type. The analog type has a moving pointer on a background scale. Measurement accuracy is within 1 percent to 5 percent range depending upon specific measurement. The digital RF voltmeters have digital readout probes with somewhat improved measurement accuracy.

3.7.1.7 RF Probes

One way to measure RF voltage is to use an RF probe with a standard dc multimeter. RF probes are sometimes referred to as detector probes. An RF probes is basically a rectifier with a filter capacitor that stores the peak value of the sine-wave RF voltage. The result is a peak value that can easily be converted to root-mean-square by multiplying it by 0.707.
Most RF probes are good for RF voltage measurement to about 25 MHz. The accuracy is about 5 percent, but that is usually very good for RF measurement.

3.7.1.8 Dummy Loads

A dummy load is a resistor whose value is equal to the output impedance of the transmitter and that has sufficient rating, which is connected to the transmission line in place of antenna to absorb the transmitter output power. These resistors are noncritical, but must be non-inductive. The resistor should be as close to pure resistance at the operating frequency as possible.

3.7.1.9 Field Strength Meters (FSM)

The FSM is a sensitive device used for detecting the presence of RF signals near an antenna. It detects the RF energy being radiated by a transmitter into an antenna.

3.7.2 MAJOR TRANSMITTER TESTS AND MEASUREMENTS

Four main tests and measurements are made on most transmitters. These are tests of frequency, modulation tests, power measurement, and the tests for harmonics and spurious output such as parasitic radiation.

3.7.2.1 Frequency Measurement

Regardless of the method of carrier generation, the frequency of the transmitter is important. The transmitter must operate on the assigned frequency so as to ensure that the signal can be picked up by a receiver that is tuned to that frequency. To measure the frequency, the transmitter output is connected to a dummy load see figure 3.24. This will ensure that no signal is radiated, but that there will be sufficient signal pickup to make as frequency measurement if the counter and its antenna are placed near the transmitter. The output of a transmitter is then measured directly to determine its frequency. The transmitted signal is independently picked up and its frequency measured on a frequency counter.
[Figure 3.24: Transmitter Frequency Measurement]

3.7.2.2 Modulation Tests

If AM is being used in the transmitter, you should measure the percentage of modulation. In FM or PM transmitter, you should measure the frequency deviation with modulation. The best way to measure AM is to use an oscilloscope and display the AM signal directly. To do this, you must have an oscilloscope whose vertical amplifier bandwidth is sufficient to cover the transmitter frequency. Figure 3.25(a)shows the basic test setup. An audio signal generator is used to amplitude-modulate the transmitter. An audio signal of 400 to 1000 Hz is applied in place of the microphone signal. The transmitter is then turned on, and the oscilloscope attached to the output load. It is best to perform this test with a dummy load to prevent radiation of the signal. The oscilloscope is then adjusted to display the AM signal. The display will appear as shown in figure 3.25(b)
[Figure 3.25: (a) Basic setup of oscilloscope (b) Oscilloscope display 3.7.2.3 Power Measurements]
Most transmitters have a tune-up procedure recommended by the manufacturer for adjusting each stage to produce maximum output power. In older transmitters, tuned circuits between stages have to be precisely adjusted in the correct sequence. In modern solid-state transmitters, there are fewer adjustments, but in most cases there are some adjustments in the driver and frequency multiplier stages as well as tuning adjustment for resonance at operating frequency to the final amplifier. There may be impedance-matching adjustments in the final amplifier to ensure full coupling of the power to the antenna. The process is essentially that of adjusting the tuned circuits to resonance. These measurements are generally made while monitoring the output power of the transmitter. The procedure for measuring the output power is to connect the transmitter output to an RF power meter and the dummy load shown in figure 3.26.The transmitter is turned on without modulation, and adjustments are made on the transmitter circuit to tune for maximum power output. With the test arrangement shown, the power meter will display the output power reading.
[Figure 3.26: Power measurement test setup]
Once the transmitter is properly tuned up, it can be connected to the antenna. The power in the antenna will then be indicated. If the antenna is properly matched to the transmission line, the amount of output power will be the same as that in the dummy load. If not, standing wave ratio (SWR) measurements should be made. Most modern power meters measure both forward and reflected power, so SWR measurements are easier to make. It may be necessary to adjust the antenna or a matching circuit to ensure maximum output power with minimum SWR.

3.7.2.4 Harmonics and Spurious Output Measurements

Harmonics and spurious signals are best measured using spectrum analyzer. Harmonics are multiples of fundamental frequency usually produced by high-power transmitters and which in most cases, undesired. Spurious signals are produced in transmitters as a result of parasitic oscillation and intermodulation distortion in mixers and non-linear circuits. To measure these outputs, the spectrum analyzer is tuned to search for signals at the second, third, and higher harmonics of the carrier frequency. If signals are detected, they can be measured to ensure that they are sufficiently low in power. The spectrum analyzer is then tuned over a broad range to ensure that no other spurious non harmonic signals are present. It may be possible to reduce the harmonic and spurious output content by making a minor transmitter tuning adjustment. If not, to meet specifications, it is often necessary to use filters to eliminate unwanted harmonics or other signals.

A radio receiver is an electronic                   and AM Receiver device which when connected to 4.7 Transceivers the receiving end of a transmitted radio signals, receives the signals                                      and converts it into the correct form for the interpretation of                           the information it carries. During transmission, carrier signal is modulated by the modulating signal and released from a radio transmitter into the space. The modulated RF wave is transmitted through space as an electromagnetic or RF wave to reach a receiving antenna which in turns sends the wave to Radio receiver via a coupling network or circuit. The transmitted signal is very weak (of micro volt range) when it reaches the receivers. The signal being weak is as a result of various degrees of interference in the transmission medium (space) such as collision with other signals, noise interference of various kinds, nature of the medium etc. As the signals pass across the receiving antenna, a. cvoltages of micro-volts range are induced in the antenna. These voltages are then coupled into the radio receiver through the antenna coupling network. The receiver provides the needed selectivity and sensitivity to the incoming signals i.e. identifying and selecting the desired carrier frequency from those present in the antenna circuit and providing sufficient amplification of the induced small a. c signal voltage. As part of the process, the receiver then extracts the carrier signals and allows the passage of intelligence sidebands signals by the process of detection and amplifies the resultant audio signals to the proper magnitude to
operate a louder speaker or earphone. In this chapter, we are going to see the general
functions characteristics of radio receiver, the configurations and the types of receiver. Every radio receiver must be capable of providing selectivity and sensitivity that permit full recovery of the original intelligence signal from the radio frequency signals. For a receiver to be able to provide these primary requirements, it has to carry out different stages of functions sequentially as listed below: 1. A receiving antenna connected to the receiver must intercept a portion of the passing radio signal from the space. 2. The radio receiver must select the desired radio waves intercepted by the receiving antenna through a coupling (tuned LC) circuit and reject others. 3. It will amplify the selected radio signals by the RF amplifier(s) 4. After sufficient amplification of the RF signal, detection or extraction of intelligence or modulating signal from the amplified RF signal must take place in the receiver. 5. The intelligence signals must be amplified to a sufficient power level suitable to drive a loud speaker. 6. The amplified intelligence signals should be fed to the speaker for reproduction into original sound.
Generally, the performance of the radio receiver can measure in terms of some basic receiver’s characteristics. Such characteristics include the following; 1.       Selectivity. 2.       Sensitivity and gain. 3.       Fidelity. 4.       Image frequency. 5.       Double spotting. 6.       Spurious frequency

4.3.1 SELECTIVITY OF RADIO RECEIVER

The selectivity of a receiver is defined as the extent to which the receiver is capable of differentiating between the desired signals and other frequencies (unwanted radio signals and noise). It can also be described as the ability of the receiver to select a desired signal frequency (while rejecting others). Selectivity is obtained in a receiver
by using tuned circuit. Tuned circuits are RLC circuits tuned to resonate at a desired signal frequency. The Q- factor of these tuned circuits determines the receiver’s selectivity. The processes by which these tuned circuits determine the selectivity of receivers follow the mathematical principle below: f BW = Qo.                                                                   …4.3.1
Where BW = Bandwidth of tuned circuit. fo = Resonant frequency of the tuned circuit. Q = quality (Q-) of the tuned circuit. The Q-factor of a tuned circuit is the ratio of inductive reactance, XL to the X resistance (Q = L ) usually determined or measured at resonance. We should R recall that XL = 2πFL and fo = 2π√LC
Where XL = inductive reactance of the tuned circuit. F = frequency of the tuned circuit. fo = resonance frequency of the tuned circuit. The bandwidth of the receiver (provided by the tuned circuit) is the difference between the upper (maximum) and lower (lower) cut-off frequencies. This difference is the selected frequency or the bandwidth. Therefore, the bandwidth of a tuned circuit is measure of the selectivity; narrower the bandwidth, better the selectivity. The later f statement can be justified from the mathematical relationship; BW = o. 4.3.2 SENSITIVITY OF RADIO RECEIVER

The sensitivity is the primary function of the overall receiver gain. It is often defined in terms of the voltage that must be applied to the receiver input terminals to give standard output power, measured at the output terminals. It is also the ability to drive the output transducer to an acceptable level. This entails its ability to pick up weak signal (usually of micro volt range) and amplifies it to sufficient level. However, in a more technical definition, receiver sensitivity is the minimum input signal (usually expressed in voltage) required to produce a specified output signal.

4.3.3 FIDELITY

Fidelity of a receiver refers to the ability of the receiver to reproduce all the modulating frequencies from the incoming RF signal (after detection) equally. If a radio receiver amplifies all the modulating signals equally well, it is said to have a high fidelity. Figure 4.1 shows the typical fidelity curve for radio receiver.
[Figure 4.1: Typical fidelity curve]
The fidelity at the lower modulating at the lower modulating frequencies is determined by the high frequency response of the Intermediate Frequency (IF) amplifier. Fidelity is usually difficult to obtain in AM receiver because good fidelity requires more bandwidth of IF amplifier resulting in poor selectivity.

4.3.4 IMAGE FREQUENCY

Image frequency is any frequency, other than the desired Radio Frequency signal, which will produce another (unwanted) frequency that is equal to the Intermediate Frequency (IF) if allowed to enter a receiver and mix with the frequency of the local oscillator. If the desired RF signal and its image frequency enter a receiver at the same time, they both mix with the local oscillator frequency and produce signal that are equal to IF. Consequently, two different stations will be received and demodulated simultaneously thereby leading to (image) interference. By definition, an image is an RF signal that is spaced from the incoming signal by a frequency that is two times the intermediate frequency above or below the incoming frequency,
fosc = fs +IF                                                       …4.3.2 Or, fs = fosc −IF                                                       …4.3.3 fim = fosc +IF                                                      …4.3.4 Putting equation4.1.2 into equation4.1.4, it becomes fim = fs + IF + IF =fs + 2IF fim =fs +2IF                                                               …4.3.5
Equation 4.3.5 is the image frequency expression, where fim = Image frequency fs = Desired signal frequency IF = Intermediate frequency fosc = Oscillator’s frequency In the vast majority of all receiver made, the local oscillator frequency is made higher than the incoming signal frequency by an amount equal to the IF. It is made equal at all times to the signal frequency plus the intermediate frequency. Thus fosc = fs +IF,
no matter what the signal frequency may be. When fs and fosc are mixed, the difference frequency, which is one of the by-products, is equal to IF. Only IF is passed and amplified by the IF stage. However, if an image frequency fim , manages to reach the mixer, such that fim = fosc + IF, then this frequency will also produce IF when mixed withfosc . Unfortunately, this spurious intermediate-frequency signal will also be amplified by the IF amplifier stage and will therefore cause interference. This also has the effect of resulting into two stations being received simultaneously and is naturally undesirable.

4.3.5 DOUBLE SPOTTING

Double spotting occurs at higher frequencies due to poor front end selectivity of the receiver. In this, receiver picks up same short-wave station at two nearby points on the same receiver dial. When the receiver is tuned across the band, a strong signal appears to be at two different frequencies, one at the desired frequency and again when the receiver is tuned to twice IF below the desired frequency. In this second case, the signal becomes the image, reduced in strength by the image rejection, thus making it appear that the signal is located at two frequencies in the band. Double spotting is harmful because a weak station may be masked by the reception of a nearby strong station at the spurious point on the dial. Double spotting can be reduced by improving image frequency rejection using RF amplifier stage in the receiver.

4.3.6 SPURIOUS RESPONSES

Spurious responses occur when a signal with a frequency near that of the desired frequency passes through the RF amplifier to the mixer with an appreciable amplitude and either it or one of its harmonics mixes with the oscillator or one of its harmonics to produce a frequency within the band pass of the IF filter. A non-linear mixer will produce these harmonics, but a linear multiplier circuit used as mixer will not. To reduce the effect of the spurious responses, the selectivity of the RF amplifier will have to be increased by increasing the Q-factor. This will reduce the effect of the spurious frequency by keeping the interfering signals from reaching the mixer. n and m are positive integers Radio receivers are broadly classified into Amplitude Modulated (AM) receiver and Frequency Modulated (FM) receivers. The AM receiver started with the simple form called Straight Radio Receiver or Tuned Radio-Frequency (TRF) receiver and later got modified to the superheterodyne receiver and double-conversion superheterodyne and other communication receivers which are commonly in use nowadays. 4.5 AM RECEIVERS The development of AM receiver started with TRF receiver and later, the superheterodyne receiver, called superhet in abbreviation, which has real practical applications or commercial significances. The TRF has many disadvantages which render it impracticable to use in commercial applications. Notwithstanding, we shall firstly study the TRF for the reasons that it is the simpler of all the types of AM receivers and it forms the basis for the development of others by improving on its shortcomings.

4.5.1 TUNED RADIO-FREQUENCY (TRF) RECEIVERS

Tuned radio-frequency receiver otherwise known as straight receivers are probably the simplest designed radio receiver available today, though not usually in use nowadays except in special applications as a fixed-frequency receiver. Despite not been popularly in use today, it still offers two distinctive advantages; its simplicity and its high sensitivity. The TRF has three stages; Radio Frequency (RF) Stage, Detection Stage and Audio Stage. The figure below shows the block diagram of the three-stage TRF receiver.
[Figure 4.2: Block diagram of TRF receiver]
Considering the block diagram above and the activities it represents, two or perhaps three Radio Frequency (RF) amplifiers all ganged (mechanically tuned together) are required to select and amplify the incoming signal frequency to a level adequate to drive the detector stage and simultaneously reject all other frequencies outside the
range it can handle. After the RF stage where the signal was amplified to suitable level, the detector being the next stage detects or demodulates it. i.e. converts the RF signal directly to information signal. The demodulated signal is then fed into the audio stage when it is in turn amplified by audio amplifier to a usable level. Finally, the amplified signal is fed to the loud speaker for output as a sound. The TRF receivers are simple and have a relatively high sensitivity, simple to design and align at broadcast frequencies (535 KHz to 640 kHz) but they have their peculiar disadvantages which include problem of bandwidth variation, problem of instability, problem of non-uniform gain over a very wide frequency range and problem of insufficient adjacent frequency rejection.

4.5.1.1 Limitations of Tuned Radio Frequency (TRF) Receiver

1. Bandwidth variation: The bandwidth of the TRF is inconsistent and varies with centre frequency when turned over a wide range of input frequencies. The bandwidth increases proportionally with the increase in frequency. Thus the selectivity of the input filter changes over any appreciable range of input frequencies. 2. Instability: The instability of TRF is due to large number of RF amplifier all tuned to the same centre frequency. Consequent upon this, high gain is being achieved at one frequency by the multistage amplifier and can lead to the receiver breaking into oscillation. 3. Non-uniform gain: The gains of TRF are not uniform over a very wide frequency range. 4. Insufficient adjacent-channel rejection: The TRF was unable to achieve sufficient selectivity at high frequencies, partly as a result of the enforced use of a single-tuned circuit. 5. Tracking of tuned circuit: In a receiver, tuned circuits are made available so that they can be set to the frequency of the desired signals. In most of the receivers, the capacitors in the tuned circuit are made variable. These capacitances are ‘ganged’ between the stages so that they all can be changed simultaneously when the tuning knob is rotated. To have perfect tuning, the capacitor values between the stages must be exactly same, but this is not the case. The differences in the capacitors cause the resonant of each tuned circuit to be slightly different, thereby increasing the pass band.

4.5.2 SUPERHETERODYNE RECEIVERS

Superheterodyne receiver (superhet) was developed to solve the many problems associated with TRF receiver. The basic principle of the receiver is to convert all incoming signal to a lower fixed frequency known as Intermediate Frequency (IF) at which a single set of amplifier is used to provide a fixed level of signal sensitivity and selectivity. Then this fixed intermediate frequency is amplified and detected to reproduce the original information since the characteristics of the IF amplifier are independent of the frequency to which the receiver is tuned, the selectivity and sensitivity of the superheterodyne receivers are fairly uniform throughout its tuning range. The mixing or heterodyning of these two frequencies produces an Intermediate Frequency signal (IF) which contains all the modulation properties of the original signal. The Intermediate Frequency is equal to the difference between the station frequency and oscillator frequency. IF = fosc − fs                                                   …4.5.1
[Figure 4.3: Block diagram of Superheterodyne receiver]
The block diagram shown in the figure 4.3 shows a basic superheterodyne receiver. From the diagram, it can be seen that superheterodyne receiver is an improved form of TRF. It has the same important components as the TRF receiver, in addition to the mixer, local oscillator and intermediate-frequency (IF) amplifier. The key circuit of the receiver is the mixer or frequency converter circuit which acts like a simple amplitude modulator to produce sum and difference frequencies. The incoming signal is mixed with a local oscillator signal to produce this conversion. Now, we shall see the circuit of each block or the stages of the receiver and their basic functions.
RF amplifier stage: at the RF amplifier stage, the antenna picks up the weak radio signal and feeds it to the RF amplifier. The RF amplifier uses a tuned (parallel) circuit which helps to select the desired radio signals or at least the frequency ranges in which the signal resides and raises the strength of the signals to the desired level. The RF amplifier stage provides the initial gain and selectivity. It offers the following advantages to a receiver in which it is incorporated; i.      It provides greater gain and better sensitivity. ii.     It improves image-frequency rejection ratio. iii.    It improves signal-to-noise ratio. iv.     It improves the rejection of adjacent unwanted signals, providing better selectivity. v.      It provides better coupling of receiver to antenna. vi.     It prevents spurious frequencies from entering the mixer and mixing to produce an interfering frequency equal to the IF from the wanted signal. vii.    It also prevents the re-radiation of the local oscillator through the antenna to the receiver. Mixer or frequency converter stage and local oscillator: the mixer is a nonlinear resistance having two sets of input terminals and one set of output terminal. The amplified output of the RF amplifier is applied to the input of the mixer. The mixer also receives an input from a local oscillator. The two frequencies (oscillator output and mixer output) now heterodyned (beat together) and produce an intermediate frequency (IF) which becomes the output of the mixer. The intermediate frequency is the difference between oscillator frequency and radio frequency. That is IF = oscillator frequency ( fosc ) – radio frequency ( fr ). The signal at this intermediate frequency contains the same modulations as the original carrier. The IF is 455 kHz (in AM).
IF amplified stage: The output of the mixer is an IF signal containing the same modulation that appeared on the input RF signal. This signal is amplified by the multistage IF amplifier and most of the receiver gain is obtained in this stage. In the receiver, a careful consideration is made as regards to the intermediate frequency to be fed to IF amplifier. The followed factors are considered while choosing the intermediate frequency. i. Very high intermediate frequency will result in poor selectivity and poor adjacent channel rejection. ii. A high level of intermediate frequency increases tracking difficulties. iii. At very low intermediate frequency, image rejection is poor.
iv. At very low value of intermediate frequency, selectivity is too sharp, cutting of the sidebands. v. The Intermediate Frequency must not fall in the tuning range of the receiver otherwise, instability will occur and heterodyne whistles will be heard, making it impossible to tune to the frequency band immediately adjacent to the intermediate frequency. Detector stage: The amplified IF signal is finally applied to the detector or demodulator, which recovers the original intelligence signal. The detector used is usually a diode circuit because of its low distortion and excellent audio fidelity. However, other types of detectors such as quadrature detector or a product detector may be used for FM and SSB respectively. AF amplifier stage: The audio signal output of detector stage is fed to audio amplifier. Here, the signal is amplified with sufficient voltage and power gain to operate the loud speaker. The speaker converts the audio signals into sound wave corresponding to the original sound at the broadcasting station. Automatic gain control and Automatic frequency control: Automatic gain control is a system by means of which the overall gain of a radio receiver is varied automatically with the changing strength of the received signal to keep the output substantially constant. The output of a detector is usually the original modulating signal, the amplitude of which is directly proportional to the amplitude of the received signals. The received signal which is usually a. c is rectified and filtered into a d. cvoltage by the Automatic Gain Control circuit (AGC). This dc voltage is fed back to the IF amplifier to control receiver gain. The AGC circuits then helps to maintain a constant output voltage level over a wide range of RF input signal levels. It also helps the receiver to function over a wide range so that strong signals do not produce performance-degrading distortion. Virtually, all superheterodyne receivers use some form of AGC which enables tuning to stations of varying signal strengths without appreciable change in the volume output signal. In addition, AGC in superheterodyne helps to smooth out the rapid fading which may occur with long-distance shortwave reception and prevents over loading of the (last) IF amplifier which might otherwise have occurred. On the other hand, Automatic Frequency Control circuit (AFC) generates AFC signal which is used to adjust and stabilize the frequency of the local oscillator.

4.5.2.1 Signal Interference in Superheterodyne Receiver

Signal interference is the additional signals that weaken or block the main signals in a radio receiver when they occur on a single frequency. They are basically two types of signal interference which can occur in a superheterodyne receiver. These are image interference and adjacent channel interference. Basically, it is the action of the former that leads to the later. Adjacent Channel Selectivity and Interference Every communication signal used in communication has a finite bandwidth. When a carrier is modulated by the information signal, sidebands are produced. The resulting signal occupies a certain amount of space in the RF spectrum. The space occupied is called channel. As the number of the communication signals and corresponding channels increase, more and more of the spectrum space is used up. Over the years as the need for electronic communication has increased, the number of radio communication stations has increased dramatically, and the RF spectrum has become extremely crowded, resulting in channels closer to each other. As channels are very closer to each other with a very narrow gap it has become more difficult for a receiver to separate two signals occupying adjacent channel without interference between them or without compromising receiver performance. Such characteristic of receiver is called adjacent channel selectivity. Adjacent channel interference occurs in the receiver when the receiver picks-up the same short wave station at two nearby points on the receiver dial. It is caused by insufficient image-frequency rejection. That is to say, the front-end of the receiver does not select different adjacent signals very well, though the IF stage of the superheterodyne takes care of eliminating almost all of them. This being the case, it is clear that the exact tuning of the oscillator is what determines which signal will be amplified by the IF stage. The receiver which badly suffers from channel interference is assumed to have no RF amplifier. Consider such a receiver at High Frequency (HF), having an IF of 455 KHz. If there is a strong station at 15.9MHz, the receiver will naturally it pick up. When it does, the local oscillator frequency will be 16.355MHz. This is from the fact that fosc = fs +IF (i.e fosc = 15.90MHz + 0.455MHz = 16.355 MHz). The receiver will also pick up this strong station when it is tuned to 14.99MHz. This is also from the fact that fs = fim − 2IF (i.e 15.9 -2x0.455 = 14.99MHz). When the receiver is tuned to the second frequency, its local oscillator will be adjusted to 15.445MHz. Since this is exactly 455 KHz (0.455MHz) below the frequency of the
strong station, the two signals will produce 455 KHz when they are mixed, and the IF amplifier will not reject this signal. If there had been an RF amplifier, the 15.9MHz signal might have been rejected before reaching the mixer, but without an RF amplifier this receiver cannot sufficiently reject 15.9MHz when it is tuned to 14.99MHz. The above illustrated situation is an instance of adjacent channel interference. An improvement in image- frequency rejection will expectedly produce a corresponding reduction in the adjacent channel interference.

4.5.2.2 The Image Frequency Rejection in Superheterodyne Receiver

Image frequency rejection is a technique use in solving the problem of image frequency interference in radio receiver. Image interference occurs only when the image signal is allowed to appear at the mixer input. To solve the image frequency interference, a single-tuned circuit that will reject that image is employed. A high Q- loaded tuned circuit is used ahead of the mixer, or a selective RF amplifier to block this. If the selectivity of the RF amplifier and tuned circuits is good enough, the image will be rejected. This is to say that image rejection depends on the selectivity of the receiver and must be achieved before the IF stage. Once the spurious frequency enters the first IF amplifier, it becomes impossible to remove it from the wanted signal. The rejection of an image frequency by a single tuned – circuit is the ratio of the gain at the signal frequency to the gain at the image frequency expressed by the term, Image Frequency Rejection Ratio (IFRR). In another way, IFRR can be described as the numerical measure of the ability of a single tuned circuit to reject the image frequency. The mathematical expression is
