4.5.2.4 Tracking in Receiver Tracking is the process of tuning receiver circuits to get the desired output signals. The need for tracking arises because the receiver has number of tunable circuits which must all be tuned properly if any given station is to be received. The tuning circuits that are involved are RF tuned circuit, mixer tuned circuit and local oscillator tuned
circuit. The expected result of proper tuning is that the incoming RF signal must be correctly gotten at the input and, at the output of the receiver, proper IF signal is gotten as well. Tracking in receiver is achieved by gang-tuning the tunable circuits. Ganged tuning involves coupling all tuning circuits mechanically so that only one tuning control knob is required. (Refer to figure 4.3) Any errors that exist in the IF after tracking, will result in an incorrect frequency being fed to the IF amplifier. Such errors are known as tracking errors. To avoid tracking errors, standard capacitors are not used in the tuned circuit, instead, ganged capacitors circuit with identical sections, which have different values of inductance and special extra capacitors called trimmers and padders are used to adjust the capacitance of the oscillator to the proper range. Using the any of the special capacitors involves altering the value of the oscillator’s section by adding series padder capacitor and/or parallel trimmer capacitor. There are three methods use for tracking. These are padder tracking, trimmer tracking and three-point tracking.

4.5.2.5 Automatic Gain Control (AGC) of a Receiver

Automatic gain control is a system by means of which the overall gain of a radio receiver is varied automatically with the variation in the strength of the receiver signal, to maintain the output substantially constant. The working principle of the AGC is that the circuitry derives the dc bias voltage from the output of the detector. It applies this derived d. c bias voltage to a selected number of RF, IF and mixer stages (of the receiver) to control their gains. When the average signal level increases, the size of the AGC bias increases, and the gain of the controlled stages decreases. When there is no signal, there is a minimum AGC bias, and the amplifiers produce maximum gain. The use of AGC in a receiver prevents severe distortion and a disturbing blast of sound which can occur when the receiver is tuned to a strong station as a resulting the signal possibly overloading the later IF and AF stages of the receiver. There are two types of AGC circuits in use. These are simple AGC and delayed AGC.
Simple AGC This type of AGC circuit is used in most domestic receivers and cheaper communications receivers. In a simple AGC receiver, the AGC bias starts to increase as soon as the received signal level exceeds the background noise level. As a result, receiver gain starts falling down, reducing the sensitivity of the receiver. Figure 4.7 shows the simple AGC circuit. A simple half-wave rectifier is the AM detector use in this circuit. This detector produces a d. clevel that is proportional to the average signal level. This d. c produced by the AM detector is put through an RC low-pass filter to remove the audio signal and then applied to bias the base of the IF and/or RF amplifier transistors and to control the gain of RF or IF amplifier. The time constant of the filter is kept at least 10 times longer than the period of the lowest modulation frequency received. If the time constant is kept longer, it will give better filtering, but it will cause an annoying delay in the application of the AGC control when tuning from one signal to another. The recovered signal is then passed through a coupling capacitor, Cc to remove the dc allowing the a. c component to pass. The resulting ac signal is further amplified and applied to the loud speaker.
[Figure 4.7:Circuit diagram of a simple AGC]
Delayed AGC Delayed AGC is used in most of the better communications receivers. This circuit is shown in figure 4.8 (a). Delay AGC circuit improves upon the simple AGC. In simple AGC circuit, the unwanted weak signals (noise signals) are amplified with high gain, but this shortcoming is corrected by the principle of operation of the
delayed AGC circuit. To prevent this, AGC bias voltage is not applied to amplifier in the AGC circuit until signal strength has exceeded a preset threshold and increases proportionally after which AGC bias is applied as with simple AGC, but more strongly so that the maximum sensitivity of the receiver can be realized when the receiving low-level signals. The threshold may be fixed by the circuit design or may be adjustable. The threshold is usually adjusted by adjusting the voltage at the positive input of the operational amplifier so that AGC starts taking effect when the signal has risen nearly to the level that produces the receiver maximum output under maximum sensitivity conditions (that means, under full gain). A delayed AGC response characteristic is illustrated in figure 4.8 (b) together with response of simple AGC and the response when no AGC is connected to the system.
Figure 4. 9(a): Circuit diagram of a delayed AGC circuit
Figure 4. 9 (b): AGC response characteristic
Advantages of Using AGC in Communication Receivers The benefits of the AGC in the superheterodyne receiver cannot be underestimated. Without the function of AGC, a superheterodyne usefulness is seriously impaired. The following list gives some of the problems that would be encountered in the receiver without this provision: 1. Tuning the receiver would be greatly difficult. To avoid missing the weak stations, an operator of the receiver would have the volume control (in the non- AGC set) tuned way up. As it tuned to a strong station, the speaker would probably blow out whereas a weak station might not be audible. 2. The received signal from any given station is constantly changing as a result of changing weather and ionospheric conditions. The AGC allows you to listen to a station without constantly monitoring the volume control. 3. Many radio receivers are utilized under mobile condition. For instance, a standard broadcast AM car radio would be almost unusable without a good AGC to compensate for the signal variation in different locations.

4.5.3 DOUBLE-CONVERSION SUPERHETERODYNE RECEIVER

All superheterodyne receivers suffer from interferences; image interference and adjacent channel interference, but some suffer more than the other because of the frequency operation, chosen IF and interfering signal frequency. Image interference occurs only when the image is allowed to appear at the mixer input. This is the reason for using a high Q- tuned circuit or selective RF amplifier ahead of the mixer. If the selectivity of RF amplifier and the tuned circuit are good enough, the image will be rejected. If not, once an image frequency has down-converted to IF as a result of not being blocked prior to the mixer, it cannot be removed. In a situation whereby high Q- tuned circuit or selective RF amplifier could not be made to achieve the desired result, a double- conversion superheterodyne receiver can be employed as a better and sure option. Double – conversion superheterodyne receiver has two intermediate frequencies (IFs), and uses two mixers and two oscillators. The principle of its operation is that the first receiver converts the incoming signal to a relatively high IF for the purpose of eliminating or rejecting images. Then the second mixer converts that IF down to a much lower frequency where good selectivity and amplification are easier to obtain. The figure 4.9 below is the block diagram of a double-superheterodyne receiver. It shows how different frequencies are obtained. Each mixer produces the different frequencies. The first local oscillator is variable and provides the tuning for the receiver. The second local oscillator, a crystal oscillator, is fixed in frequency. Since its need is to convert only one fixed IF to a lower IF, this local oscillator does not have to be tunable.
[Figure 4.9: Double conversion Superheterodyne receiver]
The double conversion receiver allows the receiver to have good image rejection and also good adjacent channel selectivity. The image rejection is assured in the first conversion as image frequency is well outside the fixed-tuned RF amplifier bandpass. The narrow bandpass required for good adjacent channel rejection is obtained in the second intermediate frequency, which may be as low as 100 KHz. Let us assume that the receiver is tuned to receive signal of 200 MHz. The first intermediate frequency is 10.7 MHz with the bandwidth of 200 KHz and the second intermediate frequency is 465 KHz with bandwidth of 20 KHz. With these values, the image frequency of the first intermediate frequency can be given as fim = fs +2IF = 200 + 2 x 10.7 = 200 + 21.4 = 221.4 MHz This image frequency is above the bandwidth limit of 200 KHz and hence it is rejected. However, at the same time bandwidth of 200 KHz allows several 20 KHz wide adjacent channels to pass to the second mixer. The bandpass for the second intermediate frequency rejects these adjacent channels since its passband is only 20 KHz. We can also use illustration to show the stages at which the frequency conversion is done in the receiver. If an input value of the signal frequency,fs and the two local
oscillator values, fosc1 and fosc2 are known, the value of the two IFs; first and second can be determined. There are two stages to this. The first stage is to determine the difference between the input signal and the first local oscillator. The result gives the first IF.i.e IF1 =fosc1 − fs In the second stage the IF1 will now become the input signal to the second mixer. Then the second intermediate frequency IF2 can now be achieved by obtaining the difference between the second mixer’s signal (the IF1 ) and the second local oscillator’s frequency, fosc2 (i.e IF2 = fosc2 − IF1 ) Take for instance, in the diagram of the receiver in figure 4.9,the value of the incoming RF signal frequency is 2MHz to 16 MHz and that of the first (variable) local oscillator is 3.7 MHz to 17.7 MHz. At the first stage, the RF signal is mixed with the signal of the first local oscillator to produce a signal difference of 1.7 MHz been the first IF. In the second stage, the first IF is fed to the second mixer as the input signal. It then mixes with the fixed frequency of the (crystal) second local oscillator which has the value 1.9 MHz to produce a much lower IF of 0.2 MHz or 200 KHz. This is the frequency conversion process of the double superheterodyne receiver. As shown in the figure, the double conversion superheterodyne receiver has number of modifications and additional circuitry. They include Beat Frequency Oscillator (BFO) which helps in the reception of pulse-modulated RF carrier (Morse code) and squelch circuit which helps in quieting loud noise. Other added circuits are the AGC amplifier, AGC detector, tuning calibration and noise limiter.

4.5.4 SINGLE SIDE-BAND (SSB) RECEIVER

SSB receiver is a High Frequency receiver that uses double conversion technique. In this technique, two intermediate frequencies are used to get good image frequency rejection and adjacent channel selectivity. Figure 4.10 shows the block diagram of a single sideband HF receiver
[Figure 4.10: The block diagram of a single sideband HF receiver]

4.5.4.1 The Principle of Working of SSB Receiver

The RF amplifier is tuned for desired frequency, and it provides initial gain and selectivity. The desired signal received by RF amplifier is then converted into fix frequency called intermediate frequency with the help of mixer and local oscillator. The output of the mixer is amplified by first IF Amplifier. The output of the first IF amplifier is converted into second intermediate frequency, which is lower than the first intermediate frequency with the help of another combination of mixer and local oscillator. The second intermediate frequency signal is then amplified by second IF amplifier. Two SSB filters are connected at the output of second IF amplifier. The USB (upper sideband) filter passes the IF upper sideband and rejects the lower sideband. The LSB (lower side band) filter passes the IF lower sideband and rejects the upper sideband. The appropriate sideband is selected by a switch that connects the output of the desired filter to the balanced demodulator. The output of the balanced or product detector is fed to the audio amplifier. The output of the audio amplifier is controlled by the squelch circuit or quieting circuit. When carrier is not present at the input, that is, in the absence of transmission on a given channel or between stations, a sensitive receiver produces a disagreeable amount of loud noise. The squelch circuit cuts off this noise by switching off audio amplifier’s output in the absence or transmission. The amplified IF signal is rectified to provide the AGC signal for the RF and IF amplifiers and for the squelch circuit.

4.5.5 INDEPENDENT SIDE-BAND (ISB) RECEIVER

Figure 4.11 shows typical diagram of ISB receiver. This receiver has a number of very interesting features, of which the first is the fixed-frequency RF amplifier. This may be wideband, covering the entire 100 KHz to 30 MHz receiving range. The second very interesting feature is the very high first intermediate frequency of the value 40.455 MHz. such high value becomes possible by the invention of VHF crystal bandpass filters. These filters offer majorly two advantages to this receiver. One is to provide image frequency rejections much higher than previously available filter. The second is that it facilitates receiver tuning. However, it will be seen that this receiver is a double-conversion superheterodyne receiver, up to lower frequency IF stages. After this, the main differences are due to the presence of the two independent sidebands, which are separated at this point with mechanical filters.
[Figure 4.11: Typical block diagram of ISB receiver]

4.5.5.1 The Principle of Working of ISB Receiver

The first stage of the receiver is a wideband RF amplifier associated with filters which converts the entire 100 kHz to 30 MHz receiving range. The very high intermediate frequency of the first stage mixer is fed to the second mixer through VHF crystal bandpass filter and the first IF amplifier. The VHF crystal bandpass filter provides high image frequency rejection and easy tuning mechanism. The outputs of these two filters are then applied to the product detector to get two separate modulating audio signals. Since the carrier is not coming with the transmitted signal as a result of carrier suppression from the transmitter, the automatic gain control
of the receiver circuit is obtained by rectifying the part of the combined audio signal and it is used to control the gain of the RF and IF amplifiers.
The FM receiver is a more complicated and modified version of superheterodyne receiver. It uses superheterodyne principle. However, it still has some similarities with the AM receiver. The two receivers (AM and FM) have also their differences both in functions of their components and in the arrangement of their components. The figure 4.12 below shows the block diagram of the FM receiver.
[Figure 4.12: Block diagram of FM receiver]
The diagram above can be of help to see the various sections of the FM receiver and thereby understand the similarities and differences between the FM and AM receiver From the figure, the differences that are apparent are the use of the word discriminator in place of detector as in AM receiver, the addition of a de-emphasis network, and limiter and the fact that AGC may or may not be used as indicated by the dashed lines. The discriminator is a device in which amplitude variations are derived in response to frequency or phase variations. It extracts the intelligence from the high-frequency carrier and can also be called the detector, as in AM receiver. The de-emphasis network following demodulation is required to bring the high- frequency intelligence back to the proper amplitude relationship with the lower frequencies. Though it may sound surprising the fact that AGC is optional in an FM receiver, we need to recall from the AM receiver section, 4.5.2.5, that the AGC is very essential to its
satisfactory operation. But, the use of limiters in FM receivers essentially provides an AGC function. Many older FM receivers also include an Automatic Frequency Control (AFC) function. The AFC is a circuit that provides a slight automatic control over the local oscillator circuit. It compensates for drift in local oscillator frequency that would otherwise cause a station to become detuned. It was important because it had not yet been discovered how to make an economical LC oscillator at a higher frequency up to 100MHz with sufficient frequency stability. The AFC system is not needed in new design. A limiter is a circuit whose output is constant amplitude for all input above a critical value. It is a form of clipping device or circuit whose output tends to remain constant despite changes in the input signals. Its function in an FM receiver is to remove any unwanted amplitude modulation and amplitude variation due to noise both of these variations would have an undesirable effect if carried through the speaker. In addition, the limiting function also provides AGC action because signals from the critical minimum value up to some maximum value provide a constant input level to the detector. In addition to the difference in the components circuit of FM receiver to that of AM receiver, the FM receivers equally have differences in their functions. Generally, FM receivers have much higher operating frequencies. There is need for limiting and de- emphasis in FM. The demodulation methods are totally different and there is difference in the method of obtaining AGC. 4.6.1 VARIOUS STAGES OF THE FM RECEIVER
RF amplifier stages: Since FM signal has a large bandwidth, it is likely to encounter more noise. For this reason, the RF amplifier is always with the main purpose of reducing the noise figure, which could otherwise be a problem because of the large bandwidth needed for FM. In addition to this function, it is also required to match the input impedance of the receiver to that of the antenna. To meet the requirement of the impedance-matching function, grounded-base or grounded-gate circuits are employed for this stage. Both of these circuits have low input impedance, suitable for matching with antenna impedance and neither circuit requires neutralization. This is because the input electrode is grounded on either type of amplifier, effectively isolating input from output for RF purpose. A typical FET grounded-gate RF amplifier is shown in figure 4.13. The circuit has no possibility of feedback and thereby instability in operation. In addition to all the mentioned good properties of the circuit, it has the features of low distortion and simple operation.
Figure4.13:FET grounded-gate RF amplifier
Oscillator and mixer stage: At the mixer stage, with the help of the local oscillator, the incoming signal is down-converted to IF which is 10.7 MHz for FM receiver. The local oscillator is usually the Clapp or Colpitts oscillator which is very suitable for VHF operation. Maintaining a constant different between the carrier frequency and local oscillator frequency (tracking) is not a problem in FM receiver unlike in an AM receiver. This is because the tuning frequency range is only 1.25:1 in FM receiver which is from 88 MHz to 108 MHz tuning range, a ratio far less than what is obtainable in the AM broadcasting. The arrangement at the front end of an FM receiver consists of FET for the RF amplifier and mixer, with local oscillator constructed with bipolar junction transistor. This is done with the consideration that FETs are less noisy than the BJTs. The mixer stage uses a tuned circuit as its load. The circuit is tuned to Intermediate Frequency of 10.7 MHz and hence selects the difference between incoming carrier frequency and locally generated oscillator frequency. Intermediate Frequency (IF) amplifier stage: The most of the gain of receiver is developed in the IF amplifier stage. We need to note that the type and operation of the IF amplifier stage in FM receiver do not vary much from that of AM receiver. However, it is worth noting that the intermediate frequency and bandwidth requirement in the FM receiver are far higher than in AM receiver. Typical figure for FM receivers operating in the 88-to-108 MHz band are an IF of 10.7 MHz and a bandwidth of 200 KHz. Two IF amplifier stages are often provided to compensate for a low gain per stage being the consequence of the large bandwidth. However, while designing these stages, shrinkage of bandwidth due to cascading must be taken into account.
Limiter stage: This stage contains the (limiter) circuit that its precise function is to remove the amplitude variation of the signal. In the FM receiver, it precedes the demodulator so as to block the spurious amplitude changes in the signal that is fed to the demodulator if signal distortion must be avoided. Frequency modulation is developed to provide a communication system which is less noise-sensitive than AM system. The most of the noise accompanying the desired signal accompanies it as AM signal. Thus, if the intelligence is contained in the frequency variation of signal; we can at the receiver, remove all amplitude variation without loss of the information content of the desired signal. This is the function performed by the limiter. At the output of the limiter stage, we get a constant amplitude signal, even though the amplitude of input signal may be varying. The limiter is thus basically a clipper circuit which clips off the undesired amplitude variations of the input signals, as shown in figure 4.14 (a). The input signal provides the bias for the FET circuit. Negative bias increases as input increases and hence it lowers the gain of the amplifier for high amplitude of the input signal and output voltage tends to remain constant. The basic function of the limiter is squaring off (flat topping) the upper and lower extremities of the signal. This is illustrated in figure 4.14 (b).
[Figure 4.14(a): Amplitude limiter]
Figure 4.14(b): Amplitude limiter transfer characteristics Although the signal is distorted, it makes no difference as far as FM is considered, since the information is contained in frequency variation and not in amplitude variation. A typical limiter response characteristic of the limiter is shown in the figure 4.15
[Figure 4.15: Typical limiter response]
It has been shown that the range of input voltages over which the amplitude limiter will operate satisfactorily is itself limited. The limits are the threshold point at one end and the reduced angle of output current at the other end. In a typical practical limiter, the input voltage B may correspond to 0.4 V, and D may correspond to 4 V. the output may be about 5 V for both values and all voltages in between (note that all these voltages are peak-to-peak values). The practical limiter will therefore be fed with a voltage which is normally in the middle of this range, that is, 2.2 V peak-to-peak or approximately 0.8Vr.m.s . It will thus have a possible range of variation of 1.8 V (peak-
to-peak) within which limiting will take place. This means that any spurious amplitude variation must be quite large compared to the signal to escape being limited. Further limiting and double limiter: It is very possible for the limiter described to be insufficient to its task, because signal-strength variations may easily take the average signal amplitude outside the limiting range. As a result, further limiting is required in practical FM receiver. When two limiters are cascaded to bring further limiting in the FM receiver, it is described as double limiter. This arrangement gives satisfactory limiting range.
Automatic gain control: AGC is a suitable alternative to the second limiter. This ensures that the signal fed to the limiter input is within the range of the limiter, regardless of the input signal strength, by reducing the gain for higher signal strength. It also prevents the over loading of the last IF amplifier stage. Both FM and AM receivers employ superheterodyne principle. However, the following are the points of differences between the two types of receivers: 1. The FM receiver is more complicated and, therefore, more expensive than the normal AM receiver. 2. FM receiver has some additional stages which are quite different from AM receiver, such as limiter, discriminator etc 3. FM receivers are free from interference and this means that much weaker signal can be successfully handled unlike in AM receiver. 4. The IF or FM receiver is 10.7 MHz whereas IF for AM is 455 KHz. 5. FM broadcast signals lie in the frequency range between 88 MHz and 108MHz whereas AM broadcast signals lie in the frequency range from 540 KHz to 1600 KHz.
Most electronic communication is a two way, and so two parties communicating have both a transmitter and a receiver. As a result, most communication equipment incorporates circuits that both send and receive signals. These units are commonly referred to as transceivers. Transceiver therefore, can be described as a device that combines a transmitter and a receiver in a single package for simultaneous transmission and reception of communication signal. Modern transceivers are based on superheterodyne architecture. Transceivers are at the core of most modern communications technology and are built into almost every communication device from satellites to electronic keys for expensive automobiles that won't start unless the code transmission in the key housing is validated by the computer built into the car's
ignition system. Even the radio frequency identification (RFID) chips built into some consumer product packaging to prevent theft and certain credit cards, contain transceivers for decoding, along with transponders to continuously send out information on the card or passport for scanners to read.
In the transceiver, all the transmitter and receiver circuits are packaged within a single housing and usually share some common circuits such as power supply. Transceiver devices vary in appearances (aesthetics), radio bands, and operating settings. But, despite the differences in models and settings, basic operating principles remain the same. Some examples of communication devices that employ transceiver circuits are, telephone, fax machines, handheld citizen band (CB) radios, cellular telephones, and computer modems. Transceivers provide many advantages. In addition to having a common housing and power supply, the transmitter and receivers can share circuits, thereby achieving cost saving and, in some cases, smaller size. Some of the circuits in the transceiver that can perform a dual function are antennas, oscillators, frequency synthesizers, power supplies, tuned circuits, filters and various kinds of amplifiers. There are various ways in which transceiver can be classified; classification based on the range of frequency of operation, classification based on nature of modulated signal transmission and classification base on mode of signal transmission.
4.7.1 CLASSIFICATION OF TRANSCEIVER BASED ON THE OPERATING FREQUENCY RANGE
Based on the operating radio frequency range, transceivers can be classified asvery high frequency (VHF) transceivers and Ultra-High Frequency (UHF) transceiver.

4.7.1.1 VHF Transceiver

A VHF transceiver operates between 30 MHz to 300 MHz. The wavelength of a VHF transceiver varies between 1 m to 10m mainly depending on the frequency used. To increase transmission reliability of VHF transceiver, HF and UHF bands are often included in the device. VHF transceiver devices are used in personal and business use. For businesses such as taxi cabs and other transportation industries, base station repeaters are used to extend a VHF device's communication range.

4.7.1.2 UHF Transceiver

An UHF transceiver is a device which usually houses a transmitter and receiver operating between the radio wave frequencies of 300 MHz to 3 GHz. Depending on the frequency used, the corresponding wavelength of a transceiver using a UHF band ranges between 10cm to 1m. Due to the relatively short wavelength, UHF transceivers devices such as walkie-talkies and citizen band (CB) radios are limited to a radius of several miles. The actual operating distance of the devices will largely depend on several factors including environmental topography, use of repeaters and antenna height. A UHF transceiver relies on line-of-sight radio propagation, which means, the devices communicate with one another in a direct path, Physical objects such as trees and buildings will often weaken or even block line-of-sight propagation, decreasing communication reliability of the transceiver devices. To increase reliability, UHF transceivers bands and multi-band transceivers such as walkie-talkies and CB radios are used for short range communications between two or more parties. Walkie-talkies and CB radios are used by a variety of sectors including public, commercial and military. In many commercial and military settings, base station repeaters are utilized to extend a UHF transceiver operating range.
4.7.2 CLASSIFICATION OF TRANSCEIVER BASED ON MODULATED SIGNAL TRANSMISSION
In this category, transceiver can be classified as FM transceiver and SSB transceiver.

4.7.2.1 FM Transceiver

The FM transceivers are types of radio transceivers that are capable of receiving and transmitting frequency modulated (FM) signal in form of voice communications, music, or any other type of audio transmission. Equipment of this type ensures the signal is within a certain band range and can be easily picked up by other transceivers that are structured to receive and send FM signals. This device differs with an FM transmitter. Unlike an FM transmitter, which can only send signals on the FM receiver that is capable of receiving the frequency
modulation broadcast, the FM transceiver is configured for both transmission and reception of signals within a certain bandwidth. FM transceiver find applications in basic communication equipment used by individuals and in sophisticated communication equipment used in the military, air traffic control and other organizations in various parts of the world. Common example of the FM transceiver is a 2 meter radio called FM meter transceiver.
FM Meter Transceiver An FM meter transceiver is basically a two-way radio capable of both receiving and transmitting. This is 2 meter radio. A basic 2 meter radio makes use of the amateur radio band in the VHF- spectrum and uses frequencies from 144MHz to 148 MHz. Since 2 meter transceivers use the VHF frequencies, height is a considerable factor on how far away it is possible to communicate clearly. To get the necessary height, repeaters are used and are located in skyscraper tops in cities or mountain range tops in country sides. Repeaters are meter transceivers that pick up 2 signals from a 2 meter transceiver and retransmit the received signal on their antenna at the same time as received and allow a 2 meter to transmit a long distance. If the repeater is high enough, reception is good for round 100 miles, though the usual repeater rate is for somewhere between 30 to 40 miles’ distance. A typical FM meter transceiver setup would have a 50 watt set and rooftop vertical antenna for transmission to the local repeaters.

4.7.2.2 SSB Transceiver

Figure 4.16 is a general block diagram of a high-frequency transceiver capable of SSB operation. The block diagram also explains the principle of operation of the transceiver. Both the receiver and the transmitter as shown in the block diagram, make use of heterodyning techniques for generating IF and final transmission frequencies, and proper selection of these intermediate frequencies allows the transmitter and receiver to share local oscillators. As shown in the figure, local oscillator 1 is the beat frequency oscillator (BFO) for the receiver product detector and the carrier for the balanced modulator for producing DSB. Later, crystal local oscillator 2 drives the second mixer in the receiver and the first transmitter mixer used for up conversion. Local oscillator 3 supplies the receiver first mixer and the second transmitter mixer.
In transmission mode, the crystal filter (another shared circuit) provides sideband selection after the balanced modulator. In the receiver mode, the filter provides sideband selection after the modulator. In the receive mode, the filter provides selectivity for the IF section of the receiver. Tuned circuits may be shared. A tuned circuit can be the tuned input for the receiver or the tuned output for the transmitter. Circuit switching may be manual, but is often done using relays or diode electronic switches. In most newer designs, the transmitter and receiver share a frequency synthesizer.
[Figure 4.16: Block diagram of a HF SSB Transceiver]
4.7.3 CLASSIFICATION             OF     TRANSCEIVER              BASED   ON   MODE   OF COMMUNICATION
In this classification, consideration is made on how the communication goes, whether there is a provision for circuits, transmitter and receiver, to interact simultaneously without interruption or interact one after the other.

4.7.3.1 Half-duplex Transceiver

Half-duplex transceivers use the principle of half-duplex transmission mode. In a transceiver of this type, transmission and reception often, but not always, are done on the same frequency. An electronic switch allows the transmitter and receiver to be connected to the same antenna, and prevents the transmitter’s output from damaging the receiver. While the transmitter is transmitting signal, the receiver is silenced. With a transceiver of this kind, it is impossible to receive signals while transmitting. This transmission mode is called half duplex.

4.7.3.2 Full-duplex Transceiver

These types of transceivers use full duplex communication mode. They are designed to allow reception of signals during transmission periods, and require that the transmitter and receiver operate on substantially different frequencies so the transmitted signals do not interfere with signal reception. Cellular and cordless telephone sets use transceiver that operates in th is mode. Satellite communications network often employ full-duplex transceivers at the surface-based subscriber points. In the case of the satellite full-duplex transceiver, transmitted signal (transceiver-to-satellite) is called the uplink, and the received signal (satellite-to-transceiver) is called the downlink.

TV               is an abbreviation of          5.6 BASIC TERMS AND TECHNIQUES the word ‘television’.        IN THE STUDY OF TV
It is a combination of two words                           “tele” and “vision”. ‘Tele’ is a Greek word which              stands for long distance while vision means to see. Therefore, television can be described as an electronic device through which events occurring at a physical far distance from an observer can be seen through electronic means. TV serves as one of the major electronic media of information exchange through which sound and pictures (moving pictures) are transmitted simultaneously majorly in broadcasting manner. TV system finds applications in various communication system such as satellite information analysis, video processing and monitoring of events (such as in CCTV), display of information, display device with computer and so on. All the mentioned applications use TV with slight modifications.
5.2 BASIC TELEVISION PRINCIPLES The basic principles involved in TV system is to convert ‘sound’ and ‘picture’ into an electric signal by modulation process, transmit the modulated signal through
appropriate electronic communication channels in form of electromagnetic wave and reproduce the picture and sound at the receiver by suitable demodulation processes. These processes require microphone, video (TV) camera, transmitters, transmitting antenna and some other devices at the transmitting end. The microphone is used as the input transducer for sound, the video camera serves as the input transducer for picture, and the TV transmitter is used for the modulation of the TV signal and antenna is used for the radiation of the modulated signal for transmission through the right medium. At the receiving end, the TV receiving antenna attracts the TV signal as electromagnetic wave in the range of micro-volts and transfers it to the TV receiver through a coupling network. The TV receiver is a special super-heterodyne receiver that recovers both the sound and picture information. It receives and demodulates the signals, separating them into the original picture and sound. The picture tube and screen display the picture while the speaker reproduces the original sound.
5.3 TELEVISION SIGNALS We have seen that picture and sound signals are to be transmitted from TV transmitting station simultaneously and received in TV receiver simultaneously. To transmit the signals (information, sound and picture) requires that they should be converted to electric analogue signals; video signal and sound signal.

5.3.1 VIDEO SIGNAL

The video signal carries the picture information to be transmitted. The information is obtained from the camera tube by scanning beams. Nevertheless, the video signal is a composite of other signals in addition to the picture information. Examples of such signals include; vertical and horizontal synchronization pulses, pre- and post- equalizing pulses, colour burst, and blanking pulses. 5.3.1.1 Amplitude Modulation of Video Signal
The video signal transmission uses Amplitude Modulation. Using this method, the video signal amplitude modulates the picture or video carrier signal. This type of the TV video signal can be achieved into different ways; positive amplitude modulation and negative amplitude modulation.
Positive AM modulation Generally, the amplitude of the carrier increases with increase in amplitude of the signals and vice versa. This is called positive amplitude modulation. In this type of AM modulation, when used in TV system, as the intensity of the picture increases, the amplitude of the modulated envelope increases. Figure 5.1 is the wave form of the positive amplitude modulation. In the waveform shown by the figure, we observe that the sync tip of the video signal lies at zero volts. This means the video signal appears to be converted in amplitude. When noise occurs in the system, it tends to increase the amplitude of the modulated signal (by adding its amplitude on the amplitude of the video signal). This overall increase causes bright blobs (spots) on the screen of TV. Suffice it to say that the major challenge of this amplitude modulation pattern is greater noise interference.
[Figure 5.1: Positive AM modulation]
Negative amplitude modulation In negative amplitude modulation, the instantaneous amplitude of the carrier decreases with increase in instantaneous amplitude of the signal. Using this modulation in TV system has the effect that as the intensity of the picture increases, the amplitude of the modulated envelope decreases. Figure 5.2 shows the waveform of negative amplitude modulation. Observe from the figure that the sync tip lies at the maximum amplitude. And as the intensity increases, the amplitude of the modulated carrier decreases. The resulting modulated signal has white levels at the lower side, black level at the higher side. So, whenever noise occurs due to increase in amplitude, the level goes towards
less brightness level, that is, gray or black colour. Thus the effect of noise interference is minimized in the transmission using this method.
[Figure 5.2: Negative amplitude modulation]
5.3.1.2 Advantages of Negative Amplitude Modulation over Positive Amplitude Modulation in TV System
1. There is a reduction in noise interference: In positive modulation, the effect of RF noise spikes produces white dot on the TV screen. But in negative amplitude modulation, the RF spikes produce black dots on the screen. Actually, fully black means electron beam is cut off. This means no effect on the picture tube screen if spike amplitude is above blanking level. Therefore, the interference of noise is less effective when negative modulation is used. i.e the RF noise will not cause adverse effect on the picture. 2. Greater peak transmitter power is possible: In the case of negative amplitude modulation, transmitter can be over modulated. This is because, the over modulation can take place only when sync pulses do not affect their shape significantly. On the contrary, in the case of positive modulation, over modulation of carrier is not permissible. This is because the non-linear distortion introduced due to over modulation will affect the high intensity area of the picture. 3. AGC circuit of the transmitter will have stable level of reference: AGC is simple in the case of negative amplitude modulation. The sync pulses are always at the peak level (100% modulation) of the modulated envelope. The AGC circuits use these sync pulses as the reference voltage. But in positive amplitude modulation, the sync pulses are at zero level in modulated envelope.
Hence, sync pulses cannot be used directly as a reference for AGC. Also, the peak amplitude of the modulated signals varies continuously depending upon brightness levels of the picture. Hence, such level is not suitable for AGC. This AGC is difficult in case of positive amplitude modulation.

5.3.2 SOUND SIGNAL

The sound signal is an audio frequency signal with bandwidth of about 50 Hz to 15 KHz. It can be converted to an electric signal with help of microphone at transmitter system. The sound signal is then amplified, filtered and modulated on some carrier for long distance transmission. In TV system the type of modulation use to impress the sound signal on the carrier is frequency modulation but the maximum permitted frequency deviation is 25 KHz, considerably less than the deviation permitted by conventional FM broadcasting. Consequently, a TV sound signal takes somewhat less bandwidth in the TV (signal) spectrum than a standard FM broadcast station. Thus the
bandwidth requirement of FM sound signal is very small compared to total channel bandwidth. Thus the FM sound signal does not increase the transmission channel bandwidth by significant amount. Also compared to the cost of TV transmission equipment, the increase in cost of transmission due to FM sound signal is insignificant. Hence FM sound transmission is widely used in TV transmission. 5.3.2.1 Advantages of Transmitting Sound Signal in FM Mode Using frequency modulation method for sound transmission in television system has the following advantages among others; 1. It gives quality sound 2. The effect of noise interference is minimized since the amplitude of the modulated carrier remains constant. The noise can be easily removed by amplitude limiter at receiver. 3. The transmission efficiency is better. This is because amplitude is independent of depth of modulation. Hence low level modulation can be used in FM and all succeeding amplifiers can be class C which are more efficient. Thus amplifiers in FM transmitter handle constant power. 4. The effect of adjacent channels interference is minimal. This is because guard band is provided between two adjacent channels. 5. Co-channel interference effect is minimal in FM. The co-channel interference means signal from some other transmitting situation which is operating at same carrier frequency. These signals are relatively weak in amplitude, but tend to interfere with the signals of interest. The limiter in FM receiver removes these interfering signals and this reduces co-channel interference.

5.3.3 VESTIGIAL SIDEBAND TRANSMISSION OF TELEVISION SIGNAL

Using FM signal for sound transmission and AM signal for video signal transmission in TV system is not a matter of accident or haphazard choice. Each method is a deliberate choice made to achieve a desired effect and each guarantees the suitability for the transmission. FM modulation minimizes noise. Therefore, it is suitable for sound transmission so as to give immunity to the noise during the sound transmission. However, the challenge for which it is then not suitable for video transmission is because it contains large number of sidebands. With the large number of the sidebands, there will be an increased channel bandwidth if the FM is used for the
picture or video transmission and the increased channel bandwidth is not affordable since the channel transmitted in the particular frequency band may reduce. For this reason, FM is not used for video or picture transmission instead, the AM transmission is used. Using AM signal for the transmission does not automatically conquer the problems of large bandwidth. Again, signal distortion can as well occur with this method. When placing these two challenges into consideration, a suitable type of AM modulation has to be chosen so as to achieve a lesser bandwidth and undistorted picture during the TV signal transmission. This informed the choice of using vestigial sideband (VSB) signal transmission. The vestigial sideband is a type of AM techniques in which one complete sideband (upper or lower) and a fraction of the other sideband (upper or lower) are used for transmitting signal. Therefore, in television system, vestigial sideband transmission can be described as the type of transmission in which the TV signals are transmitted with a complete (upper) sideband and small portion of the other (lower) sideband. Figure 5.3 shows the spectrum of broadcast TV signal channel (bandwidth) using vestigial sideband transmission.
[Figure 5.3: Vestigial sideband broadcast TV signal channel spectrum.]
The use of vestigial sideband signal transmission is not without a reason. The reason why this type of AM signal is used instead of the other types of the Amplitude Modulation techniques is because; the vestigial transmission helps in solving some major issues which could arise if Double Side Band-Suppressed Carrier (DSB-SC) transmission or Single Side Band-Suppressed Carrier (SSB-SC) transmission is used. These problems are issue of excessive band requirement and issue of distortion of signal.
The issue of excessive bandwidth requirement comes up with DSB transmission while issue of signal distortion is associated with SSB transmission. Owing to these facts, VSB is the only type of AM TV transmission that can be to solve both problems. The spectrum of amplitude modulated signal consists of lower sideband, upper sideband and carrier. If the video/picture signal is to be transmitted using both upper and lower sideband (of DSB), the minimum requirement of channel bandwidth, as shown described by figure 5.4 will be 11.25MHz. This is as a result of the following, which add up to the total channel bandwidth; Upper sideband = 5MHz Lower sideband = 5MHz Roll off characteristic of filters on both sides = 1MHz (0.5MHz each). This roll off is added to accommodate for filters roll off characteristics in receiver Guard band = 0.25MHz. This is added to separate the video signal from sound signal so that over lapping of the two signals will not occur.
[Figure 5.4: Channel bandwidth of DSB transmission]
Thus, with the total bandwidth of 11.25MHz, it is obvious that a large bandwidth is required if double sideband transmission is to be used for the transmission. The consequence is that the number of channels that can be transmitted in a particular band will be (greatly) reduced. To solve this problem, we shall target at reducing the bandwidth of the signal. Out of the three types of the AM (techniques); DSB, SSB and VSB, the only one that can reduce the channel bandwidth to good extent is SSB but it cannot solve the problem of distorted signal. With SSB, only the upper (or lower) sideband is transmitted. Figure 5.5 shows the channel spectrum of SSB.
[Figure 5.5: Channel spectrum of SSB]
As shown in the figure 5.5, the spectrum will have some roll off effect on both sides of the sideband. On the higher side of the frequency we have allotted 0.5MHz extra to accommodate roll-off characteristics of filter. But on the lower side of frequencies, we cannot do so because the sidebands start from picture carrier of 0 Hz itself. Thus the roll-off cannot be accommodated in lower sideband which is suppressed. Hence, lower frequencies of the upper sideband are attenuated because of roll-off characteristics of filter. The same problem will arise if only lower sideband is to be transmitted. This shows that it is not possible to suppress one sideband completely using physically realizable filters. And if SSB transmission is used, then, as shown in figure 5.5, the low frequency details of the picture will be lost and there will be serious distortion in the reproduced picture. We have seen that SSB transmission is not possible since one sideband cannot be suppressed fully by physically realized filters. Therefore, some part of the lower sideband is to be retained to be used to accommodate roll off characteristics of filters. This prevents the attenuation of low frequencies near picture carrier. The method of using a portion of the lower side and a complete upper side band for the transmission is called vestigial side band (VSB) transmission.
[Figure 5.6: Channel bandwidth of a TV signal with vestigial sideband transmission]
Figure 5.6 shows the channel bandwidth of a TV signal with vestigial sideband transmission. As shown in the figure, a full upper sideband picture carrier to 5MHz is transmitted. The sound inter-carrier is placed at 5.5 MHz from picture carrier. A guard band of 0.25MHz is also provided. The frequencies of lower sideband up to 0.75MHz are not suppressed. Thus the frequencies up to 0.75MHz are present in both sidebands. This means low frequencies are transmitted in both sidebands. Since the outputs due to both sidebands are added at the receiver, the frequencies up to 0.75MHz will have double output (amplitude) at the receiver compared to remaining frequencies. Therefore, vestigial sideband correction is required at the receiver to cut these low frequencies to the required level. As shown in the figure, a 0.5MHz of lower sideband is also given (after 0.75MHz) to accommodate the roll off characteristics of filters. Thus the frequencies from 0.75MHz to 1.25MHz in lower sideband will have decay according to roll off characteristics of filters. The total bandwidth on this system is 7MHz which consist of: Complete upper sideband = 5MHz Fraction of lower sideband = 0.75MHz Roll off of USB = 0.5MHz Roll off of LSB = 0.5MHz Guard band = 0.25MHz
Comparing this bandwidth (7MHz) with that of DSB, which is 11.25MHz, it is clear that a total of 4.25MHz bandwidth is saved with VSB. Hence vestigial sideband transmission is used for TV signal transmission. It offers the advantages of using a lesser bandwidth which accommodates many channels in the transmission band and it enhances undistorted pictures at the receiver.

5.3.4 TV SIGNAL BANDWIDTH

The TV signal bandwidth varies according to the two major TV standards. The composite TV signal for America TV system is about 6 MHz while that of Europe is about 7 MHz.

5.4 TELEVISION BROADCASTING

The term ‘broadcasting’ in electronic communication means to send out radio wave that carries information signals in all direction. For commercial television broadcasting, the TV signal is sent from the transmitting station via a transmitting antenna, in all direction in form of Radio Frequency radiation. This radiation is a combination of two Radio Frequency carrier waves modulated by desired information in sound and video signals. Amplitude Modulation (AM) is used for the video signal modulation while frequency modulation is used for the sound modulation. The modulated signals are broadcasted from the transmitting station and they are picked up by receiving antenna of any destination tuned to the particular frequency of the transmitted TV signal. Four processes are involved in TV signal transmission and reception system. These processes are TV signal generation, and signal transmission which takes place at the transmitting station and signal reception and signal demodulation which occur at the receiving end. TV signals are generated in the TV transmitter by modulation circuits after which they are transmitted in radiated or broadcasted form via a transmitting antenna. At the receiver, the signals are intercepted by a receiving antenna and send to the TV receiver for proper demodulation and recovery of the original signal.

5.5 TV SIGNAL TRANSMISSION AND RECEPTION

Transmission and reception in TV system involve the components of a television system that generate, transmit, and utilize the television signal.
[Figure 5.7: TV signal transmission-reception system]
Figure 5.7 shows a simplified block diagram of the TV signal transmission-reception system. From the figure, the system has two ends; transmitting system and receiving system, each comprising of different devices that perform particular functions.

5.5.1 THE TV TRANSMITTING SYSTEM

From the figure 5.7, the transmitting end of the TV system is made up of the TV camera, AM transmitter, microphone, FM transmitter, diplexer and the transmitting antenna. TV camera In the TV camera, the scene to be televised is focused by a lens on an image sensor located within the TV camera. This produces the picture or video signal. The camera picks up the picture or video signals, scans it and converts the scanned signal into electrical signals, which is fed to the AM transmitter.
The AM transmitter The AM transmitter of the TV does mainly two functions; the modulation of the carrier signal with the video signal and generation of synchronization signal and blanking pulse. The synchronization signal is used for transmitter-receiver synchronization. Then the synchronization and blanking pulses are added to the modulated signals, establishing the complete composite video wave form. The microphone It serves as sound input transducer that converts the sound signal into equivalent electrical signal for input into FM transmitter for the sound modulation process. The FM transmitter In the FM transmitter, the modulation of sound signals ready to be fed to the antenna for transmission via the diplexer occurs. Diplexer The diplexer is a set of sharp band filters device in TV transmitting system that allows both the video AM signal and the audio FM signal to feed the same antenna. It feeds both the video and sound signals to the antenna while not allowing either to be fed back into the other transmitter Transmitting antenna The transmitting antenna converts the TV signals (combination of sound and video modulated signals) into electromagnetic energy required for transmission and radiates same to the space. 5.5.2 THE TV RECEIVING SYSTEM
At the receiving end, the TV signals are translated back into a corresponding sequence of lights and shadows, and sound by detection process. The TV receiving system contains the receiving antenna, the receiver; AM receiver and FM receiver, the picture tube and the loud speaker.
Receiving antenna
The first call in the TV reception process is the TV receiving antenna. The antenna collects the transmitted TV signal (the sound and picture carrier waves) in form of modulated electromagnetic wave of a very low voltage Radio Frequency which produces on it the currents that are identical in form to those flowing in the transmitting antenna but much weaker than it. The received RF signals generates (induces) some currents and voltages on the antenna. The signal is conducted to a booster (usually attached to a Yagi-Uda antenna) which does further processing (signal amplification and removing of some noise) on the signal before sending it to the TV receiver circuits by a lead-in transmission line.
A good TV receiving antenna, in addition to signal reception attenuates the interferences coming with the signals such as interference due to adjacent channels, signal reflection, switching etc. It should as well have sufficient wideband so that it can be used for reception of good number of channels. Finally, it should be able to withstand adverse effect of the environment like temperature, wind raining, dust and others.
The receiver
The detection of the TV signals occurs at the receiver. The entire receiver system is made up of the AM receiver and FM receiver. While the AM receiver detects the in- coming picture or video signal, the FM receiver demodulates the in-coming sound signal.
Picture tube
The picture tube is the device on to which the AM receiver channels the demodulated video signal for display on the TV screen.
Loud speaker
This is the output transducer for the TV sound signal. Here, the detected sound signal is amplified and gives out in audible manner and in such a way that it is synchronized with the picture on TV screen.
5.6 BASIC TERMS AND TECHNIQUES IN THE STUDY OF TV SYSTEM There are basic terms and techniques use in the general study of television system. Some of them are treated in this session and will be seen throughout the books.
5.6.1. PICTURE ELEMENTS
The idea of picture element is likened to a draft board of two colours; black and white. The draft board is formed by many squares bounded by horizontal and vertical lines. The squares are analogous to picture elements while the area of the board is analogous to the TV screen. The picture element which is called the pixels serves as the smallest element of a picture upon which the visual information of a scene or picture depends. The resolution or details or picture quality of a scene depends on it. As the number of the pixel’s increases, the picture quality becomes better. The idea of what a picture element is can be better understood by taking a closer look at a picture printed in a newspaper. When a picture is printed on a photoengraving, there are many small black printed dots which form the image. If you can observe a photo on a newspaper closely, you can see that the printed picture is composed of small elementary areas of black and white. On examining very closely, the dots will be seen because the picture elements are relatively large. Each small area or shade is a picture element or picture detail. All the elements contain the visual information in the scene. If they are transmitted and reproduced in the same degree of light or shade as the original and in proper position, the picture will be reproduced.

5.6.2 PICTURE DEFINITION

Picture definition is determined by the pixel. For good picture definition, the TV screen will have close to 150,000 pixels. The number of pixels which a screen has is determined by the number of scan lines of the screen. This is because, the time to scan each line reduces when the scan line increases, thereby leading to increase in bandwidth. High bandwidth leads to high picture definition. Suffice it to say that the quality of the picture definition which is also refer as picture resolution or picture detail depends on the number of picture elements that can be reproduced. With many small picture elements, the fine detail of the image is evident. Therefore, as many picture elements as possible should be reproduced to have a picture with good definition. This technique makes the picture clearer. Small details can be seen, and objects in the image are outlined sharply. Good picture definition also gives apparent depth to the picture by bringing in details of the background.
Good picture definition is determined by the quality scanning of the picture elements across the horizontal and vertical viewing dimension of the TV camera or picture tube. Figure 5.8 is a checkerboard pattern of alternating black and white pixels and screen parameter definition.

5.6.3 ASPECT RATIO

In order to incorporate the horizontal motion that predominates in virtually all televise events, the width of the TV screen rectangle is greater than its height. The ratio of the width to the height of the picture frame is defined as the aspect ratio which is mathematically expressed as, Horizontal dimension (width) Aspect ratio= Vertical dimension (height)
It also expresses the picture shape. The standard value chosen for aspect ratio is 4:3 in standard definition television (SDTV), while in high definition television (HDTV), the aspect ratio is 16: 9. Nevertheless, the HDTV aspect ratio is just an increase from the SDTV by multiplying the ratio by itself. It should be noted that the aspect ratio just sets proportions. The actual frame of the TV set can be any size from a few square inches to 20 x 15 ft as long as the correct aspect ratio of 4:3 or the multiple is maintained. If the picture tube does not reproduce the picture with this proportion of width to height, object in the scene look too thin or too wide. Therefore, on the picture tube rectangular screen of 4:3 width to height, the reproduced picture has correct aspect ratio when the horizontal scanning amplitude just fills the width of the TV screen and the vertical scanning just fills the height.

5.6.4 VIEWING DISTANCE

The size of the picture tube and the distance of the viewer from the screen affect the apparent resolution seen by the viewer. Close to the screen of the TV, we see all the details. However, the individual scanning lines are visible. Also, we may see the fine grain of the picture reproduction. In television, the grain consists of small white speckles called snow produced by noise in the video signal. The best viewing distance is compromise therefore, about 4 to 8 times the picture height. SDTV is designed on the assumption that the viewers in the typical home setting are located at a distance equal to 6 or 7 times the height of the picture screen- on average some 3 meters (10 ft) away. Even HDTV assumes a viewer who is seated no closer than three times the picture height away.
To illustrate this, suppose we have an SDTV system feeding a receiver with a 48.25 cm (19-in) diagonal picture. If the viewer is seated about 2.3 m (7 ft) from the screen, he or she will not see any details of the scan lines on the screen. However, if the viewer moves closer, he or she will see some of the line details. If the viewer moves farther from the screen, he or she will have sensation of improved definition, although the picture will appear to be smaller because it is farther away. Again if the viewer sits at 2.3 m (7 ft) from a 76 cm (30-in) diagonal screen, he or she will again see line details, so for a good picture the viewer must move farther from the screen. Alternatively, if the system were changed to “high definition” so that the pixel densities available were higher, then the viewer could move closer or could use a large screen without degradation of the picture. The limit of definition for human eye is such that it can discern an object that is large enough and close enough to subtend a viewing angle of about 1 minute of arc. Again, a viewer will have a feeling of “in the picture” if the picture width subtends an angle greater than 30° From the foregoing discussion, it obvious that screen dimension, viewing distance and viewing angle are related.
