5.6.5 SCANNING IN TV SYSTEM

Scanning is a technique in TV system in which a rectangular scene is divided up into individual lines. This process takes place in TV video camera during video signal generation and modulation and at the picture tube of the TV receiver. At the transmitter, scanning occurs when the TV video camera focuses an object on its pickup device which can be the photosensitive cells in the camera tube or an imaging charge couple device (CCD). The variable light on the video image pick-up devices (sensors) results in a similar variable voltage being developed at the sensor’s output. As a result, the visual scene has been converted to a video (electrical) signal and can now be suitably amplified and used to amplitude-modulate a carrier for the TV broadcast. Scanning also occurs at the picture tube during the TV signal reception to display the original picture picked from the transmitting end. In the video camera tube and picture tube, the scanning process involves the movement of electron beams from the end of one line to the start of the next line.
5.6.5.1 Electron Beam Movement in TV Tubes During Scanning The movement of the electron beam during scanning is from left to right and then back to the left (horizontal scanning) or from the top to bottom and then back to the top (vertical scanning). In either case, the movement of the scan beam is such that when the beam reaches its destination, the right corner end or the bottom, from the starting point, it breaks it “journey” and returns back to its original position, getting ready for the next movement. The first movement from its original position is called trace and when it breaks its movement at the destination, to begin afresh from the original position, we describe it as retrace or fly-back. Therefore, the total movement of the scan beam during the scanning process is a trace-and-retrace (trace + retrace) movement. The sequence of the scanning is that the electron beam sweeps across the horizontal line, covering all the picture elements in that line. At the end of each line, the beam is retraced very quickly to the left side in a fly back mode to begin scanning the next horizontal line. No picture information is scanned during the retrace because both the camera tube and picture tube are blanked out at this period. Therefore, the retrace must be very rapid since they are wasted time in terms of picture information. Whenever the beam is returned to the left side, its vertical position is lowered so that the beam will scan the next lower line and not repeat over the same line. This is accomplished by the vertical scanning motion of the beam which is provided in addition to the horizontal scanning. The time it takes an electron beams to move from end of one line to the start of the next lower line is described as retrace Interval. Retrace interval can be Horizontal retrace interval or Vertical retrace interval.

5.6.5.2 Horizontal and Vertical Scanning

Scanning in TV system is done in the same way comparable to one reading a page of a paper, when one reads to cover all the words in a line and all the lines on the page. Reading to cover all the words in a line is like making a horizontal scanning while reading to cover all the line in a page is like vertical scanning. In horizontal scanning, electron beam moves rapidly from left to right along each line. In vertical scanning, the slow downward progression
scanning lines are spread to fill the frame top to bottom. This movement involves horizontal and vertical retraces. In horizontal retrace, the electron beams starts at the upper left-hand corner and sweeps horizontally to the right side and then rapidly returned to the left side. This is comparable to the movement of your eye as you read one line in a page of text book (as you are doing now) and quickly retrace to the left side and drop slightly for the next line. In vertical retrace, the electron beams moves from the lower right - hand corner up for the next picture when all the horizontal lines have been traced. This type of retrace is analogous to the time it takes the eye to move from the bottom of one page of a text to the top of the next page.

5.6.5.3 Scanning Process

In TV transmission, the pictures are scanned frame by frame and transmitted. On the TV screen also, the scanning beams ‘paints’ the picture frame-wise. The scanning rate is so fast that the picture details do not change much when the picture frame is being scanned. Such picture frames are transmitted one after the other in succession to represent the moving picture. To create the picture, the scene is subdivided into many fine horizontal lines called scan lines or scene lines. Each line represents a very narrow portion of light variations in the scene. The number of scan lines determines the resolution of the picture and the observed details. If the scan line increases, then the resolution becomes higher and greater the detail that can be observed. According to US NTSC TV standard, the maximum division of the scene is 525 horizontal lines. Of these, about 40 lines are lost as a result of vertical retrace interval. This leaves 485 visible lines that one can actually see if TV screen is viewed at close range. The number of the visible lines does not depend on the TV screen size. Because this scanning occurs rapidly, persistence of vision and CRT phosphor persistence cause us to perceive these 485 lines as a complete image. Persistence of vision is the storage characteristics of human eye which makes the sensation of vision by the eye to persist up to 1/16 th of a second if the object, scene or picture (light) is removed. While persistence is a property of TV system which makes use of principle of persistence of vision and it is defined as length of time an image stays on the screen after the electrical signal is removed.
Let us use some examples to illustrate the scanning process.
Figures 5.10 (a): Scanning of a letter F on a white background
[Figure 5.10 (b):Serial transmission of the video electrical signals derived from each scan line]
Figure 5.10(a) is simplified drawing of scanning process. As shown in the figure, the scene is a large black letter F on a white background. The task of TV camera is to convert this scene into an electrical signal. The camera accomplishes this by transmitting a voltage of 1 V for black and 0 V for white. The scene is divided into 15 lines numbered 0 through 14. The scene is focused on the light-sensitive area of a camera tube or CCD imaging device which scans the scene 1 line at a times, transmitting the light variations along that line as voltage level. The figure also shows the light variations along several of the lines. Where the white background is being
scanned, a 0-V signal occurs. When a black picture element is encountered, a 1-V level is transmitted. The electrical signals derived from each scan line are the video signal. They are transmitted serially one after the other until the entire scene has been sent as shown in figure 5.10 (b).This is precisely how a standard TV picture is developed and transmitted. Again, figure 5.11helps us to understand how these tiny individual outputs of the scanning process can serve to represent an entire scene.
Figures 5.11: Scanning of a letter T on photosensitive cells
In this simplified system as shown by figure 5.11(a), the camera focuses the letter “T” onto the photosensitive cells in the CCD imaging device, but instead of a million cells, this system has just 30, arranged in 6 rows with 5 cells per row. Each separate area is the picture element (pixel). The letter “T” is focused on the light-sensitive area of the camera so that all of row 1 and 6 are illuminated as shown in figure 5.11(b), while all of row 2 is dark and the centres of rows 3,4, and 5 are dark. If each row is scanned sequentially, and if the retrace time is essentially zero, then there will be a sequential breakup of information. Figure 5.12(a) shows this sequential breakup of information.
This sequence continues at every retrace interval and usually accomplished very rapidly. The variable time light on the photosensitive cells results in a similar variable voltage being developed at the CCD’s output as shown in figure 5.12(b).The result is that the visual scene has been converted to a video (electrical) signal and can now be suitably amplified and used to amplitude-modulate a carrier for TV broadcast.
[Figure 5.12: (a) Sequential breakup of information during scanning (b) The variable time light (the resulting electrical signal) on the photosensitive]

5.6.5.4 Needs for Scanning

1. Scanning makes it possible for one video signal to include all elements for the entire picture. At one instant of time, the video signal can show only one variation. In order to have video signal for all the variations of light and shade, all the picture details are scanned in a sequential order of time. 2. Scanning makes a TV picture reproduction different from a photographic print. In a photo, the entire picture is reproduced at one time. In TV, the picture is reassembled line after line and frame over frame.

5.6.6 SCAN LINE

To create a picture on TV screen, the scene is sub-divided into many fine horizontal lines called scan lines. Each line represents a very narrow portion of light variation in the scene. The total number of scan lines proportionately, determines the picture resolution on the TV screen.

5.6.7 FRAME RATE AND FIELD RATE

There is certain numbers of scan lines contained in a TV screen. The number is determined by the type of TV system. In America’s TV system, the total number of the scan line is 525 while in Europe’s system, the total number is 625. This total number in a screen makes up a frame. Suppose we assign numbers to each scan line of a frame, we shall have a set of even numbers and a set of odd numbers. The set of all the odd numbers of the frame makes half of the frame while the set of even numbers gives the other half of the frame. Each of these halves is called a field. This implies that one field of a frame contains scan lines of odd numbers and the other field contains scan lines of even numbers.

5.6.8 FLICKER

Flicker is an undesired effect that occurs during scanning process as a result of discontinuity between two picture frames. In this process, motion of pictures appears jerky in the TV screen due to insufficient scanning frequency. This is to say that flicker arises because of insufficient frame frequency and this effect is made more serve when the screen is made black and white alternatively. Flicker effect is solved by a type of scanning method called interlaced scanning.

5.6.9 PERSISTENCE OF VISION

As we have said, in TV transmission, the pictures are scanned frame by frame and transmitted. On the screen also the scanning beam paints the picture frame-wise. The scanning rate is so fast that the picture details do not change much when the picture frame is being scanned. Such picture frames are transmitted one after another in succession to represent the moving picture. It is necessary to present this picture frames on TV screen in such a way that an illusion of continuity is created. Because of this, the motions in the scene from frame to frame are integrated by human eye and picture on the screen appears smooth and continuous. This illusion of continuity of the TV picture is created because of persistence of vision of the human eye. The persistence of vision is related to storage characteristics of human eye. When the light is incident on eye’s retina, the nerves of the retina are stimulated and the
sensation is carried out to the brain by these nerves. If the light is removed from an eye, the stimulation of the nerves persists for about 1/16th of a second. Hence the scanning rate of the TV picture frame is made higher than 16 frames per second. Because of this, the stimulation created by one picture frame on the nerves of the retina in the eye persists till the next picture frame is shown. Thus the stimulation of the nerve of the retina is modified according to second picture frame without any discontinuity. Subsequently, the nerves of the retina always remain stimulated and the ‘stimuli’ of successive picture frames are integrated. Hence, the brightness changes of the picture frame are sensed as smooth and continuous by the eye and overall picture appears continuous to an eye.

5.6.10 IMAGE CONTINUITY IN TV

The advantage of persistence of vision of human eye is employed in TV system. The individual picture frames are created on the TV screen with help of scanning. There is also no need to blank the screen at the end of picture frame since sequential scanning is used. Because of this sequential scanning, the element or point on the screen is blanked by itself between the two successive scanning processes.

5.6.11 KELL FACTOR AND VIDEO BANDWIDTH

Theoretically, there are expected maximum lines which a scanning beam should produce for a distinct resolution. The maximum lines depend on the television system. However, in practice, if the size of the scanning beam is more than width of the line, then it may scan two lines at a time partially. Again, because of small errors in the deflection circuits and alignment of the scanning system, the beam spot may fall equally on two consecutive lines. The above factors are the practical limitations. Because of these practical limitations, the vertical resolution is reduced than the theoretical value. Experiment has shown that around 70% of the total lines get scanned while the remaining 30% lines get merged due to finite beam size and alignment error. Thus, this factor by which the theoretical maximum lines are reduced to give effective scanning lines is referred to as Kell factor or resolution factor. Mathematically, the relationship between the theoretical maximum horizontal scanning line, the effective scanning lines and the Kell factor can be represented by the formula; ne =knv                                                                  …5.6.18 Where
ne = the effective horizontal scanning line nv = ideal number of the horizontal scanning line K= Kell factor For example, in a system where the ideal maximum scanning line is 860 line, with 70% Kell factor, the effective scanning line will be K= 70% = 0.7;nv = 860 ne = knv = 0.7 x 860 ne = 602

EXAMPLE 5.3

In a TV system that uses 625 scanning lines, 40 lines are lost in vertical retrace period. Determine the number of effective scanning lines for vertical resolution.
Solution The total of scan line = N; N = 625                 The ideal scanning line is 585, that is, the value from calculation. But the practical Number of scan lines lost (suppressed)              value of the scanning line is; during retrace period = Ns; Ns = 40 ne = knv = 0.7 x 585 = 409.5 Number of active line = Nv;Nv = N -Ns ne ≈ 410 Nv = 625 – 40 = 585 Width of the scan line is the ratio of the vertical dimension of the viewing area of the camera to the number of active line

title: Monochrome Television System
text:
CHAPTER OUTLINES

6.1 INTRODUCTION

6.2 NTSC TV STANDARDS 6.1 INTRODUCTION                               6. 3 MONOCHROME TV (VIDEO) CAMERA

6.4 TV CAMERA’S IMAGE PICK-UP DEVICES

T he first popular analogue TV is a 6.5 TYPES OF VIDEO CAMERA IMAGE monochrome or black and white           SENSORS TV developed in America in the 6.6 TYPES OF TV CAMERA TUBES year 1954 by the National Television Standard Committee(NTSC). The NTSC             6.7 MONOCHROME TV PICTURE TUBE
is a body in the US which sets the             6.8 MONOCHROME TV TRANSMITTER AND analogue television standard for the           RECEIVER
United States. This first TV by the NTSC becomes the first America                       standard television version and it is rightly called NTSC TV system.     Nevertheless, the TV system is not without certain limitations Some major limitations that associate with this TV system include incompatible scanning standard, issue of excess bandwidth and the issue of phase error.

6.2 NTSC TV STANDARDS

The NTSC system has basic standards which are the features or the characteristics of the system. These basic characteristics of the TV system are strongly dependent on the mains electricity supply for America which is 60 Hz frequency. Some of these characteristics include scan lines, field rate, frame rate, scanning frequency, retrace interval etc. The NTSC TV contains 525 horizontal scan lines per a picture frame.
The value for a (picture) frame is half of the frequency of mains electricity supply, that is, 30. A frame contains 525 scan lines and it takes 1 sec for electron beam of the TV camera tube to scan 30 frames. Consequently, 15,750 horizontal lines are scanned in every 1 sec (i.e. 525 lines x 30 frames). This is the line scanning frequency. A frame is made up two fields. That means, a field is half a frame. Each field contains 262.5 lines. The time it takes electron beam to scan 1 line in a frame is 63.5 𝜇s (1/15,750 Hz) and this called the line rate or line interval. When a complete scanning of a line is made, the electron beam retraces to begin the scanning of the subsequent line. The time it takes for this retrace to be made is described as retrace interval. With the consideration of the retrace interval, it happens that the actual time to scan 1 line in an NTSC TV system is 53.5 𝜇s. This actual time is the difference between a line rate and the retrace interval. In addition to the above mentioned standard, NTSC TV has an aspect ratio of 4:3, and TV composite signal bandwidth of 4.2 MHz.

6.3 MONOCHROME TV (VIDEO) CAMERA

The TV camera is the “eye” of the TV system. It is a very sophisticated electronic device that employs optical system (lenses) and image sensors (image pick-up devices) mostly camera tubes, or charge couple devices (light-sensitive image sensors) transducers and it is used for generating video signals. The lenses and the sensors work together to convert optical images (scenes, objects or pictures to be viewed) into sequence of electrical signals (by optical-to-electrical conversion process). That is, they generate the primary components of picture signal that are used to modulate a carrier signal.

6.4 TV CAMERA’S IMAGE PICK-UP DEVICES (SENSORS))

The image sensors of the camera which is the most important part, started firstly with the introduction of mechanical spinning disk in 1884. After some decades, by the middle of 20th century, the spinning disks were replaced by vacuum tubes, which utilized an electron beam to scan an image of a scene that was focused on a light- sensitive surface within the tube. Today, in most cameras, the camera tubes have been replaced by smaller, cheaper solid-state image sensors such as charge-coupled devices, though, the camera tubes still have suitable application on the design of studio televisions.

6.4.1 WORKING PRINCIPLE OF CAMERA IMAGE SENSORS

Generally, TV camera image sensors work on the principle of optical-electrical conversion process, which is based on the phenomenon of photoelectric effects on certain materials. There are two modes of this photoelectric effect, namely; photoemission and photoconductivity.

6.4.1.1 Photoemission

The working principle of photoemission is that when light falls on the surface of certain metals, they emit electrons. These emitted electrons are called photo electrons. This is from the fact that light consists of photons and these photons possess energy. So, when these energies of the photon strike the surface of the metals, they give away their energies to the valence electrons of the metals. Some metals or oxides are readily photo – emissive. Cesium – silver or bismuth silver – cesium oxides are used as photo – emissive surface for TV cameras. The spectral response of these materials is close to human eye. Figure 6.1 illustrates the basic principles of operation of camera tube using photo emission. The face plate has photo emissive coating. It deposits charges on the target plate depending upon the light intensity variations of the scene. The electron beam strikes the target with almost zero velocity to avoid secondary emission. The beam is moved back to the target. This reflected beam is collected by an electrode which is mounted very close to the cathode from where it was emitted. Thus, the circuit or path of an electron beam is completed from cathode of an electron gun, target, collecting anode, load resistance RL, d. c bias voltage and back to grounded cathode. The intensity of the reflected beams depends upon the charge deposited (or electron image) on the target plate. The beam current flow through load resistance R L and produces video signal across it. Thus, the video signal across RL represents the intensity variations of the picture. The photo-emissive coating on the face plate alters the electron image on target according to intensity variation of the scene. The TV camera tube that mostly uses the principles of photoemission for its operation is the image orthicon.
[Figure 6.1: Basic principles of operation of camera tube using photo emission]

6.4.1.2 Photo Conductivity

Photoconductivity materials have the property that when light falls on them, their resistance varies according to intensity of light. The semi-conductor metals such as selenium, and Lead and their oxides show this phenomenon. The materials are used in the tellurium plates of TV camera tubes. Figure 6.2 shows the principle of operation of camera tube using photo conductivity. The light rays from the scene are made incident on the face plate having photoconductive coating. The resistance of each picture element varies according to the light intensity at that point. When an electron beam scans a particular element, the beam’s current will flow according to the resistance offered by the picture element (pixel). The electron beam current path is completed through cathode of electron gun, variable resistance offered by the target, load resistance RL d. c bias voltage and back to grounded cathode. Thus, the voltage developed across RL represents video signal. The vidicon camera tube and plumbicon camera tube work on the principle of photo conductivity.
[Figure 6.2: The principle of operation of camera tube using photo conductivity]

6.5 TYPES OF VIDEO CAMERA IMAGE SENSORS

The image sensors of a TV camera are those sensitive devices contained in the video camera and which pick up images of scenes or objects, scan them and channel them to the video camera. From the time of its invention, TV image sensors have passed from a mechanical spinning disk, to (CRT) camera tubes and to photosensitive cells called charge couple devices.

6.5.1 MECHANICAL SPINNING DISK

The mechanical spinning disks were developed based on the prototype patented in 1884 by a German engineer, Paul Nipkow. The disk worked in such a way that as it rotated, light reflected from the scene passed through a series of apertures in the disk and entered a photoelectric cell, which translated the sequence of light values into a corresponding sequence of electric values. In this way, the entire scene was scanned, one line at a time, and converted into an electrical signal.

6.5.2 CAMERA TUBES

The video signal for picture begins at the camera tube, inside the camera head. The input is light from the focused scene to be televised, and the output is electric signal corresponding to the picture information. All camera tube; monochrome and colour tube follow the same process for generating signal. Light from object or scene is focused by the lens onto the photoelectric image plate. The photoelectric properties of the image plate then convert the different light intensities into corresponding electrical variations. With electron beam scanning across the image plate, line by line, and field by field, the camera signal is produced for the entire picture area. We shall discuss in detail, the camera tubes in the next section.

6.5.3 CHARGE COUPLED DEVICES (CCDs)

The development of charge coupled devices (CCDs) and its utilizations in modern television video camera are to offer solutions to the limitations suffered by the camera tube. CCDs are solid-state image sensors constructed as large-scale integrated circuits on semiconductor chips. The basic sensor elements include a photodiode and field effect transistor. Light falling on the junction of the photodiode liberates electrons and creates holes, resulting in an electric charge that accumulates in proportion to the intensity and duration of the light falling on the diode. The photosensitive cells (sensor elements) in typical CCDs are up to hundreds of thousands or millions. The cells are arranged in a two-dimensional array; vertical columns and horizontal rows and analyses image into a corresponding number of pixels by the principle of photoemission. In this form, when light energy (photons) strikes its surface, the light information will be converted to an electronic analogue of the light, a video signal. In one type of the image sensor, the charges accumulated inform of light information by the sensor elements are transferred one row at a time by a vertical shift register to a horizontal register from where they are shifted out of the device in a serial fashion called bucket brigade to form the video signal. An important limitation of CCD device is the maximum speed at which the information placed on the device can be easily shifted out to storage.

6.5.3.1 Advantage of CCDs over Camera Tubes

The major benefits of CCD centre on the providing high sensitivity, high resolution, low noise level, proper spectral response, stability, good constant range, and easy processing of the output signal. They are lightweight and portable. They do not require large amount of power or voltage for their operation. They are less costly compared to camera tube.

6.6 TYPES OF TV CAMERA TUBES

The main types of camera tubes, in their order of development, are the image orthicon, the vidicon and the plumbicon. The orthicon works on the principle of photoemission while the vidicon and plumbicon work on the principle of photoconductivity. Among the three, plumbicon offers more advantages. Before delving into the types of the camera tubes, let us see the basic terms associated with performance characteristics of the camera tubes.
6.6.1 TERMS ASSOCIATED WITH PERFORMANCE CHARACTERISTICS OF TV CAMERA TUBES
1. Dark Current: This is the current which flows for zero light input. This current flows because of finite value of resistance of the photoconductive layer. The magnitude depends upon the type of the photoconductive material use. The value of this current is normally very small in few nano-amperes. 2. Image Lag: This is described as the time delay in following the signal current according to new scene illumination on the plate of the camera tube. The two factors that contribute to image lag are photoconductive lag and beam lag. Photoconductive lag is an effect that takes place due to the reluctance of photoconductive target. It does not follow the fast changes in the brightness of the scene. Beam lag takes place because of the capacitive effect of the photoconductive target. This is also called capacitive lag. 3. Light Transfer Characteristics: This is a graphical plot of signal output current versus illumination on the tube face plate with the dark current.
4. Resolution: This is the ability to resolve picture elements. It depends upon the diameter of the electron beam (beam aperture) when it lands on the target of the camera tube.

6.6.2 IMAGE ORTHICON

[Figure 6.3: Image Orthicon 6.6.2.1 Working Principle of Image Orthicon]
Figure 6.3 shows the diagram of image orthicon TV camera tube. Image orthicon works on the principle of photoelectric emission and it is a sensitive tube capable of handling a wide range of light values and contrast. It includes three sections in a single envelope. These sections are image section, scanning section and electron multiplier section. Image section This is the part where image pick-up occurs. The section includes three basic parts; Photocathode, Target plate, and a screen The photocathode: This is a photosensitive surface that emits light. It operates at a very large negative potential on to which the optical image is focused. When an optical image is focused on it, photoelectrons, in proportion to the amount of light impinging, are emitted. The target plate: This plate is a thin plate of glass of low resistivity. The thickness is less than 2 x10−4 inch. Most of the photoelectrons which are emitted from the
photocathode that pass through the screen hit this target plate. Secondary electrons are liberated from the surface of the target plate by high accelerating photoelectrons from the photocathode. The emission of the secondary electrons from the target plate leaves a distribution of positive charge on its surface. The resistivity of the target plate resists the lateral charge flow on its surface and thus the image charge pattern formed on the plate. Since the plate is thin, this charge pattern also appears on the other side of the plate. The Screen: This is located very close to the target plate and has about 500,000 openings per square inch. The screen collects the several secondary electrons emitted by the target plate. Scanning section In this section, the scanning of the image generated at the image section occurs. The low velocity beam generated by the electron gun scans the picture. The beam is deflected on the plate in vertical and horizontal directions and enables the electron beam to scan the whole plate. This beam gives up the number of electron required to neutralize the positive charge at that point and thus the returning electron beam varies in magnitude in accordance with the brightness variation of the image. The electron multiplier section This section is located within the pick-up tube for amplifying the electron density variation in the returning beam, thereby providing the desired output signals. The process of producing the camera signal output by the image orthicon is summarized briefly in the following steps; 1. Light from the televised scene is focused onto the photocathode, where the light image produces an electron corresponding to the picture elements. 2. The electron image is accelerated to the target to produce secondary emission from the glass plate. 3. The secondary emission produces on the target a pattern of positive charges corresponding to the picture elements in the scene. 4. The low-velocity scanning beam from the electron gun provides electrons that land on the target to neutralize the positive charges turn back from the target and go towards the electron gun. 5. As the beam scans the target, therefore, the electrons turned back from the glass plate provide a signal current that varies in amplitude in accordance with the charge pattern and the picture information.
6. The returning signal current enters the electron multiplier, where the current is amplified. The amplified current flowing through the load resistor in the multiplier’s anode circuit produces the camera signal output voltage.

6.6.2.2 Advantages of image orthicon

1. It has high sensitivity. 2. Its signal-to-Noise ratio is better and the typical value is 30 dB. 3. Its spectral response is close to eye. 4. It produces no lag.

6.6.2.3 Disadvantages

1. The size is bulky in nature. 2. Its operation is complicated. 3. It is very costly 4. It has a limited life time of nearly 1500-6000 hours.

6.6.3 VIDICON

[Figure 6.4:Vidicon camera tube]

6.6.3.1 Working Principle of Vidicon Tube

The vidicon is a very small tube of relatively simple construction. It uses the principle of photo conductivity for its working. The resistance decreases with the amount of incident light on it. The internal construction of the vidicon camera tube is shown in figure 6.4. It consists of majorly two sections with other various components as shown in the figure. The two sections are the signal plate and the scanning system. The Signal Plate The signal plate is a conducting metallic plate film, very thin so as to be transparent. The side of the film facing cathode is coated with a very thin layer of amorphous selenium, which is photoconductive material. This side is scanned by electron beam. The optical image is focused on the other side of this film. The Scanning system This section contains the following device; the cathode, control grid-1, accelerating grid-2, anode grid-3, focusing coil, deflecting coils and alignment coils. In the scanning process, the electron beam for scanning is formed by the combination of cathode, control grid-1, accelerating grid-2, and anode grid-3. The focusing coil produces an axial field which focuses the beam on the film. Deflecting coil brings about the vertical and horizontal deflection of the beam by passing saw-tooth current waves through it, so as to scan the whole film. The vertical and horizontal deflected beams thus produce transverse horizontal and vertical magnetic fields respectively. The alignment coils are for the initial adjustment of the direction of the beam. Figure 6.4 shows the various parts of the vidicon tube. The cathode is heated by the heater. The accelerator grid G2 is at about 300 V. It is used to attract electrons from heated cathode. The control G1, which is at – 30 V, is used to control the number of electrons in the beam. G3 is a long focus electrode. Its voltage is 260 V. it is used to make the beam sharp on target plate. The last electrode is G4. It is in the form of mesh and its bias voltage is 400 V. It is used to increase the velocity of electrons. The deflection coils are used for deflecting the beam horizontally and vertically for scanning the target. The focus coils are used to make the beam narrow and sharp. The front end converter consists of a glass faceplate, transparent signal electrode, photoconductive layer and a target ring. The photosensitive target plate has two layers; one layer which is facing the light is a thin coating. This coating is made of tin oxide SnO. It is a transparent and electrically conductive. The target ring is electrically connected to this layer. The other side of the
target plate is coated with a photosensitive material, usually antimony trisulphate. It is photoconductive material and its resistance varies according to light intensity. When the scanning beam passes over the photo conductive material of the signal plate, it deposits electron so that the potential of this side of the plate is reduced to that of the cathode. But the other side of the film (plate) is still at its original potential. As a result, the potential difference across a given point to the photoconductive material is created, which approximately 30V. Before the next scanning, the charge leaks through photoconductive material at a rate determined by the conductivity of the material which in turn depends upon the amount of the incident light. White portion of the object (scene) will project more light on the film and make it more conductive. This charge leaked to photoconductive side of the film will vary according to the illumination of the object. Consequently, potential at every point on the photoconductive side will vary. Now the electron beam again starts scanning photoconductive side of the film but this time, the charge deposited by the beam in order to reduce its potential zero (cathode potential) will vary with time. Therefore, current through RL (and hence the output voltage) will follow the changes in potential difference between two surfaces of the film and hence follows the variations of light intensity of successive points in the optical image. 6.6.3.2 Advantages 1. Low cost. 2. It has simple adjustment. 3. Its sensitivity is large. 4. It has good image resolution.

6.6.3.3 Disadvantages

1. Owing to the fact that the resistance of the photoconductive film does not change instantaneously with change of light intensity, different levels of light intensity are adjusted with slight time slag. 2. It has non-linear response characteristics.

6.6.4 PLUMBICON

[Figure 6.5:Plumbicon TV camera tube]
Similar to vidicon, plumbicon TV camera tube uses the principle of photo conductivity. Its construction is similar to that of vidicon except for the photoconductive target material which is a Lead oxide of the form PbO and the structure. The target plate of plumbicon has different structure as shown in figure 6.5 The faceplate consists of conducting transparent film of tin oxide just inside the glass. On this film, a layer of lead oxide is deposited. This layer is doped in such way that a PIN junction is formed as shown in figure 6.5. This PIN junction acts like a semiconductor diode.

6.6.4.1 Principle of Operation

The operation of the pumbicon can be best explained from the figure 6.5. Initially, when there is no light input, the PIN diode is reverse biased due to a positive potential appearing on SnO2 coating (n-type) and p-type stabilized at a potential
slightly below the cathode due to negatively charged scanning beam. This results in a very small output current which is almost negligible. This is the greatest advantage of a pumbicon camera tube especially when used with colour systems. The photo electronic conversion is almost similar to that of standard vidicon except for the method of discharging each storage element. In a standard vidicon, each element acted as a leaky capacitor with leakage resistance decreasing with more light. Here, when the light falls on the target, the diode becomes forward biased upon the extent depending upon light intensity. The forward bias on each diode results from the photo excitation of the pure PbO and doped PbO junction. Thus the target behaves as capacitor in series with PIN diode. 6.6.4.2 Difference between Vidicon and Plumbicon
The difference between vidicon and plumbicon will be well understood by presenting them inform of electrical equivalent circuits. Figure 6.6(a) is the electrical equivalent circuit of vidicon camera tube and figure 6.6(b) is the electrical equivalent circuit of plumbicon.
Figure 6.6(a): Electrical equivalent of vidicon camera Figure 6.6(b): Electrical equivalent circuit of plumbicon camera tube tube
In the figure 6.6(a), the target plate is represented by equivalent resistors at various picture elements (pixel). Each pixel acts as variable resistance in parallel with a capacitor and the resistance is altered (increases or decreases) according to the variation of light intensity falling on it. Whenever scanning beam falls on the particular picture element, the electrical circuit is completed through the photo resistance target ring, load resistance RL, d. c bias voltage, cathode of the electron gun and electron beam. In the electrical equivalent circuit of plumbicon, as shown in figure6.6(b), each element on the target plate acts as a capacitor that is in series with a reverse biased light controlled diode (PIN diode). The conductive film of tin oxide (SnO2) is connected to the d. cbias of 40V through load resistance RL. The light from the picture is focused on the PbO layer, that is, on the PIN junction. This light creates photo excitation of junction between intrinsic and doped PbO layer. Hence, current starts flowing and video signal is generated. In other words, when electron beam scans a picture element, an equivalent photo diode formed, conducts through equivalent capacitor and video signal is generated across the load resistance. 6.6.4.3 Advantages of Plumbicon Camera Tube
Apart from the difference in the equivalent electrical circuit, the plumbicom camera tube has some advantages it offers over the vidicon and by extension the orthicon camera tube. The advantages are as follows; 1. It has the least lag of all the TV camera tubes 2. The dark current is extremely low and independent on temperature 3. The spectral response is similar to that of human eyes, hence it is preferred over vidicon 4. It has small size, light weight and low power requirement 5. It has better light transfer characteristic than vidicon. Its light transfer characteristics are straight line with higher slope compare to vidicon.

6.6.6 LIMITATIONS OF TV CAMERA TUBES

Camera tubes need frequent adjustment and replacement. They are sensitive to mechanical vibration and shock. They are large and bulky. They suffer from various image problems such as bloomy with bright lights, smearing and retained images. They use a lot of power.

6.7 MONOCHROME TV PICTURE TUBE

Picture Tube is a display device in the TV system that converts the electric voltage into picture element. It is basically a Cathode Ray Tube (CRT), housed in a fully evacuated closed bell-shaped glass with a display screen. Figure 6.7 is the basic elements of picture tube and the illustration of its operations.
[Figure 6.7: Monochrome picture tube]
The electron gun placed inside the neck of the picture tube generates an electron beam. The electrons are emitted from the heated cathode towards the anode, that is, towards screen of the picture tube. The heater is the small filament mounted very close to the cathode. Face plate is the screen of the picture tube coated inside with very fine particles of phosphor. When high velocity electrons from the gun hit this phosphor coated layer, it emits light. This effect (emission of light) is called luminance. After the beam is removed, the phosphor continued its emission of light following excitation of the screen. This condition is called phosphorescence. This persists till the electron beam comes to that point again. It is only when this happens that we will be able to see the complete picture on the screen produced by the scanning beam. Otherwise, if the sufficient persistence is not there, then as the electron beam scan further, the following point on the screen will lose their intensity and only a moving dot will be visible. For this process to create a good persistence to human eyes, the duration must be up to 1/30 sec so that complete picture will be produced.
Around the neck of the picture tube is a structure of magnetic coil called deflection yoke. The yoke contains horizontal and vertical deflection coils and various magnets for different adjustments. The horizontal and vertical current linear saw-tooth waves generated by the sweep and synchronizing circuits are applied to the yoke coils, which produce magnetic fields inside the tube that influence the position of the electron beam. When electrons flow, a magnetic field is produced around the conductor through which the current flows. The magnetic field that is produced around the beam is moved or deflected by the magnetic field produced by the deflection coils in the yoke. Thus the electron beam is swept across the face of the picture in interlaced pattern. As the beam is being swept across the face of the tube to trace out the scene, the intensity of the electron is varied by the luminance signal which is applied to the cathode or in some cases to the control grid. The control grid is an element in the electron gun that is negatively biased with respect to the cathode. By varying the grid voltage, the beam can be made stronger or weaker, thereby varying the intensity of the light spot produced by the beam when it strikes the phosphor. Any shade of gray, from white to black, can be reproduced in this way.

6.8 MONOCHROME TV TRANSMITTER AND RECEIVER

The transmitter and receiver of a monochrome TV form the major part of the monochrome TV system. The transmitter uses the monochrome video camera to generate image to be transmitted, together with microphone as sound transducer to generate sound signal. Both signals are integrated into a composite monochrome TV signal and propagated. The monochrome receiver receives the transmitted TV signal from the transmitter and processes it into the original video and sound signals. The demodulated video signal is displayed by the monochrome picture tube and the sound reproduced by the loud speaker. Both processes in the transmitter and receiver occur in step through synchronization. Our discussion of monochrome TV transmitter and receiver in this section and subsequent sections will be based on NTSC TV system.

6.8.1 MONOCHROME TV TRANSMITTER

The block diagram of figure 6.8 shows a simplified monochrome (NTSC) TV transmitting system. The system is composed of TV camera, a microphone, a coupling network, transmitting antenna and the TV transmitter.
The monochrome (NTSC) TV transmitter is actually two separate transmitters; the sound transmitter and video transmitter. The sound transmitter is an FM transmitting system similar to broadcast FM radio. It is a high-fidelity system just as the broadcast FM transmitter. The major difference between the broadcast FM and the TV audio transmitting system is that TV uses a ±25 kHz deviation while the broadcast FM uses a ±75 kHz deviation. Thus, the TV sound signal transmitter has the same fidelity with that of broadcast FM transmitter, but it is less effective in canceling the indirect noise effects. The output stage in the sound transmitter circuitry is followed by a vestigial sideband filter which is a band-pass filter. This band-pass filter is an LC filter capable of handling the high power at this point. The video or picture transmitter is an AM transmitter. In this transmitter, picture or video signal is amplitude-modulated onto a carrier. 6.8.1.1 The Transmitter Microphone and TV Camera Tubes
Attached to the transmitter is a microphone. The microphone serves as the sound input transducer that converts the sound signal into an equivalent electrical signal. The sound electrical signal is fed into the transmitter for onward modulation of sound carrier. The video sequence at the transmitting station beings with the TV camera tube which is a transducer that converts a visual picture or scene into equivalent (video) electric signals. Detailed descriptions of the various camera tubes have been discussed in section 6.6 of this chapter. Very basically, a camera tube has a mosaic screen, onto which the real images are focused through the lens system of the TV camera. An electron gun forms a beam which is accelerated toward this photoelectric screen. The beam scans the screen, from left to right and top to bottom, covering the entire screen 30 times per second. The beam intensity is affected by the charge on the screen at that point, and this in turn depends on the brightness of the point. The current-modulated beam is collected at a target electrode, located at the screen. The output voltage from this electrode is varying (video) voltage, whose amplitude is proportional to the screen brightness at the point being scanned. This voltage is now applied to video amplifiers.
[Figure 6.8: Simplified monochrome television transmitter block diagram]

6.8.1.2 Video Stages in the Transmitter

The output of the camera is fed to a video switcher. The function of this switching system is to provide the many video controls required. It is at this point that the mixing or switching of various inputs, such as fading in of one signal and fading out of another, will take place. At this point, various visual effects involving brightness, contrast or hue will be inserted. The output of this mixing and switching amplifier goes to more video amplifiers, whose functions are to raise the signal level until it is sufficient for modulation. Along the chain of video amplifiers, certain pulses are inserted. These are the vertical and horizontal blanking and synchronizing pulses, which are required by the receivers to control their scanning processes. These pulses are generated by blanking generators and sync generators respectively. The final video amplifier is the power amplifier which grid-modulates the output RF amplifier. Because certain amplitude levels in the composite video signal must correspond to specific percentage modulation values,
this amplifier uses clamping to establish the precise values of various levels of the signal which it receives. Thus, the composite transmitted TV signal is a combination of both AM and FM principles. This is done to minimize interference effects between the two at the receiver because an FM receiver is relatively insensitive to amplitude modulation and an AM receiver has rejection capabilities to frequency modulation. The output of the sound and picture transmitters is fed to the antenna via a coupling network (diplexer). The network ensures that, although both the picture and sound transmitters are connected to the antenna with a minimum of loss, neither is connected to the other. Hence, the entire composite TV signal is driven into an antenna that converts the electrical energy into radio (electromagnetic) waves. These waves travel through the atmosphere to be intercepted by a TV receiving antenna and fed into the receiver once again as an electrical signal. That signal consists of video signal, audio signal, and synchronizing signal. 6.8.1.3 The NTSC Composite TV Signal
The maximum modulating rate for the video signal is 4 MHz and maximum video bandwidth is 4.2 MHz. The FCC allows only a 6 MHz bandwidth per station which also includes the FM sound signal. The TV signal that is transmitted is shown in figure 6.9
[Figure 6.9: NTSC composite TV signal]
From the figure, the lower video sideband extends only to 1.25 MHz below its carrier with the remainder filtered out, but the upper sideband is transmitted in full. The sound
is 4.5 MHz above the video carrier with FM sidebands as created by its ± 25 KHz deviation. The lower sideband is mostly removed by filters that occur near the transmitter output. While only one sideband is necessary, it would be impossible to filter out the entire lower sideband without affecting the amplitude and phase of the lower frequencies of the upper sidebands and carrier. Thus, part of the 6 MHz bandwidth is occupied by a “vestige or fraction” of the lower sideband (about 0.75 MHz out of 4 MHz). It is therefore commonly referred to as vestigial-sideband operation. This type of TV signal transmission offers the added advantage that carrier re-insertion at the receiver is not necessary as it is the case when SSB signal is used because the carrier is not attenuated in vestigial-sideband transmission systems. 6.8.1.4 The NTSC TV Channel Allocations
