6.8.2 MONOCHROME TV RECEIVER All TV receivers work on the principles of heterodyne receiver, as do almost all other type of receivers and therefore carries with it all characteristics associated with superheterodyne receiver which we have discussed in detail in chapter 4. What this means is that whatever is the incoming channel frequency, it is converted to intermediate frequency (IF) by a mixer and local oscillator of the receiver. This IF is then amplified, filtered and demodulated to get back the TV signal, a replica of the modulating signals (sound and picture) at the transmitter. In the overall TV receiver system, separate IFs are used for picture and sound. The TV receiver is a bit more complex and sophisticated than most other receivers. The technological sophistication of this device enables it to handle effectively the processing and recovering of the video and synchronizing signals as well as sound signal so as to present the pictures and sound output in a high-quality manner.
The receiver is made up of some basic sections which include RF tuner section, video (intermediate frequency) section, video detector section, sound (intermediate frequency) section, synchronizing and deflection section, power supply section and display (picture tube) section. Figure 6.10 is the block diagram of the receiver.
[Figure 6.10: Block diagram of monochrome TV receiver]

6.8.2.1 Tuner Section

The tuner section of the receiver is made up of RF amplifier, mixer and local oscillator. It is placed as the first gadget in the receiver serving as the input terminal of the receiver where the signal from the antenna or the TV cable is connected to. As a result, it is referred to as ‘the front end’ of the receiver. The Radio frequency (carrier) TV signals, comprising of picture and sound carrier signals that are collected by the antenna before this point is usually at their weakest level, ranging from microvolts to millivolts. The signals are immediately transferred to the receiver front end. The first job it does is for the IF amplifier component to amplify the received RF signals, selecting the desired TV channels’ carrier frequency signal and reducing it to the intermediate frequency (IF) by the heterodyning action mixer and local oscillator, which can be said to be overall output of the tuner. These three different major functions of the tuner are achieved due the three major circuits that make up the tuner and are they are briefly discussed below.
RF amplifier
The Radio-Frequency amplifier is the first circuit in the tuner section of the receiver. It is particularly designed for low-noise amplification. It is used for amplifying the input signal, that is, the voltages of the incoming picture and sound carriers signals and their side bands by about 10 times the original value, and improves its signal-to- noise ratio. It equally prevents local oscillator frequencies from going to antenna and rejects the image frequency signal.
Mixer
The mixer in the tuner section of the receiver is a device that converts the incoming RF signal frequencies from different channels into a common IF bandpass of the receiver. The signals from the Radio Frequency are passed to the mixer which then converts the frequencies of the sound and picture carriers to values better suited to subsequent amplification processes.
Local oscillator
The local oscillator generates the continuous sine wave frequency which can be adjusted precisely with help of the fine tuning. The generated signal amplitude is large compared to Radio Frequency signal. These generated sine waves are heterodyne in the mixer with the RF signal. The heterodyne process produces sum and difference of frequencies. The difference of frequencies is the intermediate frequencies (IF). It remains the same, irrespective of what the channel receiver is tuned to.
To illustrate, the mixing action causes an exchange in the carrier frequency position because there are two carriers transmitted 4.5 MHz apart. Therefore, for example, if channel 2 assigns the station picture carrier at 55.25 MHz and sound carrier at 59.75 MHz, and the local oscillator for this channel is set at 101 MHz, the difference between the oscillator frequency of 101 MHz and the picture carrier is 45.75 MHz. But with two carriers being received, the sound carrier also mixes with the oscillator frequency, for a difference frequency of 41.25 MHz, and then the difference in frequency will remain unchanged (45.75-41.25 = 4.5MHz). Consequently, no difference in performance will be seen in the operation of the receiver. The IF is passed through the pass filter while the filter blocks all other frequencies.

6.8.2.2 Types of Tuning

Types of tuning in the TV receiver are of two types; stagger tuning and electronic tuning.
Stagger Tuning
Stagger tuning is the techniques of cascading several tuned circuits with slightly different resonant frequencies, as shown in figure 6.11. In this method, a number of tuned band pass filters, each having a slightly offset band pass frequency, are cascaded to form a wider flat band pass with steep high- and low-frequency roll-off skirts. As shown in the figure, the response of three separate LC tuned circuits is used to obtain the total resultant passband shown with dash lines. The use of a Lower-Q tuned circuit in the middle helps provide a flatter overall response than would otherwise be possible.
Another interesting point illustrated in the figure is the attenuation given to the video side frequencies right around the picture carrier. This is done to reverse the vestigial- sideband signal characteristics generated at the transmitter.
The need for this tuning technique arises as a demand for getting a wide enough band- width but still have relatively sharp falloff at the passband edges, unlike in radio receiver where relatively High-Q tuned circuits are required since the desired bandwidth is often less than 10 KHz. In a TV IF amplifier, the required passband is about 6 MHz because of the wide frequency range necessary for video signals. Hence the problem here is not how to get a very narrow bandwidth with High-Q components, but instead how to get the required band-width but still have relatively sharp falloff at the passband edges, hence the use of stagger tuning in solving the problem.
[Figure 6.11: Frequency response of stagger tuning.]
Electronic Tuning
Most TV receiver use electronic tuning. Varactor is used for electronic tuning. Varactors are silicon diodes whose junction capacitance can be changed for tuning. As the reverse bias across the varactor diode varies, capacitance varies inversely. Figure 6.12 shows how varactor diode can be used for tuning. In the circuit, by changing R3, voltage across varactor diode D is changed. This changes the capacitance of the circuit and hence tuning.
[Figure 6.12: Circuit diagram of varactor diode circuit use for electronic tuning.]

6.8.2.3 General Functions of the Tuner in TV receiver

In addition to performing the functions of selecting the desired station to be viewed and the conversion of the carrier signals (picture and sound) into intermediate frequency, there are some other functions which the tuner section performs in the TV receiver. The functions are;
1. It provides amplification for the RF carrier signals. 2. It prevents the local oscillator signal from being driven into the antenna and thus radiating unwanted interference. 3. It steps the received RF signal down to the frequency required for the IF stages. 4. It provides proper impedance matching between the antenna-feed line combinations into the tuner itself. This allows for the largest possible signal into the tuner and thus the largest signal-to-noise ratio.

6.8.2.4 Video IF Section

The video IF section is made up video IF amplifier stages and the video detector stages. At the video IF amplifiers, bandpass type amplifiers, the sound and video IF are together properly amplified. The amplified IF signals are then sent to the video detector. The video detector in the monochrome TV receiver is a simple AM diode detector. The diagram of the video detector is shown in figure 6.13
Figure 6.13:Circuit diagram of AM diode (video) detector In section 3 of chapter 5, we emphasis that negative amplitude modulation is suitable for the TV signal transmission, for this reason, the diode, D of the detector is connected in the reverse form. As shown in the figure, capacitors C1 and C2 are used to bypass the high frequency carrier signal. Inductors L1 and L2 are the filters to further remove all other unwanted frequencies. If the composite video signal is positive amplitude modulated, then the diode D in the figure 6.13 will be reversed. The rectifying action of the diode in the video detector results in frequency translation of the sound IF signal. The video IF heterodyne with the sound IF to produce sound intercarrier signal modulated with sound. This sound intercarrier is extracted by a trap circuit as shown in the figure 6.13. It is also blocked from passing to video amplifiers. This implies that the output of the detector is composite video signal and frequency modulated intercarrier sound signal. Or, it can simply be said that the detector separates the sound IF signal from the video signal at the output. While the sound IF signal is given to the sound section of the TV receiver, the other output signal of the detector is fed separately to sync separator for deflection circuits, video amplifier section for picture display of demodulated picture and, AGC circuit for gain stabilization.

6.8.2.5 Synchronization Pulse Separator and Deflection Section

This section is made up of various circuits that perform different functions that are related and which enhance each other. Figure 6.14 shows the different components of this section. The function(s) of the component units are discussed below.
[Figure 6.14: Synchronization and deflection section]
Synchronization Circuit The video detector provides a takeoff point for the synchronization signal. The synchronizing pulse is made up of horizontal and vertical synchronizing pulses. These pulses need to be separated at this section into their horizontal and vertical components. The circuit that does the separation function is the sync separator. The sync separator can therefore be defined as a circuit that separates the horizontal and vertical component of the sync pulse signals which are used to calibrate precisely and periodically, the vertical and the horizontal oscillators. It is able to achieve this function from the fact that vertical sync pulse is of long duration, while the horizontal sync pulse is of extremely short duration. Other work of the sync separator outside separating vertical pulse from horizontal pulse is to clip the sync pulse of the video signal. This prevents the sweep instability that could occur because of false synchronization of sweep oscillators at the receiver by spurious video signals. Because of this function, the sync separator is sometimes referred to as the clipper. Once the sync separator has clipped the sync signals from the lower-level video signal, the two types of the separated signal are applied to both low- and high-pass filter.
Low-and High-pass Filters The vertical and horizontal sync pulse signals are then given to low pass filter (LPH) and high pass filter (HPF) to generate triggering pulses for horizontal and vertical oscillators. A low-pass filter is an integrator, while a high pass filter is a differentiator. The output of the low-pass filter will be the lower-frequency vertical sync pulse at 60 Hz because it is wide pulse rich in low-frequency components. The output from the high-pass filter will be the horizontal sync pulse at 15750 Hz because it is a narrow pulse that is rich in high-frequency content. Vertical and Horizontal Oscillators The vertical sync pulse is applied to the vertical oscillator. It then operates at 60 Hz and generates a linear ramp signal. By itself, the vertical oscillator generates a signal at about 60 Hz but must be precisely the same frequency as the transmitter’s vertical oscillator to prevent the picture from ‘rolling’ in a vertical direction. The horizontal oscillator generates linear lamp signal at 15750 Hz. In function, it follows the same process as the vertical oscillator except that their frequencies differ; 15750 Hz for horizontal oscillator and 60 Hz for vertical oscillator. AFC circuit This circuit generates triggering pulses for horizontal oscillator. It takes keying pulses as output /feed-back signal. Vertical and Horizontal Amplifier The horizontal and vertical oscillators’ outputs are then amplified by horizontal amplifier and vertical amplifier respectively for use to control precisely the horizontal and vertical movement of the electron beam that is scanning the phosphor of the CRT. They are applied to a coil around the yoke of the CRT tube, whose magnetic fields cause the electron beam to be deflected in the proper fashion. The coil around the tube yoke is the deflection coil. The vertical output amplifier is the driver circuit for vertical deflection coils. The horizontal deflection circuit works in feed-back mode. AGC Circuit The AGC circuit provides gain stabilization for the receiver. The function of the AGC is to examine the strength of the signal at the output of the video detector and converts it to a d. c voltage which is used to adjust the bias on the IF amplifiers, controlling gain in a manner that will maintain a constant signal level to the low-frequency
amplifier. The average d. cvoltage in the wave is a direct result of scene brightness as well as signal strength. The only part of the wave that truly represents the signal strength is the amplitude of the blanking and sync pulses. Consequently, a pulse from the horizontal deflection section is applied to the AGC network so as to turn on the AGC amplifier only during the horizontal blanking time. This will make the AGC independent of scene brightness. Such a system is called gated AGC or keyed AGC. The circuit diagram of the AGC is as shown in figure 6.15.
[Figure 6.15: AGC circuit]

6.8.2.6 Video Amplifiers Section

The video amplifier of the TV receiver drives the picture tube, adjusting the instantaneous voltage between its cathode and grid in proportion to the video voltage. This modulates the beam current and results in the correct degree of whiteness appearing at the correct point of the screen, which is determined by the deflection circuits. Again, the contrast and brightness controls are located in the circuitry of the output video amplifier. The contrast control is the direct video equivalent of the volume control in a radio receiver. 6.8.2.7 Power Supply Section
The TV receiver requires a low-voltage power for the function of its delicate circuits and high-voltage power for the picture tube. These powers are generated in the power supply section.
The power supply section contains two power-converting circuits; low-voltage power supply circuit and high-voltage power supply circuit. The low-voltage power supply circuit converts alternating current from the power line into direct current needed for low powered solid-state circuits and other low power required circuits in the receiver. This low-power voltage is otherwise referred to as B+ voltage and the value is 10-12 V. On the other hand, the high-voltage power supply circuit produces high-voltage power. This is shown in figure 6.16.
[Figure 6.16: Power supply section of TV receiver]
Referring to figure 6.14, the high voltage power produced by the high-voltage supply circuit is of two natures; the boosted B+ or B++ and EHT. The B++ which is about 110V is used to provide acceleration for the picture tube anode while the EHT which is in the range of 10-20 KV is supplied to the final anode in the picture tube to accelerate the electron beam and create scanning spots in the tube. (The picture tube filament is heated by its own separate low-voltage heater supply, not by EHT.) These two high-voltage powers are generated in the horizontal deflection section in the TV receiver.

6.8.2.8 Sound Section

The sound signal at the output of the video detector is an FM signal. It is then sent to the sound section of the receiver. This sound section of the receiver is a complete FM receiver system in itself. The sound section contains sound carrier trap, sound IF amplifier, FM detector, audio amplifier and speaker. The block diagram of this section is shown in figure 6.17. The sound carrier trap is the narrow bandpass filter which passes only a 4.5 MHz signal and suppresses the remaining signal. The Intermediate Frequency amplifier amplifies the FM signal being the output of the sound carrier trap and sends the amplified signal to FM detector. The FM detector detects the FM signal and converts it to audio signal form, similar to the original form from the transmitter. The next in the section is audio amplifier stage. At this stage, the audio amplifier amplifies the
amplitude and power of the audio (detected) signal. Volume control is added to this stage for volume control/adjustment. Loud speaker is the last stage of the sound section. The loud speaker collects the signal current of the amplified audio signal and converts it into sound.
[Figure 6.17: Sound section of a TV receiver]

6.8.2.9 Television Display Section

The traditional means of displaying television picture has been the use of picture tube. Picture Tube is a display device in the TV system that converts the electric voltage into picture element. Though, it is not a part of the receiver, it takes the output signal of the receiver and displays it. It is basically a Cathode Ray Tube (CRT), housed in a fully evacuated closed bell-shaped glass with a display screen.

6.9 TV SIGNAL PROPAGATION AND THE SIGNAL INTERFERENCES

TV signals are transmitted in the VHF and UHF electromagnetic wave frequency bands. There are three types of electromagnetic wave propagation. They are ground wave propagation, sky wave propagation and space wave propagation. The most suitable mode of propagation for TV signal is space wave propagation. The frequency range for ground wave propagation is very low and limited to 1500 kHz. Long distance communication uses sky wave propagation, but it is not suitable for frequencies above 30 MHz. For frequencies above 30 MHz, space wave propagation is most suitable.
6.9.1 TV SIGNAL TRANSMISSION USING SPACE WAVE PROPAGATION FOR TV SIGNALS
The space wave propagation is also called line of sight communication. In this type of propagation, the electromagnetic waves travel straight from transmitter to receiver. All VHF and UHF range of frequencies of TV signal are signals band are transmitted mainly by space wave propagation. However, for this type of propagation and range of frequency, signal attenuation is a major challenge. The attenuation is high because frequencies of the space wave propagation suffers mainly due to obstacles like hills, tall buildings etc. hence shadow zones are created. Also the interference result because of reflected signals.

6.9.2 INTERFERENCE PROBLEMS IN TV SIGNAL TRANSMISSION


6.9.2.1 Shadow Zones

Shadow zones are created because of obstacles like hills and tall building and so on. The signal power is received in such shadow zones because of diffraction and tropospheric bending. But the signal strength in shadow zones is reduced. The problem of shadow zones can be corrected by mounting antenna at the top of the obstructing object and using community antenna TV (CATV) system. This means the signal is given through the cable to each user from the common antenna which is mounted on the top of the obstructing object.

6.9.2.2 Co-channel Interference

Co-channel interference occurs when the signals from the two stations which operate at the same carrier frequencies are received at the same receiver. For example, when a station (of interest) is transmitting signals on a particular channel, it is quite possible that some other stations at long distance may be transmitting on the same channel. Therefore, the receiver picks up signals from this station (which is not our interest) also. These signals are weak in amplitude but tend to interfere with the required station. This interference produces horizontal bars on the screen. If the signals from interfering station are weak, then these bars are not visible on the screen. The co- channel interference was the serious problem when only VHF band was used for TV
transmission. Normally many stations transmit on the same channel. But these stations are located at long distances from each other, so that their signal does not interfere with each other. Now the transmission has been started on UHF band also. Therefore, many channels are available and co-channel interference is reduced. 6.9.2.3 Adjacent Channel Interference The signals due to adjacent channels interfere with the required channel. This is called adjacent channel interference. The picture carrier of adjacent channel interferes with sound carrier of required channel. This is because they are located close to each other’s. Similarly, sound carrier of required channel can interfere with picture carrier of required channel. Their sidebands interfere with each other and produce interference on the screen. Adjacent channel interference also results if guard band between the two channels is reduced. 6.9.2.4 Ghost Interference
Ghost interference arises because of multipath transmission. The signal received at the antenna can direct as well as reflected from the buildings, bridges, hills, tower etc. the reflected signal also contribute to picture since it is received by antenna. The reflected signal arrives late since it travels more distance compared to direct signal. Therefore, same image is created on the screen because of the direct and reflected signals. This image is slightly weak in brightness since reflected signal is weak. This image is called ghost image. The ghost interference is reduced by using the directional antennas so that radiations from other sides are not received.

6.9.3 SOLVING THE PROBLEMS OF TV SIGNAL INTERFERENCES

To reduce the problems dues to reflection and shadow zones, the transmitting antennas are mounted on the top of the hills. Increasing height of receiving antenna can also reduce such problems. Therefore, the range of transmission is also increased by increasing the heights of the antennas. The range of transmission is 60 km for 225 meters’ height of antenna above ground level. If the receiving antenna height is 16 meters above level, then the range of transmission is increased to 76 km. For any transmitting station the range is normally limited to 100 km since the radiated power is limited. In the VHF range of frequencies, the transmission range is limited only up to 60km.

title: TV Image Formation (Synthesis) and Composite Video Signal
text:
CHAPTER OUTLINES

7.1 INTRODUCTION


7.2 SCANNING AND SYNCHRONIZATION


7.3 SCANNINGRAD


7.1 INTRODUCTION                                7.4 SYNCRONIZATION IN TV SYSTEM


7.5 COMPOSITE VIDEO SIGNAL

I mage formation in TV system is the most vital process toward the         7.6 TV BROADCAST CHANNELS
video signal transmission. Transmitted                                      video signal is a combination of some other components                 such as sync and blanking pulses. At the receiver, the transmitted image is analyzed and reassembled to produce the original form of the image. To be able to achieve an unaltered image at the receiver, both the transmitter and receiver’s sequence of action will have to be in step. This is achieved by synchronization. This therefore, entails that for proper image formation for video signal and the analyses of the image into a quality picture at camera tube, two complimentary processes are involved. These are scanning and synchronization.

7.2 SCANNING AND SYNCHRONIZATION

In order for the camera tube to convert picture information into video signal, the image is dissected into series of horizontal lines. Similarly, the picture tube reassembles the image line by line at the receiver. These are achieved through scanning. The scanning is done by electron beam from the camera. The electron beams scan the picture across
the screen (of the camera) which is referred to as horizontal scanning or scan the line from top to bottom of the screen which is described as vertical scanning. Scanning processes have been fully discussed in chapter 5 The scanning at the camera tube and the picture tube must be synchronized or timed with respect to the video signal. The synchronization is necessary to reassemble the picture information on the correct lines. These functions are provided by scanning and synchronization circuit in-built in both the TV transmitter and TV receiver. The order of the complimentary process in TV transmitter is scanning-synchronization while in the receiver, it is synchronization-scanning.

7.3 SCANNING

Scanning is a process use in image formation for video signal transmission. We have discussed the process of scanning in chapter 5. In this section, we shall discuss the various terms that apply in scanning process and the scanning techniques.

7.3.1 TERMS USE FOR SCANNING PROCESS


7.3.1.1 Scan Line

To create a picture on TV screen, the scene is sub-divided into many fine horizontal lines called scan lines. Each line represents a very narrow portion of light variation in the scene. The greater the number of scan lines, the higher the resolution and greater the details of the scene (picture) that will be observed.

7.3.1.2 Frame Rate and Field Rate

A video frame is made up of many horizontal scan lines. In European system, there are 625 horizontal scan lines in a frame (i.e. 625 lines per frame) while the NTSC contains 525 horizontal scan lines per frame. Assume these lines are assigned numbers; we shall have collection of two sets of numbers; the set of odd numbers and set of even numbers. The set of odd numbers make half of the entire frame while the set of even numbers make another half of the frame. Suppose we separate them as
shown in figure 7.1, figure7.1(a) is the full frame, figure 7.1 (b) is one half of the frame containing odd numbers of the scan line lines and figure7.1(c) is the other half containing even numbers of the scan lines. The separation of the numbers into different sets is what we call field. Therefore, a field is half of a frame.
[Figure 7.1: Frame and fields]

7.3.1.3 Fly back

The movement of electron beam in TV screen during picture scanning is usually from the left side to the right side of the horizontal line, till it reaches the bottom of the screen. At the end of each scan line, the electron beam is returned very quickly to the left side of the screen to begin scanning the next horizontal line, maintaining this pattern till it reaches the bottom of the screen; the right side of the last line. It then, returns back to the top to continue the process. This movement of electron beam from the right side to the left of the next scanned line or from the right bottom line to the left top line is called flyback or retrace. The movement from the left to the right side and back to the next scanned line is horizontal retrace while the movement from the right bottom to the left top is called vertical retrace. These patterns are shown in figure 7.2
[Figure 7.2: Retrace movement of scanning beam]

7.3.2 SCANNING FREQUENCIES AND (TIME) INTERVAL


7.3.2.1 Horizontal and Vertical Scanning Frequencies

Horizontal scanning frequency is the rate at which the electron scanning beam completes its cycle of horizontal motion from left to right on a picture frame and back to left again, ready to start the next horizontal scan. It is also called line frequency. The value of line frequency is 15750 Hz for NTSC TV system and 15625 Hz for European system. The number of horizontal scanning lines in a complete picture frame is 525 lines and 625 lines for NTSC and European TV system respectively. During the (interlaced) scanning, 25 frames of European TV screen or 30 frames of NTSC TV screen are scanned in 1 second. Since there are 625 lines in a frame for European system, suffice it to say that 625 x 25 lines (15625 lines) will be scanned in one second. So, the scanning frequency for 25 frames of the TV screen is 15625 Hz. For NTSC TV system, the line frequency is as a result of scanning 30 frames of 525 lines each which gives 15750 Hz (i.e 525 lines x 30 frames). The time (period) for each scanning line is 1/15,750 Hz (= 63.5𝜇sec) for America TV system and 1/15,625 Hz (= 64𝜇sec) for European system. This is also referred to as horizontal line interval or simply, line interval which is defined as the time it takes electron beam to scan or trace out one horizontal scan line. Vertical scanning frequency is the frequency (field rate) at which the electron beam completes its cycle of vertical motion from top to bottom and back to top again ready to start the next vertical scan. The value of this field rate is 60 Hz for NTSC TV and that of Europe is 50 Hz. Therefore, vertical deflection circuits for the camera tube and picture tube operate at 60 Hz or 50 Hz. The time of each vertical scanning cycle for one field is 1/60 sec or 1/50 sec.
7.3.2.2 Trace and Retrace Time As we have mentioned, a horizontal scan line has a period of 63.5 usec and 64 usec for NTSC TV system and European TV system respectively. These line periods cover trace and retrace movement of the electron beam. In each of the TV system, about 10 usec is given for line retrace of the beam which is about 16% of the line interval. This is called retrace interval and it expresses the time it takes an electron beam to
move from the end of one line to the start of the next lower line. During this time, there is no scanning, therefore there is a blanking in the scene. Hence the active time to trace a line in both systems is the total period of a scan line minus the retrace time. This therefore, gives approximately 53.5 usec and 54 usec for NTSC and Europe’s TV system respectively.

7.3.2.3 Vertical Trace and Retrace Time

The time period to for a vertical scan is the reciprocal of the of the field frequency. The field frequency for NTSC TV system is 60 Hz and that of European system is 50Hz. Hence the duration (time period) for vertical scanning is 1/60 Hz for NTSC TV and 1/50 Hz for European system. Following these, the time period for the vertical scanning for the respective TV systems are 0.0167 sec and 0.02 sec (16.7 msec and 20 msec). Out of these given periods, experiments showed that 21 horizontal scan lines are used up during the vertical retrace in NTSC TV and 20 in European system. If we remember that each horizontal line scan takes period of 63.5 usec for NTSC TV and 64 usec for European TV system, we can then determine the vertical trace and retrace time of the electron scan beam. The vertical retrace time are given as: NTSC TV system: 21 used horizontal scan line during vertical retrace, that is, 21 scan lines x 63.5 usec = 1.333msec European TV system: 20 used horizontal scan line during vertical retrace, that is, 20 scan lines x 64 usec = 1.28 msec. The active vertical trace for each of the TV system is the difference between the (total) vertical scan period and the retrace time. Therefore, following the results above, the (active) time for the vertical retrace of the TV systems is; NTSC system: 16.7 – 1.333 = 15.4 msec European TV system: 20-1.28 =18.7 msec

7.3.3 SCANNING TECHNIQUES

During scanning, horizontal scan lines are scanned one after the other from one side of the TV display to the other until it gets to the last line. In the scanning process, each of the lines can be scanned one after another consecutively or can be scanned in
alternate manner, that is, when one line is scanned, the next consecutive line is jumped after which the process starts again from the beginning to scan the lines skipped. The former method is called progressive scanning while the latter is called interlaced scanning.

7.3.3.1 Progressive Scanning

In progressive scanning, image is created and displayed on the screen by scanning each horizontal line (or row of pixel) in a sequential order rather than alternate order. In other words, in progressive scanning, the image lines are scanned in numerical sequence (1, 2, 3…) down the screen from top to bottom, instead of an alternate order where the odd lines 1, 3, 5… are scanned first followed by even lines of 2,4,6…Progressive scanning is much simpler than interlaced scanning because each line is scanned consecutively until a complete frame is drawn. The major disadvantages are that it occupies more bandwidth and it is more susceptible to flicker. This type of scanning is used in high definition television (HDTV) system.

7.3.3.2 Interlaced Scanning

In this scanning method, the scan lines of a scene (full picture frame) are scanned in alternate manner and the full frame is scanned twice to produce a complete picture. This is because the scan lines of the picture frame in this technique are divided into odd and even lines. Each set of the lines makes a field, which is half of the frame. A field in NTSCTV system contains 2621/2 lines. The 2621/2 lines are scanned in 1/60 of a second at the first beam movement after which there is a fly back. The other field (scan lines of even numbers) of the remaining 2621/2 lines are scanned at the second movement of the beam in such a way that the scan lines fall in-between those of the first field. This brings the total time it takes to scan one full frame to twice the time it takes to scan one field, that is, 1/30 sec (1/60x 2) for NTSC TV. The total scanning (first and second beam movement) produces the interlaced scanning, with a total of 2 x 2621/2 lines (= 525 lines). In European system where the field rate is 50 Hz with 3121/2 lines per field, the interlace scanning produces a total of 625 scan lines (2 x 3121/2 lines) scan at a time period of 1/25 ( 1/50 x 2) sec During the entire interlace scanning process, if we could stop video scanning of a picture frame to observe a single video field, we would see that every alternate line is missing in a frame. The first scan process will contain only the odd lines (1,3,5,7…)
of the frame while after the flyback, the second process will contain the even lines (2,4,6,8…). Each of the scanned field appears like a comb. The two interlaced fields produce a complete frame of video. With this rate of the interlaced scanning, as it is very fast enough, human eye cannot detect individual scan lines and therefore sees a stable picture.
Figure7.3: Interlace scanning of picture
As shown in figure 7.3, when the two fields are interlaced, we have a clearer picture as shown in the figure. This is how video camera produces image of a scene using interlace scanning. However, in practice, a further reduction occurs beyond the ~485 NTSC / ~585 European visible lines already established (Chapter 5) from vertical-blanking line loss. The Kell factor further reduces the effective resolution of these visible lines (as detailed in Chapter 5, section 5.6.11), rather than being the cause of the 485/585-line figures themselves. The major advantage of interlace scanning is that it is used to reduce flicker effect. Flicker is annoying to the eye but, as the fields are changing at twice the frame rate, there will be less perceived flicker than if each frame was scanned progressively. However, interlace scanning creates some distortion due to the slight delay during the refresh time between the odd and even lines of the field.

7.3.3.2 Solving Flicker Effect Using Interlace Scanning

Flicker is an undesired effect of discontinuity between the two picture frames which occurs during scanning process as jerky appearance of motion due to insufficient scanning frequency. In TV system, 30 picture frames or 25 picture frames are scanned per second. This implies that a complete scene (frame) is traced between every sec or        sec depending on the TV system.
The 30 picture frames or 25 picture frames scanned per second is not enough to create an illusion of continuity to the eye or “trick” the eye from observing discontinuous between two picture frames (flicker). This is to say that flicker arises because of insufficient frame rate and this effect is made more severe when the screen is made black and white alternatively. To “kill” flicker, a way of increasing the frame frequency to double (i.e 60 picture frames per second or 50 frames per second) has to be devised. If the frame frequency were increased to the double directly, the flicker would no longer be noticeable, but the video signal bandwidth would have to be doubled leading to the bandwidth that is out of requirement for the video transmission. Instead of that solution of doubling the picture frame, the process of interlaced scanning is used to “trick” the human eye into thinking it is seeing 60 or 50 picture frame per second.

7.4 SYNCRONIZATION IN TV SYSTEM

Synchronization is a very important process in TV system which facilitates the transmitter and receivers to work at the same pace without any delay, making the receiver stays in step or run at exactly the same speed with the transmitter. Without synchronization, the receiver will run at different speeds with the transmitter, either slower or faster, causing the scanned image on the screen of the picture tube to skew diagonally to left or diagonally to the right. To enhance the synchronization process, synchronizing pulses are generated at the transmitter and are added to the picture information generated by scanning process. It is this synchronization requirement of TV system that makes video transmissions more complex than sound transmission. As with the case of scanning, synchronization is of both horizontal synchronization and vertical synchronization. For the horizontal and vertical synchronization, both line and vertical synchronizing pulses are generated in the transmitter and transmitted together with the picture information.

7.4.1 TRANSMITTER- RECEIVER SYNCHRONIZING PROCESS

The ways in which synchronization process helps in transmitter – receiver “interaction” are as follows; 1. When the TV camera starts scanning line 1, the receiver (must) also start scanning line 1 on the CRT output display. This prevents the top of the scene (picture) appearing at the center of the TV screen. 2. The receiver scans each line with exactly the same speed the transmitter scans each line during scanning process. This helps to avoid distortion in the receiver output. 3. Synchronization makes it possible for the time when the electron beam is returned back to the left-hand side to start tracing a new line (horizontal flyback) occur coincidentally at both transmitter and receiver. This prevents the horizontal lines starting at the centre of the TV screen. 4. When a complete set of horizontal lines have been scanned, moving the electron beam from the end of the bottom line to the start of the top line (vertical flyback) must occur simultaneously at both transmitter and receiver. This is possible due to synchronization.

7.5 COMPOSITE VIDEO SIGNAL

[Figure 7.4: Composite video signal for three arbitrary lines]
Figure 7.4 shows the arbitrary signal of video signal components in three different lines. (They do not represent consecutive lines). In the figure, various components of the video signal are marked. The composite video signal consists of various major components. These are picture information, blanking pulses, synchronizing pulses, and equalizing pulses. The picture information is obtained due scanning beam in the camera tube. The blanking and synchronization pulses work together. A blanking pulse comes first to put the video signal (picture information) at black level, then a synchronizing pulse comes to start the retrace. The sequence applies to blanking horizontal and vertical retraces during picture formation (scanning) process. The equalizing pulses are used for proper field synchronization.

7.5.1 BLANKING PULSES

In television system, ‘blanking’ means going to black. As part of the video signal, the blanking voltage is at the black level. Video at the black level cuts off electron beam current in the picture tube at the receiver to black out light from screen during the time the beam must retrace to get ready for the next scan. Then, blanking pulses are added to the video signal to make the retrace of the beam invincible. As shown in figure 7.5, the amplitude of the video signal during pulses is made 75% of maximum value.
[Figure 7.5:Blanking pulses]
The video signal remains at the level of 75% during complete horizontal and vertical blanking interval. Normally the picture becomes fully black and electron beam is cut- off when video signal goes above 72%. Thus extra 8% amplitude is allowed for blanking pulses. The blanking pulses are of two types, namely; horizontal blanking pulse and vertical blanking pulse.

7.5.1.1 Horizontal Blanking Pulses

The horizontal blanking pulse comes along after a scanned line to blank out the (scan) retrace from right to left for each line. This pulse lasts about 16% of scan line period (63.5𝜇sec) for each horizontal line. The width of the horizontal blanking pulse is 10.2𝜇sec. (That is, 63.5𝜇secx 0.16). This width is the horizontal blanking time. This entails that the retrace from the right to left must be completed within 10.2𝜇sec, before the start of visible picture information of the horizontal scanning.

7.5.1.2 Vertical Blanking Pulses

The vertical blanking pulses blanks out the picture tube during the vertical retrace. Together with synchronizing pulses, it initiates the retracing of electron beam from bottom to top of the scene at the end of each field so that the next field can be scanned. The time period for the vertical blanking pulse is approximately 8% of the time for each vertical field. The total time for vertical scan is 1/60sec, including the downward trace and upward retrace. Therefore, the vertical blanking time for each field is 1/60 x 0.08 (= 0.0013 sec or 1.3 ms) for NTSC TV. For the European system, the value is 1.6 ms (i.e. 1/50 x 0.08). It (the vertical blanking time) therefore, means that within 1.3 ms or 1.6 ms, as case may be, the vertical retrace must be completed from bottom to top of the picture.

7.5.1.3 Blanking Level

The video signal due to picture is allowed to vary from 10% to 75% of its maximum level. The peak white level is fixed at 10 to 12.5% of the maximum level of the signal. Thus, the video signal due to picture will not go below 10% of its maximum value. The maximum value of the video signal due to pictures details is 75%. This level is called blanking level. At the blanking level, the picture is fully black as a result of electron beam cutoff.

7.5.2 SYNCHRONIZING PULSES

Synchronizing pulses are used to maintain synchronization of frame/fields and horizontal scanning lines. To produce a true and undistorted picture on the TV screen, it is necessary that the scanning process at the transmitter camera tube should be quite in step with that at the receiver picture tube. Thus, the timing pulses called synchronizing pulses, referred to as sync pulses, are generated by the synchronizing generator to perform this function. The sync pulses are added to video signal, during the retrace periods of the beam and above blanking pulses, to ensure that the scanning sequences of transmitter and TV receiver are the same. The video (picture) to sync pulses amplitude ratio becomes 10:4. This ratio is found optimum. The pulses occupy the amplitude range of 75% to 100% in the composite video signal. This does not affect the video signal since no information is sent during retrace periods. In this sort of mechanism, the sync pulses are time multiplexed with video signal. The sync pulse can be classified as horizontal sync pulse and vertical sync pulse.

7.5.2.1 Horizontal Sync Pulses

The horizontal sync pulses, otherwise referred to as line synch pulses, are transmitted to synchronize the horizontal scanning at receiver with that at transmitter. Each line sync pulse is inserted in the video signal within the time of horizontal blanking pulse. The line sync pulse occupies the amplitude range from 75% to 100% of composite video signal. That is, the line sync pulse is present above blanking level (Darker than dark). The width of the line sync pulse is 0.075H, that is 0.075 ×64 µsec = 4.8 µsec. Given allowance for tolerance, the width of the line pulse can be from 4.5 to 4.9 µsec. There are two points at the line synch pulses; the point that is before the line synch pulse and the point that follows it. The former is called front porch while the latter is called back porch. Front Porch The front porch is present before the line sync pulse. The amplitude of front porch is at blanking level, that is, 75% of composite video signal. The width of the front porch
is 0.025H, which gives 0.025H x 64 µsec = 1.6 µsec. With tolerance, the width of the front porch can be from 1.3 to 1.8 µsec. During the front porch the video signal reaches to blanking level which is fixed. This allows every line sync pulse to build up from fixed amplitude level. Hence the amplitude of the line sync pulses remains uniform at the receiver. But, if front porch is absent, the line sync pulse has to go to 100% level from varying amplitude levels of the video signal. Thus, as shown in figure7.6, whatever level of the picture signal at the end of nth line, the sync pulse always starts from fixed amplitude levels.
[Figure 7.6: Detail of horizontal synchronization and blanking pulse]
Because of front porch, the video circuits get some time to settle down to blanking level. Also the sync circuits at the receiver are isolated from the effect of varying amplitude levels of picture signal at the end of every line. Therefore, the start of the scanning line is normally measured from line sync pulse. This is because front porch is present at the end of scanning line. Back Porch The back porch follows line sync pulse. The duration of the back porch is 0.09 H, that is about 5.8 µsec width (0.09 X 64 µsec, = 5.76 µsec). The amplitude of the back
porch remains fixed at blanking level i.e. 75%. The back porch serves following purposes: 1. It is used to restore the d. c content of the video signal at the receiver 2. Since the amplitude level of the back porch is independent of the picture details, it is used by AGC circuits to develop AGC voltage proportional to signal amplitude during this period. 3. The back porch is used to send the colour subcarrier during colour transmission.
[Figure 7.7: Horizontal synchronization and blanking signal]

7.5.2.2 Vertical Sync Pulses

The vertical sync pulses are added at the end of every field. Therefore, the frequency of vertical sync pulses becomes 50 Hz. The width of the vertical synch pulse is 2.5 to 3 times the horizontal line period or 160 𝜇sec. The longer width is essential to distinguish between horizontal sync pulse and vertical sync pulse at the receiver. Figure 7.8 shows the composite video signal waveforms during vertical synchronization.
[Figure 7.8: composite video signal waveforms.]
As shown in the figure 7.8, we observe that the vertical sync pulse width is equal to 2.5 horizontal lines. During the vertical sync pulse period, the video signal amplitude is 100% except serrations. Serrations are basically narrow slots in the vertical sync pulses at a half line interval (32 𝜇sec) which are used to prevent the lost in the receiver’s synchronization scanning sequence due to absence of horizontal sync pulse at a particular period. 7.5.2.3 Line Blanking Period
During the line blanking period, the electron bean is cutoff. The line blanking period is the sum of front porch width, line sync width and the back porch width. The total width (time duration) value is around 0.19 H. For the horizontal scan period of 64 µsec, the line blanking period becomes 0.19 x 64 µsec= 12.16 µsec.
Width of the line blanking pulse = front porch width + line sync width + Back porch width
Width of the line blanking pulse = 1.6 µsec + 4.8 µsec+ 5.76 µsec =12.16 µsec

7.5.2.4 The Visible Line Time

The visible line time, or again referred to as active trace period of line is the difference between the horizontal scanning period and the line blanking period.
During the line blanking period, the electron bean is cutoff. Thus, the visible line time or active trace period of line becomes about 51 µsec. This value is gotten from the difference between the horizontal scanning period and the visible line time
The visible line time =64 – 12.16 =51.84 µsec

7.5.2.5 Separation of Sync Pulses

The horizontal and vertical sync pulses are separated at the receiver by a sync separator.
[Figure 7.9: Sync separator]
Figure 7.9 shows the simplified diagram of a sync separator. As shown, the sync separator is normally a transistor amplifier. It is biased such that only vertical and horizontal pulses of amplitude levels above 75% are passed at the output. These pulses are given to the integrator and differentiator of the sync separator circuit simultaneously. The integrator capacitor C2 charges during vertical synchronization period. This is because, the ON period of the signal is more compared to its OFF period. Therefore, voltage builds up across C2 as shown in figure 7.9, C2 does not charge during horizontal sync pulses since the duty cycle of the wave form is very
small. That is, C2 charges to some small amplitude during horizontal sync period, but discharges fully because of large OFF time of the signal. Thus, the voltage builds up across C2 only during vertical sync period. This voltage is compared with some threshold and used as vertical sync pulse for the deflection circuits.
The differentiator differentiates the input wave form and produces spikes across R1. These spikes are produced during vertical pulses and they are used as trigger signals for the horizontal deflection circuits.

7.5.3 EQUALIZING PULSES

Equalizing pulses are used for proper field synchronization. These pulses are used to remove the effect of half-line discrepancy in the charging action of a capacitor in sync separator circuit. With the addition of equalizing pulses in the video signal, the waveform appears as shown in figure 7.10
Figure7.10:Composite video signal waveforms with equalizing pulses
From the figure 7.10, it is shown that five equalizing pulses are added before the vertical sync pulse starts and another five equalizing pulses are added after vertical sync pulse. The former are called pre-equalizing pulses while the later are called post- equalizing pulses. In the figure 7.10 we observe that the pre-equalizing pulses occupy 2.5 lines before vertical sync pulse starts. Similarly, post-equalizing pulses occupy
2.5 lines after the vertical sync pulse. Again, the equalizing pulses are added just like horizontal sync pulses at half line intervals and the width is 2.3 𝜇sec. 7.5.3.1 Vertical Field Blanking Interval
This is the sum of vertical sync pulse, pre-equalizing sync pulse, post-equalizing sync pulse and blanking lines. This is equal to about 20 horizontal lines or approximately 1280 𝜇sec. 7.5.4 AMPLITUDE RANGE OF (COMPOSITE) VIDEO SIGNAL

7.5.4.1 Darker Than Dark

This is the amplitude range of the video signal above blanking level (i.e 75% to 100%). This amplitude range is used for sync pulses. 7.5.4.2 Whiter Than White
This is the amplitude range of the video signal below peak white level (i.e 0 to 10%). This amplitude range is used to accommodate excessive bright spots in the picture without causing amplitude distortion in the modulator.

7.5.5 PICTURE BRIGHTNESS OF THE COMPOSITE VIDEO SIGNAL


7.5.5.1 DC Level of the Signal

The video signal always has d. c component. This d. c component represents average brightness of the picture. In figure 7.4, we observe that the video signal due to three lines has some d. c value. Since these lines are from different frames, their d. c levels are different. This is because the average brightness of these frames may not be same. However, we should note that the d. c value of the video signal remains almost same with consecutively scanning lines. This is because the consecutive scanning lines combinely represent one picture frame and average brightness of the picture frame remains same. Hence d. c level of these lines will also remain same. 7.5.5.2 Pedestal height
Pedestal height is the distance between blanking level and d. c values of the signal. This height represents the true level of brightness of the picture, since it represents
how much the average value differs from black level. Hence, the pedestal height is used to indicate average brightness of the picture. 7.5.5.3 Brightness control
When we adjust the brightness of the picture with help of brightness control, the pedestal height or d. c level of the video signal is adjusted. 7.5.5.4 Contrast control
Contrast is the difference between black and white. This difference is indicated by peak to peak variation in the video signal. These peak to peak variations of the video signal take place around the d. c level. As the contrast is more, the peak to peak variations of video signal increases.

7.6 TV BROADCAST CHANNELS

Contents It is not possible to directly transmit the video signals. This is because, video signal have low frequency and antennas required will be very large in size. Also if TV signals from two different stations are to be transmitted in the same area, then the signal will interfere with each other. Hence video signal is transmitted in various channels by modulating the carrier frequencies. From our previous discussions, we see that video / carriers are amplitude modulated by video signal and sound carrier is frequency modulated by sound signal. Two different video signals can be transmitted over two different broadcasting channels. Since the channel frequencies are different, they do not interfere with each other. Thus it is possible to receive many TV programmes simultaneously. The frequencies of TV broadcast channels are normally in the VHF and UHF range, hence, they travel long distances. The sizes of antennas to transmit and receive such frequencies are small. It is essential that the carrier frequency be chosen about ten times of the highest modulating frequency. Hence, the frequencies used to transmit television channels should be above 40 to 50 MHz. 7.6.1 FREQUENCY ALLOCATION OF TV CHANNELS
The TV channels are specified in two frequency ranges; UHF and VHF. The frequencies allocated for various bands in those ranges are shown in table 7.1

title: Principles of Colour TV
text:

8.2 COLORIMETRY IN ANALOGE COLOUR TELEVISION

In colour TV signal transmission, the Uadvantage is made of how human eyes perceive colour in nature either by colour subtractive mixing or colour additive
mixing. As we may know, natural light contains all colour range which mixed up to give the white light. The white light can be made to split into all colours it contains with help of glass prism and all those colours which are visible to the eyes are actually part of the electromagnetic wave emitted by the sun. If the human eyes see a particular colour of object or scene as against white colour, it simply means that the object has absorbed all other colours of white light and reflected (throw off) that particular colour which the eyes see. For instance, if an object appears green, it is interpreted that all other colours of the white light have been absorbed by the object but it throws off (reflected) the green colour which the eyes see. In two extreme cases; we have a situation where the whole light of the nature are absorbed or reflected. When the whole natural white light areabsorbedby an object, the scene appears black but when they are all reflected, the scene appears white to the eye. Using the instances of the above natural phenomenon, scientists and artists can manipulate the human eyes into seeing any colour they wish them to see and the range of colour to manufacture is endless. This can be achieved with either colour subtractive mixing or colour additive mixing. The former is used by artists for painting while the latter is used by scientists and engineers. It is also the techniques involved with the later that is used in development of colour television system.

8.2.1 SUBTRACTIVE COLOUR MIXING

[Figure 8.1: Subtractive colour mixing circle]
In subtractive colour mixing, two or more colours are mixed. These mixed colours absorb all the wave length but reflect their characteristics colour wavelengths which are common to both. For example, when white and blue colours are mixed, we get sky blue. Sky blue reflects the wavelength of white as well as blue. Thus subtractive mixing of colour is used in artistic painting and colour printing. The subtractive colour mixing can be illustrated as shown in figure 8.1. The figure shows three primary colours; Green, (G) Blue (B) and Red (R) mixed on a white background in subtractive mode.

8.2.2 ADDITIVE COLOUR MIXING

Additive colour mixing does not make use of the principle of colour reflection. Here, the lights of two or more colour light sources are combined. The colour of the combined light is different from the new colour. Figure 8.2 shows additive mixing of colours. If we compare figure 8.2 with figure 8.1 we shall notice that they are the same colours in the three circles, but the colours in figure 8.1 are gotten as effect of after reflection from white object while the colours in figure 8.2 are perceived by the eye without any reflection. So, the colours of figure 8.2 are the results of direct mixing from the source. Thus, with the help of Red, Green and Blue as primary colours, it is possible to generate wide range of colours with an additive colour mixing.
[Figure 8.2: Addictive colour mixing circle]
8.2.3 HUMAN EYES AND THE BRAIN INTERACTION IN INTERPRETATION OF COLOUR MIXING
The human eye, according to scientists, has two light sensitive organs called rods and cones. The function of the rods is to provide the brightness information of the radiation coming to the eye. They sense all the shades from white to black and convey the information to the brain. On the other hand, the cones are sensitive to only colour information. There are three groups of cones, one group that is sensitive to only red colour, the second group is sensitive to only green and the third group is only sensitive to blue. Thus, the relative amounts of only red, green and blue colours are sensed by each group of the cones respectively. These amounts (proportions of the primary colours) are integrated in the brain along with brightness information provided by the rods to produce actual colour of the scene or object. This integration is exactly the additive mixing of Red, Green and Blue colours. Therefore, only red, green and blue colours are used by human eye to generate complete range of colours. It is this principle of human eyes and brain interaction in interpretation of colour that is employed in colour TV system.

8.3 TELEVISION COLOUR SIGNAL; application of colorimetry

The television colour signal actually consists of two components, luminance and chrominance which are the quantities by which any coloured lights are possibly specified in colour television system. The luminance is the measure of the colour brightness while the chrominance is the colour difference resulting when the luminance has been extracted from the primary colours. Red, Green and Blue colours are the primary colours and are used as fundamental colours to generate complete colour range. Those complete colour range can be shown on one circle called colour circle. The colour circle is as shown in figure 8.3.
[Figure 8.3: Colour circle]
As can be seen from the colour circle, the colour difference signals (R-Y) and (B-Y) are the right angles, on the colour circle. (R-Y) represents the purplish red hue and (B-Y) represents the purplish blue hue. The location of other colours like red, green, blue etc. are also shown on the circle. Since the colours are plotted on the circle, the colours with 180° phase shift with each other are also possible. These 180 phase shift colours are called complementary colours of each other. For example, the complimentary colour of magenta is green which is at 180° from magenta. + (R-Y) represents purplish red colour. Its complementary colour is bluish green at 180° phase shift and written as -(R-Y). Similarly, + (B-Y) and -(B-Y) are complementary colour of each other. 8.3.1 COLOUR LUMINANCE
This is otherwise referred to as brightness or brilliance of a colour. It is the intensity level of light which does not depend on the colour. Every colour has different luminance level if excited by equal light intensity. The eye’s response in respect of sensitivity to different colours varies. For instance, Green, Yellow and Blue have more luminance level compared to Violet and Red. Thus on Black and white TV set, Green and yellow will appear as light gray or white, Blue will appear as gray but Violet and Red will appear as black.

8.3.2 COLOUR CHROMINANCE

Chrominanceis defined as that part of the colour specification remaining when the luminance is removed. In itself, it has two aspects that combine to make it. These are hue (colour of the light) and saturation (colour intensity). These two are independent qualities.

8.3.2.1 Hue

It is the predominant spectral colour of the light perceive by the eyes. It can be said to be the “colourness” of the light such as the redness, orangeness, blueness, greenness etc of the light.

8.3.2.2 Saturation

Saturation represents the spectral purity of colour. It is rare that we see colour of only one wavelength. Always, other colours are mixed in the dominant colour by small amount. Saturation therefore, indicates by what amount the colour is diluted due to other colours. For example, dark green is fully saturated whereas light green contains some white. Same is applied to other colours. In summary, hue, saturation and luminance are three parameters which represent the colour completely. When Hue and saturation information of colour are combined, then it is called chrominance of the colour. Thus we can further say that chrominance and luminance can represent the colour completely.
8.3.3 CHROMINANCE–LUMINANCE SIGNAL GENERATION IN COLOUR TV SYSTEM
In any colour television broadcasting system, the colour (chrominance) signals must be transmitted along with the luminance information in the same bandwidth allotted to the TV signal. The transmitted information is combined into two chrominance signals and the luminance signal instead of being transmitted as separate three primary colour signals in their original forms. The chrominance signals are also known as colour difference signals. Generally, the colour difference signals are represented as R-Y, B-Y and G-Y. This is because the combination of the three colour signals produces the effect of subtracting the luminance signal (Y signal) from the R, B and G signals, that is, they contain information about the hue and saturation of a colour
and no luminance. Usually, the G-Y signal is mostly not used because it has the least magnitude and it is more easily affected by noise and distortions during transmission. Therefore, during transmission, it is the luminance and two of the chrominance signals, R-Y and B-Y that are usually in use. The manner in which these signals are transmitted is that they are used to modulate a subcarrier signal which is in turn mixed with the luminance Y signal to form a complete, or composite video signal. During the process of the colour signal transmission, R-Y and B-Y colour difference signals are modulated differently before they are combined as a phasor addition. The results of the phasor addition are two chrominance components of the combined information signals: hue or tint, which is the phase, and the saturation, which is the amplitude.
