8.4 COLOUR TV VIDEO CAMERA

[Figure 8.5: Colour TV video camera]
Colour TV video camera is more complex than the monochrome types. It is actually three-different TV (monochrome) cameras in one package, each with a colour band- pass filter for one of the three primary colours, red, green, and blue, an optical system that cast an identical image on the sensitive surface of each one and a summing network which is a matrix circuit. Each part of the camera carries out a particular function in the process of colour image signal generation. This is shown in figure 8.5. The optical system consists of lens and four mirrors that reflect the image rays from the lens on to the three tubes. Two of the mirrors are of a colour-selective type (a dichroic mirror) that reflect the light of one colour and transmits the remaining colours. The mirrors, augmented by colour bandpass filters that perfect their colour- selective action, directed a blue image to the first tube, a green image to the second, and a red image to the third. The overall process in the three tubes (are designed to) produce identical scans of the scene, so that their respective picture signals represents images of the same geometric shape, differing only in colour. The three signals are independently transmitted to the receiver, where each colour signal may be applied to a separate monochrome CRT, which produces the appropriate colour.

8.4.1 COLOUR SIGNAL GENERATION IN THE COLOUR TV CAMERA

The TV colour signals consist of the two components of an object or a scene’s colour; luminance level and chrominance. The video luminance is black and white version of the scene. The chrominance, been the colour details of a scene or object, is somehow represented by an electrical signal. The colour signals in analogue electrical signal forms, as shown analytically in last section, are generated by colour TV video camera. However, the video camera does not produce these colour components of a scene directly. What it actually does is to produce picture signals that represent the amounts of the three primary colours (blue, green and red) present at each point in the image pattern. This is done by dividing the light in each scan line into three (3) separate signals, each representing one of the three primary (basic) colours. From these three
primary colours signals, the luminance and chrominance components of the object are derived by manipulation in electronic circuits of the camera. In the video camera, the processes of the colour picture generation and conversion into electrical signal that is used for modulation takes place.

8.4.2 THE PROCESS OF GENERATING COLOUR SIGNAL IN THE VIDEO CAMERA

There are a few steps involved in the operation of the video camera. These steps are in order of image focusing, input image splitting, image colour filtering, colour image scanning and colour summation. An object or a scene focuses on the lens of the video camera. The lens then channels the object on colour separator. The colour separator as shown the circuit in figure 8.5 above is an assembly of beam splitters and mirrors. The beam splitter splits the input image into three (3) images. The mirrors are diachronic mirrors that pass only one wavelength and reject all other wavelengths. By the action of the mirrors in passing only one wavelength, one serves as red filter, passing only red (R) portion ofthe scene. The same process is achieved by the blue (B) and green (G) filters to generate blue and green colours of the scene respectively. Each of the filters has an image sensor (image pick-up) device placed directly in front of it. The image sensor device placed in front of filters scans the resulting filtered colour and converts it into an equivalent electrical signal. By this process, R, B and G electrical signals are generated from the filtered R, B and G colours. After the signal generation, these three separate colours are fed into a summing electrical network for the signal processing. The processing action of the summing network results in luminance signal and chrominance signal. The luminance signal represents brightness information of the scene. To achieve the luminance in the right proportion of red, green, and blue, the resistors RR, RG, and RB of the summing network (adder circuit) are selected such that the summation of the voltages across each in the set proportion gives the value of the luminance signal. The voltages across each of the resistors, RR, RG, and RB are respectively, VR, VG and VB . Therefore, the luminance signal in terms of the voltages across each of the resistors is given as;
Y= 0.3VR+0.59VG+0.11VB                                               …8.4.1
The maximum value of Y is 1 unit when the values of VR, VG, and VB are 1 unit as well. VR is electric voltage from red camera image pick-up sensor. VG and VB are from green and blue camera image pick-up sensors respectively. These voltages are generated by scaling each colour signal with a tapped voltage divider. These generated signals are then passed to transmitter where they are used for modulation. It is this resulting Y signal that a Black and White TV set will see during the signal reception.

8.4.3 CHARGE COUPLE DEVICES (CCDS) IN COLOUR TV CAMERA

The colour cameras that use CCDs use separate CCDs array sensors. A colour CCD image sensor uses a checkerboard pattern of transparent colour filters. These filters can represent the three primary colours of Red, Green and Blue, thereby generating the electrical signals corresponding to the three primary colours. Alternatively, glass prism can be used to separate the image into its three primary colours. In this mode, the image from the lens is passed through a colour splitter system comprising a prism and special filtering mirrors to separate the image into three, each containing one of the primary colour components of the original image; in that case, three separate CCD sensors are used, one for each primary colour. These images are aligned on the three sensor arrays which are scanned synchronously to produce the three colour signals need to produce the luminance signal and two chrominance components for transmission.

8.5 COLOUR PICTURE TUBE

The operation of a colour picture tube is identical to that of monochrome picture tube which was described in section 7 of chapter 6. However, to produce colour in the picture tube, the inside face is coated with many tiny Red, Green, And Blue phosphor dots arranged in groups of three called triads or arranged in a pattern of red, green and blue stripes. The tube contains separate cathodes and three identical electron guns that are energized and driven by the red, green, and blue colour signals to develop three separate beams of electrons. These beams of electrons hit the colour phosphor. When
the electron beams bombard the phosphor colour dots or stripes, one will glow Red, another will glow Blue, and the third will glow Green. In between the electron guns and colour phosphor screen (triad screen called dot-triad screen for the colour dot or stripe phosphor screen for phosphor stripe) is placed a metallic plate holes called shadow mask. The function of the shadow mask is to ensure that the correct beam strikes the correct colour dot or stripe for each colour on the phosphor screen. By varying the intensity of the colour beams, the dot triads or the stripe can be made to produce any colour. These fine particles of the primary colours in the phosphor are small enough so that the eye cannot see them individually at a distance. What the eye sees is a colour picture swept out on the surface of the tube.

8.5.1 TYPES OF COLOUR PICTURE TUBES

There are three types of colour picture tube depending on how the phosphor colours (red, green and blue) are arranged in the electron gun used in the construction. These three are delta gun colour picture tube, precision in line (PIL) colour tube and, Trinitron colour picture tube.

8.5.1.1 Delta Gun Colour Picture Tube

[Figure 8.6: Delta gun colour picture]
In this type of colour picture tube, the red, green and blue colour phosphors are in dots form and are arranged in triangular format called dot triads. This arrangement is shown in figure 8.6. There are around 1 x 106 dots on a screen called dot-triads screen. The screen is divided in three colours. A round hole perforated metal sheet called shadow maskis placed behind the screen, in between the electron guns and the dot- triads screen. The holes of this sheet are arranged in such a way that the electron beams hit their respective phosphor dots only, producing any colour when the intensity of the colour beams is varied. In the working of the Delta gun colour tube, most of the parts of electron beam are blocked by the shadow mask. Since the mask is conductive, it samples this beam and returns it to the ground. The hole only allows to pass the electron beam to screen. Only 20% of electrons pass to screen through shadow mask. Therefore, to maintain the required brightness, the beam current is increased. To avoid this, higher final anode voltages are used. Thus all colour picture tube use high final anode voltage compared to monochrome picture tube. 8.5.1.2 Precision in line Colour Picture Tube
[Figure 8.7:(PIL) colour picture tube]
In this type of picture tube, the electron guns from the tube are placed in line such that the electron beams of the red, green and blue colour signals are emitted in lines. In the colour phosphors screen, the three colours are arranged in vertical strips. There is a continuous strip from top to bottom of the screen for each colour. They are placed one after anode on the screen. In between the screen and electron gun is placed a transparent shadow mask which has slot shaped opening. The in-line electron beams pass through the slots of the perforated shadow mask and hit the respective strip. The principle of operation of precision in line (PIL) colour picture tube is shown in figure 8.7. The PIL offer better advantages than the delta gun. The electron transparency is better than that of delta gun since the shadow mask is slotted, therefore offering a better efficiency. The convergence adjustment is simple because of the in-line guns. 8.5.1.3 Trinitron colour picture tube
Figure 8.8 shows the working principle of the Trinitron colour picture tube. Though it may appear that the structure is the same with that of PIL, the difference and the specialty of the Trinitron is that that there is a single electron gun instead of three. The gun consists of three cathodes for red, green and blue beams.
[Figure 8.8: Trinitron colour picture tube]
Figure 8.8 shows the structure of this tube. As seen in the figure, there is a presence of a control grid G1. The control grid is a single unit with three apertures for the three beams. The convergence is achieved electrostatically by four convergence plates.
The advantage associated with this picture tube is that electron transparency is more, hence the brightness and efficiency of the tube increases. Again, the convergence becomes simple because of in-line beams.

8.5.2 BEAM CONVERGENCE IN COLOUR PICTURE TUBE

Beam convergence is important in colour picture tube and the main objective is to get the proper electron beams to strike its respective coloured phosphor dot. To make the three beams converge correctly on their colour dots or stripes of phosphor throughout the face of the tube requires special modification to the horizontal and vertical deflection systems. The beam convergence is of two modes; static convergence and dynamic convergence. Static convergence refers to proper beam convergence at the centre of the CRT’s face. This adjustment is made by d. c level changes in horizontal and vertical amplifiers. In dynamic convergence, the beams are converged away from the centre and it becomes more of a problem. But, it is necessary because the tube face away from the centre is not a perfectly spherical shape (it is more nearly flat), and thus the beams tend to converge in front of the shadow mask away from the tube centre. Special dynamic voltages are derived from the horizontal and vertical amplifier signals and are applied to a special colour convergence yoke placed around the tube yoke.

8.5.3 COLOUR PICTURE TUBE CIRCUITS

Any type of colour picture tube has a common circuit that summarises the working principles. Figure 8.9 shows how all the signals come together at the picture tube to produce the colour picture. The R, G and B signals are mixed with y signal (luminance) to control the cathodes of the CRT. Thus the beams are properly modulated to reproduce the colour picture. Note the various controls associated with the picture tube. The R-G-B screen, brightness, focus, and centering controls vary the d. c voltages that set the levels as desired. The convergence controls and assembly are used to control the positioning of the three electron beams so that they are centered on the holes in the shadow mask and the electron beams strike the colour dots or strip dead centre. The deflection yoke over the neck of the tube deflects all three electron beams simultaneously.
[Figure 8.9: Circuit diagram of colour picture tube]

8.5.4 DEGAUSSING OF THE PICTURE TUBES

Degaussing of the picture tube is the process of providing magnetic shielding to the tube so as to maintain or improve the colour purity of the tube. This is necessary because, localized magnetic fields effect and terrestrial magnetism affect the electron beam deviation. Due to the deviation, colour purity is affected. Again, when the location of the TV receiver is changed, stray field changes and affects also the picture purity. To overcome these drawbacks, degaussing is provided.

8.6 COLOUR TV RECEIVER

In the chapter 6, we treated the principle of monochrome TV receiver. It is worth noting that both monochrome and colour TV are somehow similar in function in many aspects such as in the tuner section,the IF amplifiers, the deflection circuits and the audio circuits. The basic TV signal reception processes are similar in both systems equally. Notwithstanding, there are a few modifications in some circuitry of the colour TV receiver in other to make it adequately handle the demodulation and display of the colour signals. Examples of such modification are in the video amplifier which has different features from that of the monochrome receiver, the
decoder section of the colour TV receiver decodes the three colour signals from the chrominance signal, while the equivalent section in the monochrome receiver decodes only one signal, and the picture tube of the colour TV receiver has three separate electron beam guns. In addition to some of these modifications, another major difference between the colour and monochrome TV receiver is the addition of colour decoder (camera) section which its major function is to detect and decode the three colour signals: R signal, B signal and G signal from the transmitted chrominance signal and controls the convergence of the three electron beams in the picture tube. The block diagram of the receiver is shown in figure 8.10 (see page 282)
8.6.1 DIFFERENCES BETWEEN MONOCHROME TV RECEIVER AND COLOUR TV RECEIVER
From the diagram of figure 8.10, (see page 282) when compared with the diagram of monochrome TV receiver in chapter 6, we will be able to draw some differences between the two. Some of such differences include the modification in tuner section. While the monochrome TV receiver uses a simple tuner section, the colour TV receiver uses VHF/UHF type of tuner. In colour TV receiver, there is the presence of a SAW device, connected in-between the tuner section and the video IF amplifier. Another difference is in RF the signal takeoff point. In monochrome TV receiver, the TV signals fed to the video amplifier, sound section, AGC and sync separator, all emanating from one takeoff point: the video detector. In colour TV, the feed point is from video amplifier (after video detector) to a four-way split that follows. The first path is to the input of sync separator circuit and deflection circuits, which functions in exactly the same manner as those in a monochrome set. The second path is to the AGC circuit. The third and the fourth are respectively to the colour matrix (Y signal) and colour decoder. Another difference is the type of detector used. While simple diode detector is used in monochrome receiver, synchronous demodulator is used in colour TV receiver. The colour TV CRT are driven by the amplified three colour signals, while the CRT of monochrome TV receiver does not have provision for the separate colour signals. These differences will form the bases of our discussion of the colour TV receiver in the following section.
[Figure 8.10: Block diagram of the colour TV receiver]

8.6.2 THE BASIC SECTIONS OF COLOUR TV RECEIVER

The basic sections of the TV receiver which mostly distinguish the receiver from the monochrome TV receiver are discussed below. Refer regularly to figure 8.10 for the sections in the colour receiver. 8.6.2.1 UHF/VHF Tuner
The tuner section of the colour TV receiver is the UHF/VHF tuner type. This type of tuner is a two-tuner-in-one, packaged in sealed and shielded enclosures, one for the VHF signals and another for the UHF signals. Figure 8.11 is a block diagram of the VHF/UHF tuner. The VHF tuner usually uses low-noise FETs for the RF amplifier and the mixer. UHF tuners use a diode mixer with no RF amplifier or a FET RF amplifier and mixer. In the UHF amplifier as shown in the figure by the portion inside the dashed lines, the antenna goes directly to the mixer.
The working of the tuner is such that when the tuner is switched to VHF channel 1, power is automatically removed from the VHF oscillator and applied to the UHF local oscillator. At the same time, the tuned circuits of the RF amplifier and the mixer to its right are switched to 45MHz, effectively converting them to IF for the output of the UHF diode mixer. This compensates for the gain lost because of the missing RF amplifier and brings the UHF output up to equal the level of the VHF output.
Switching the tuner to a VHF channel removes power from the UHF oscillator and sends it to the VHF local oscillator. In this way, only one oscillator operates at a time, thereby preventing the generation of signals that could cause interference. VHF signals are RF amplified, mixed and sent to the 45.75 MHz IF amplifier.
[Figure 8.11: Block diagram of the VHF/UHF tuner]

8.6.2.2 SAW Filter

[Figure 8.12:(a) Constructional feature of SAW filter(b) Frequency response of SAW filter device]
These devices are extremely High-Q filters used in modern TV and radar applications. In colour TV receiver, the SAW is placed in-between the tuner and IF amplifier to obtain a high selectivity of signal. It is a fixed tuned filter designed to provide the exact selectivity required to pass both of the IF signals (sound and video) with correct response to match the vestigial sideband signal transmitted. The SAW device works on the principle of piezoelectric effect. The only difference it has with the quartz crystal is that while the crystal relies on the effects in an entire solid of piezoelectric material to develop a frequency sensitivity, SAW devices rely on only the surface effects in piezoelectric materials (such as quartz or lithium niobate). With this device, it is possible to cause mechanical vibrations that travel across the solid’s surface, that is, the surface acoustic waves at about 3000m/s. The construction of SAW device is with electrode and piezoelectric substrate (quartz or lithium niobate). The electrode structure consists of interdigitated metallic strips. The electrode structures are referred as interdigitated transducers (IDT). The surface is set up at the input IDT. It travels along the surface in both directions. On one side, it reaches to the output IDT. On the other side, it is absorbed by absorber to avoid any reflections. The signal at the output IDT is bandpass filtered and shape according to the response of filter. Figure8.12(a) is the constructional feature of the SAW filter device and figure 8.12(b) is the frequency band response between the Video IF signal and the sound IF signal which the device control.

8.6.2.3 Video IF and Demodulation Section

The IF section is a stage where the IF signals produced after the heterodying processes at the tuner section are processed. In this section, there are two basic stages that take place; the amplification of the IF signals by IF amplifier and the demodulation of the IF signals by the video detector. We should remember that the IF signals is made up of the Video IF signal and the sound IF signal, and the standard TV receiver’s IFs are 41.25MHz for the sound and 45.75 MHz for the picture. Therefore, the entire demodulation after the IF amplifier, involves the video demodulation and sound demodulation. The sets that process the sound and video in the same IF stages are known as intercarrier system.
IF amplification is achieved using the IF amplifier. In this system, the IF amplifiers are specially designed to preserve the chrominance subcarrier signals during the amplification stages. This device is connected to the mixer’s output of the tuner, immediately after the SAW device. The IF signals (combination of sound IF and video IF signals) resulting from the heterodyning process in the tuner are next sent to it for proper amplification. The amplifier then magnifies the amplitudes of the IF signals and keep them at relatively fixed level.
The amplification of these IF signals at this stage is automatically adjusted, by a process known as automatic gain control through AGC circuit, in accordance with the strength of the signal, full amplification being accorded to a weak signal and less to a strong signal.
The tuning of the IF amplifiers need not be changed as the channel is switched, as a result, they can be adjusted for maximum performance in intermediate frequency range. After the amplification stage, the IF signals are demodulated by the video detector. The video detector used in colour TV receiver is a synchronous balanced
detector unlike the monochrome TV receiver that uses simple diode detector. The carriers and side bands are passed to it from the last IF amplifier stage. The detector develops the luminance component (Y signal) of the picture signal. This system is often referred to as video IF, even though it is also processing the sound signal. From the detector output, an averaging circuit or filter is placed which then at this point separates the picture and sound signals forming a picture signal, which is a close replica of the picture signal produced by the camera and synchronizing generator in the transmitter, and a frequency-modulated sound signal. The sound signal is passed through a sound intermediate amplifier and frequency detector (discriminator, or ratio detector) that converts the frequency modulated signal back to an audio signal current. This current is passed through one or two additional audio-frequency amplifier stages to the loudspeaker.

8.6.2.4 Video Amplifiers Section

The luminance component of the picture signal developed at the video detector output is applied simultaneously to all three electron guns of the colour picture tube through the video amplifier. The amplifier takes the output signal of the video detector and amplifies it to sufficient level capable to drive the CRT (picture tube cathode). The signal is then applied simultaneously to all three electron guns of the colour picture tube. This part of the signal thereby activates all three primary-colour images, simultaneously and identically, in the fixed proportion needed to produce white light. When tuned to monochrome signals, the colour receiver produces a black-and-white image by means of this mechanism, the chrominance component being absent. The separation of the luminance information from the composite picture signal can be accomplished through the use of a comb filter. This signal varies or modulates the electron beam strength of the CRT once applied to it, so that white and black spots of a scene are white and black spots on the CRT face. Of course, it causes electron beam strength of in-between magnitudes to provide various shades of gray.

8.6.2.5 Colour TV Decoder Section

This section is one of the major differences between monochrome TV receiver and colour TV receiver. The function which this section performs is usually, the reverse
of what happens in the transmitter’s camera, in accordance with the TV system of the receiver. It is the addition of this section, as a colour TV picture tube, that makes a colour TV receiver.
As the composite colour signals developed by the video detector as the output signals are amplified by the video amplifier, the Y signal component is used to create an AGC voltage for controlling the gain of the IF amplifiers, the tuner (RF) amplifier and mixers. From the video amplifier output, the composite colour signal is separated by a filter and fed to colour-balanced demodulator circuits. These circuits are called the colour decoder circuits. They perform the inverse operations of the addition and subtraction circuits at the transmitter. The end result of this manipulation performed by the decoders is the production of three colour-difference signals that represent respectively, the difference between the luminance signal (already applied to all three electron guns of the picture tube) and the primary-colour (R, G and B) signals. Each colour-difference signal reduces the strength of the corresponding electron beam to change the white light, which would otherwise be produced, to the intended colour for each point in the scanning line. The net control signal applied to each electron gun bears a direct correspondence to the primary-colour signal derived from the respective camera sensor at the transmitter.

8.6.2.6 Deflection Generator

When the receiver is tuned to a colour signal, the chrominance subcarrier component appears in the output of the video detector, and it is thereupon operated on in circuits that ultimately recover the primary-colour signals originally produced by the colour camera. Recovery of the primary-colour signals starts in the synchronous detector, where the synchronizing signals are passed through sync separator, a circuit that separates the horizontal and vertical synchronizing pulses. The pulses are then passed, respectively, to the horizontal and vertical deflection generators, which produce the currents that flow through the electromagnetic coils in the picture tube, causing the scanning spot to be deflected across the viewing screen in the standard scanning pattern. The mechanism for this circuit has been discussed fully in the previous chapter.

8.6.2.7 Television Display Section

The traditional means of displaying television picture has been the use of picture tube. Picture Tube is a display device that converts the electric voltage into picture element. It is so called because it is used in TV receiver to generate the picture. The picture tube is basically a Cathode Ray Tube (CRT) housed in a fully evacuated closed bell- shaped glass with a display screen. For colour TV, the colour tube is coated with fine colour phosphors that give the displayed picture a colour appearance. This tube has three different electron guns for the three colour signals.

9.2 AMERICA STANDARD: NTSC COLOUR TV SYSTEM

9.1 INTRODUCTION                                       9.3 THE PAL TV SYSTEM


9.4 SECAM TV SYSTEM

T he two major world television standards are the America’s             9.5 THE DIFFERENCES AND standard called National Television     SIMILARITIES BETWEEN EUROPEAN AND AMERICAN TV SYSTEMS Standard Committee (NTSC) adopted and approved by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the European’s standard controlled by International Radio Consultative                            Committee (CCIR). The America standard (NTSC) was the first analogue TV system developed as a monochrome version in the year 1954 and later advanced as colour TV version. Europe’s standard later came into being to improve upon the NTSC system by correcting some major challenges associated with it such as mechanical problems, incompatible scanning standard, excess bandwidth and so on, but mostly the issue of phase error. The European’s TV standard is of two systems; the PAL system and the SECAM system. Each of these two systems was developed differently in different countries of Europe. PAL was developed in Germany in the year 1967 and SECAM was developed in France in the same year. PAL is a close resemblance of NTSC system in many aspects; both use the same scanning pattern, but at the same time it is designed to correct its drawbacks. SECAM on the other hand has some similarities with PAL however differs with it in many aspects.
In general, the major difference between the NTSC TV system and Europe’s system is due to the difference in the respective electricity supply of the continent. While the mains electricity supply in America is 60 Hz frequency, that of Europe is 50 Hz. This condition brings differences in the value of some similar parameters of the two television systems such as scan lines, field rate, frame rate, scanning frequency, retrace intervaletc. The America’s standard television contains 525 horizontal scan lines per frame but that of the Europe’s contains 625 horizontal scan lines per frame. The frame value of each system is the same as half of the frequency of mains electricity supply, that is, 30 frames for the America and 25 frames for Europe. During scanning process, it takes the electron beam of the CRT of the television 1 sec to scan 30 frames of NTSC TV system and also 1 second to scan 25 frames of Europe’s systems. Consequently, in America’s standard, 15,750 lines are scanned every 1 sec (i.e. 525 lines x 30 frames). In Europe’s standard, 15, 625 lines are scanned every 1 sec (i.e. 625 lines x 25 frames). Therefore, the line scanning frequencies are 15,750 Hz and 15, 625 Hz for NTSC system and Europe’s standard respectively. The 15750 Hz line frequency for NTSC is for the monochrome version. The colour version is approximately 15734 Hz. This is because, the 60 Hz mains supply electricity is scaled by a factor of 1.001 during the designing of the colour TV so as to give allowances, preventing the overlapping of the monochrome and the colour signals. The result of the scaling is a 59.94 Hz such that when half of this value (29.97 Hz) multiplies one frame of the TV screen (29.97 x 525 lines), the line frequency will be the 15734 Hz. On the same hand, the time to scan one line (line rate) is 63.5 𝜇s (1/15,750 Hz or1/15,734 Hz) for America’s standard and 64 𝜇s (1/15,625 Hz) for Europe’s standard. All the three colour TV systems make use of luminance-chrominance signalsfor transmission of TV information signal, however, differ only in the way these signals are being added in their respective encoder circuits and demodulated in their decoder circuits.
9.2 AMERICA STANDARD: NTSC COLOUR TV SYSTEM No table of contents entries found.
The National Television Standards Committee (NTSC) is a body in the US which sets the analogue television standard for the United States. This standard started with monochrome (or Black and White) TV as the first (old) standard and presently, this old standard has been replaced by colour TV standard by adding chrominance
information on a 3.58 MHz subcarrier, but retaining compatibility with older black- and-white NTSC television receivers. Though, the use for the NTSC in TV broadcasting started in the United States in 1954, it had been adopted for use by Canada, Mexico, Japan and several other countries in America’s continent and it is the first colour television system that used the luminance-chrominance signal for colour TV signals transmission. Every other colour TV system is as a result of improvements done on the NTSC system.
9.2.1 NTSC TV COMPATIBILITY Compatibility in NTSC TV transmission is a system which provides that a colour transmission can be reproduced in Black-and-White by a monochrome receiver, and a monochrome transmission is reproduced in Black-and-White by a colour receiver. It took quite a number of years after the monochrome version of NSTC TV was invented before the colour version was developed. The delay in production of colour TV is due to the major challenge of making colour TV compatible with existing monochrome and using single transmission for both without totally abandoning the old version. However, these challenges were later overcome by television engineers when they provided the compatibility requirements of the TV system and since then colour TV has been in regular use. 9.2.1.1Compatibility Requirements of Colour TV The main requirement of colour TV was to make it compatible with existing monochrome TV system. To remain compatible, the same total frequency bandwidth (used in monochrome transmission) must be used in colour transmission, but more information (colour) must be transmitted. There are two required aspects of this compatibility. These are 1.      The colour TV must be compatible with existing monochrome. In this case, if the transmission is black and white, colour TV should produce that black and white picture. 2.      Colour TV should be transmitted in the same manner with black and white. This entails that for colour transmission, black and white TV should produce (black and white) picture without any receiver’s modification.
The above two requirements are two stringent and very important compatibility requirements for the monochrome and colour TV transmission. To satisfy these
requirements, the combine composite NTSC TV signal must satisfy some conditions which are as follows; •      The bandwidth of colour signal should be less than or equal monochrome signal bandwidth. •      The brightness information of colour signal and monochrome signal should be same for the same scene. •      The picture and sound carriers’ frequencies should not be changed. •      The picture intermediated frequency (IF) and sound IF should remain same for monochrome as well as colour signal. •      The colour signals should be accommodated in the same channel bandwidth. •      The synchronization and blanking signals should be carried as well without any effect on the colour signals. •      The colour information should not affect monochrome signals.
9.2.2 NTSC COLOUR TV STANDARDS The NTSC system has basic standards which are the features or the characteristics of the system. The standards of the TV system are from the parameters that characterized the video format and the modulation techniques. 9.2.2.1 Video Format The field rate is 59.94 Hz fields/sec for colour version. Line rate is 525 lines/frame or 262.5 lines/field The image aspect ratio is 4:3 The line interval is 63.5 𝜇s The active lines are about 485 lines per frame.
9.2.2.2 Signal Modulation Techniques The Video signal is band limited to 4.2 MHz The audio signal is band limited to 100 KHz Audio and video are multiplexed into a single signal by modulating the audio signal to 4.5 MHz using frequency modulation. The combined signal has bandwidth of 4.6 MHz
9.2.3 NTSC COLOUR TV TRANSMITTER SYSTEM The basics of the NTSC transmitter system is shown in the simplified block diagram shown in figure 9.1.As depicted by the diagram, the NTSC transmitter system is a combination of an AM transmitter (use for video TV signal generation) and FM transmitter (use for sound signal generation). The two transmitters are connected to a diplexer which in turn is connected to transmitting antenna.
[Figure 9.1:Block diagram of NTSC transmitter]
9.2.3.1Sound Transmitter The sound transmitter in NTSC transmitter system is an FM system similar to that of broadcasting FM radio stations in the 88-108 MHz band. Also, it is still a high-fidelity system because the same 30Hz to 15 KHz audio range is transmitted as in the case of broadcast FM transmitter. However, unlike the radio broadcast FM that uses a ± 75 KHz frequency deviation, the TV audio system uses FM audio transmission of ± 25 KHz frequency deviation, making analogue television audio signals sound softer than FM radio signals as received on a wideband receiver. Consequently, the TV sound signal has same fidelity but less effective in cancelling the indirect noise effects which is a major advantage of FM as regards to noise suppression. 9.2.3.2 The Video Transmitter The video transmitter is an AM transmitter. In the transmitter, the video or picture signal is amplitude-modulating onto a carrier. Here, the modulation process is quite complex than the frequency modulation in the audio system. The composite video signal resulted from the modulation process in the transmitter is multiplexed with the sound signal from the audio system. Thus, the composite transmitter signal is a product of both AM and FM principles. This is done to minimize interference effects between the two at the receiver because an FM receiver is relatively insensitive to amplitude modulation and an AM receiver has rejection potentials to frequency modulation.
9.2.4 NTSC TV SIGNAL GENERATION AND MODULATION NTSC transmitter uses the chrominance signals and luminance signal for colour picture (video) signal generation and transmission. In this system, the chrominance signals are encoded as I and Q which stand for in-phase and in-quadrature respectively. The I and Q signals are made up of different proportions of the Red, Green and Blue primary colours and contain information about the hue and saturation of the chrominance signals. As shown in figure9.2, the process by which these signals form follows that R, G and B colour signals are passed through the encoder section of the transmitter. After the mixing process in the encoder, Y, I and Q signals are formed.Mathematically I and Q signals and the proportion of the primary colour they contain are represented as; I = 0.6 R − 0.28 G – 0.32B and Q = 0.21R - 0.52G + 0.31 B. The minus sign in mathematical expression means that the colour signals have been phase-inverted before the mixing process.These signals are then passed through the band limiting filters of 4.2 MHz, 1.5 MHz and 0.5 MHz respectively. To produce colour picture at the CRT of the receiver, luminance signal and chrominance signals are required to be transmitted combined. Luminance signal is transmitted on standard picture carrier, but only one carrier at 4.43MHz is available to transmit chrominance signals. This poses a problem, but the challenge is solved by generating one more sub-carrier from the same frequency generator called sub-carrier oscillator, and given to the phase shifting network which shifts the signals 90° out of phase, producing a second chrominance subcarrier signals with the same amplitude and frequency with the main subcarrier but differ in phase by 90°. After this stage, the next stage is modulation process. The entire modulation process in this system involves two stages. In the first stage, the two encoded signals (I and Q) are fed into balanced modulators along with the 3.58 MHz sub-carriers to simultaneously modulate the amplitude and phase of the sub-carrier. Here, each of the chrominance signals amplitude modulates each of the 3.58 MHz sub-carriers (which are 90° phase shift or out of phase with each other) to
represent changes in intended saturation and phase modulates it to represent changes in intended colour value (hue). This type of amplitude modulation that occurred in this process is called Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (QAM) because the 900 phase shift or out of phase is called quadrature. Thus, the two modulated carriers are said to be in quadrature. In each of the balance modulator, the carrier of each of the amplitude modulated signal is suppressed. Therefore, output signal of each of the balanced modulator is a Double Sideband Suppressed Carrier (DSB-SC) AM signal. The resulting (modulated) signals are then combined to form a single sine-wave DSB- SC with varying phase relative to a reference carrier and with varying amplitude. The varying phase represents the instantaneous color hue captured by a TV camera, and the amplitude represents the instantaneous color saturation. The modulated 3.58 MHz subcarrier (DSD-SC) is then added to the Luminance signal. At this point in the transmitter, a pulse signal generator in the transmitter’s circuit generates signals that are used to produce colour burst, and synchronizing and blanking pulses which are all together, added to the combination of the luminance and chrominance signals. The colour bursts are used to control the synchronous detectors during the transmitter-receiver synchronization process, while the blanking pulses are used to blank out lines during retracing. The combination of these signals (two DSB signals and the Y-signal with the added pulses) forms the ‘composite colour TV signal’ and is further used as a modulating signal to modulate the picture carrier signal during the second stage of the modulation. In the second stage of this modulation process, the overall (combined) signal gotten in the first stage is used to modulate the picture carrier signal. Here, the (picture) carrier is simultaneously amplitude modulated by the luminance signal to represent changes in the intended brightness and the DSB-SC signal to present changes in the in intended saturation value and hue. The final resulting signals of this process are called NTSC composite video signal. The phase of these signals with respect to the original 3.58 MHz subcarrier signal determines the colour to be seen by the viewer at receiving end. Finally, the composite video signals and the frequency modulated sound signal are multiplexed to form a single NTSC composite TV signal.
9.2.5 NTSC COMPOSITE TV SIGNAL The NTSC composite TV signal and its sidebands are within the 6 MHz TV signal bandwidth. The complete spectrum of the transmitted colour signal is shown in figure 9.2
[Figure 9.2: Channel spectrum of NTSC composite colour TV signal]
The NTSC composite TV signal as transmitted is a complex one and it occupies a total channel bandwidth of 6 MHz. five separate components are included in the signal; sound, picture brightness or luminance, vertical and synchronization pulses, colour or chrominance information of the picture and colour burst. The actual video signal is transmitted as amplitude-modulated vestigial sideband carrier signal located between 500 kHz and 5.45 MHz above the lower bound of the channel. The video carrier is 1.25 MHz above the lower bound of the channel. The entire upper sideband is transmitted, but only 1.25 MHz of the lower sideband, referred as vestigial sideband, is transmitted. This is known as vestigial sideband transmission. The colour subcarrier which is quadrature-amplitude-modulated with a suppressed carrier, as indicated in the figure, is approximately 3.58 MHz above the video carrier. The frequency-modulated audio signal (as the main audio carrier) is 4.5 MHz above the video carrier, making it 250 kHz below the top of the channel.
9.2.6 NTSC COLOUR TV SIGNAL RECEPTION AND DEMODULATION; NTSC TV Receiver The colour TV receiver performs a major task of receiving and demodulating the composite colour TV signals into its original form and components as generated by the transmitter. In CRT picture tube of the televisions’ receiver, the NTSC signals, Q and I, are turned into three the original colour signals; Red, Green and Blue, each controlling the colour electron gun of the picture tube. TV sets with digital circuitry use sampling techniques to process the signals but the end result is the same; colour images.
For an NTSC colour TV receiver to recover hue information from the colour subcarrier accurately, it must have a zero phase reference to replace the previously suppressed carrier. To achieve this, the NTSC signal includes a short sample of this reference signal, known as the colour burst,located on the 'back porch' of each horizontal synchronization pulse. The colour burst which are generated in a precise electronic oscillator in the transmitter, consists 8-10 cycles of the unmodulated (fixed phase and amplitude) colour subcarrier of 3.58 MHz value and are injected into the signal wave form during the blank period between line scans, just after the horizontal synchronizing pulses. These samples are employed in the receiver to control the synchronous detector.
The TV receiver has a "local oscillator", which is synchronized with these colour bursts. Combining this reference phase signal derived from the colour burst with the chrominance signal's amplitude and phase allows the recovery of the 'I' and 'Q' signals which when combined with the Luminance information allows the reconstruction of a colour image on the screen.
[Figure 9.3:NTSC colour TV Receiver]
The figure 9.3 on page 299 is a complete block diagram of colour NTSC receiver.In the NTSC receiver, the process involved in receiving the NTSC TV signal and recovering it to present the picture and sound in a high-quality manner is quite a complex one. As shown in the block diagram, figure 9.3, the RF signal intercepted by the antenna is connected to the tuner, which consists of an RF amplifier, mixer, and local oscillator. The tuner is used to select which TV channel is to be viewed and to convert the picture and sound carriers plus their modulation to an intermediate frequency (IF) signal.

9.2.6.1 Video Signal Demodulation

The IF signals from the tuner section are sent to the (video) IF amplifier. The SAW filter placed in-between the tuner and the IF amplifier is used to provide exact selectivity required to pass both of the IF signal with the correct response to match the incoming vestigial sideband signal. This device greatly attenuates the sound IF to prevent it from getting into the video circuits. The IF signals are next amplified by IF amplifier and the other demodulation processes follow in the decoder section. The decoder section is the major section in the receiver, outside other sections that we have discussed in chapter 8 It is the decoder’s process of operations; of course that distinguishes the NTSC receiver from other TV receiver system.
[Figure 9.4:The decoder section of an NTSC colour TV receiver]
The decoder section, as part of the NTSC receiver, contains colour signal filter circuits, two balanced detector circuits, phase detector circuit, phase shifter circuits, signal amplifiers, colour burst circuit,and matrix networks. This is shown in figure 9.4 above. Each of the circuits in the decoder section has its specification function.
The video detector, an AM detector, takes the amplified IF signal at its input and recovers the composite (colour)video signals at the detector output. These outputs are amplified by the video amplifiers. From the video amplifier, the recovered luminance (Y) signal component of the composite signal is sent to the AGC circuit where it is used to create an AGC voltage for controlling the gain of the IF amplifiers and tuner (IF) amplifier and mixers and also sent directly to a linear (matrix) circuit after passing through a filter.
The chrominance/colour signal component is also taken from the video amplifier output by the colour signal filter and fed to colour-balance detector circuits. The colour burst (coming with the TV signal) is picked up by a gating circuit called colour burst gate or burst keyer and sent to phase detector whose output is used to synchronize a sub-carrier oscillator that produces a 3.58 MHz subcarrier signal of the correct frequency and phase. The output of this oscillator is fed to the two balanced detector circuits that demodulate and recover the I and Q chrominance signals after passing through a 90° phase shifter. The 90° phase shifter shifts the I and Q carriers fed to the two balanced detectors90° out of phase to each other. From figure9.3,we take note of another phase shifter, outside the 90° phase shifter. The 57° phase shifter circuit is used to correctly position the colour phase for maximum recovery of colour detail. The Q and I signals are then amplified by the signal amplifier and are combined in the matrix circuit, a linear mixer, with the Y signal, and the outputs are R, G and B colour signals. These primary colour signals are amplified and applied to the three electron guns of the colour picture tube, which produces the picture.
9.2.6.2 Sound Signal Demodulation We shall remember that the carrier frequency for sound channel transmitted from the broadcasting point (transmitter) in NTSC system is spaced 4.5 MHz above the picture carrier. Then at the receiver, this sound (part of the composite TV signal) is separated from the picture carrier signal by appropriate circuitry. The sound IF signal is separated from the IF video signal by a filter circuit at the output of the IF amplifier and allowing only the passage of the sound signal to the
sound section. At the sound section, the sound IF signal is first passed through sound IF detector. The resulting modulated sound signal is passed through a sound IF amplifier and to an FM detector (discriminator, or ratio detector) that converts the frequency modulated sound signal back to an audio signal current which in turn passes through one or two additional audio-frequency amplifier stages to the loudspeaker.
9.2.7 THE LIMITATIONS OF NTSC COLOUR TV SYSTEM The major problem associated with NTSC TV transmission system is that the system suffers phase error for the fact that the suppressed carrier has to be re-inserted back at the receiver during the signal detection. Achange in the amplitude of the alternation of the signal at any instant, corresponds to a change in the saturation of the colour (because the amplitude represents the saturation) being passed over by the scanning spot at that instant whereas a shift in line of its alternation (a change in phase) similarly corresponds to a shift in the hue (since phase represents the hue). As the different saturations and hues of the televised scene are successfully uncovered by scanning in the camera, the amplitude and phase respectively of the chrominance signal change accordingly. These become the major setback suffered by the system. Outside the challenge of phase error, NTSC TV system requires that a subcarrier will be re-inserted at the receiver, if there must be proper demodulation of the signal. Again, transmission of colour burst along with the colour TV composite signal is required. The 525-line resolution of NTSC produces in a lower quality image than the hardware is capable of.
9.2.8 REMEDY TO THE CHALLENGES OF NTSC TV SYSTEM In order to keep the signals in constant phase, it is injected with a colour burst during the blank period between line scans, just after the horizontal synchronizing pulses. These injected signals are employed in the receiver to control the synchronous detector. Also, subcarriers are re-inserted at the receiver.

9.3 THE PAL TV SYSTEM

PAL TV system is one of the European TV system. PAL system is short for Phase Alternating Line system. The system was first introduced in Germany in 1967. It is the analogue video format used in television transmission in most of European countries (except France, and some other countries in Eastern Europe, where SECAM is used), Australia and some Asian, South American countries, and African countries including Nigeria. This system is a close relative of the NTSC but it was invented to correct the phase error encountered by NTSC system.
The name "Phase Alternating Line" describes the way that part of the colour information on the video signal is reversed in phase with each line, which automatically corrects phase errors in the transmission of the TV signal.
Like NTSC, the PAL system uses interlaced scanning format and uses B-Y and R-Y signals to modulate a colour subcarrier. The colour subcarrier is a line-locked subcarrier at 4.43 MHz frequency. The PAL colour system is usually used with a video format that has 625 lines per frame and a frame rate of 25 frames per second. Each frame consists of two fields (half-a-frame), each field has half of the lines of a frame (one has all the even lines, one has all the odd lines). There are 50 fields per second.
In terms of signal modulation, PAL is also similar to NTSC system. It uses QAM techniques such that the chrominance signal is simultaneously modulated in amplitude to carry the saturation aspect of the colours and modulated in phase to carry the hue aspect, but it corrects the main draw-back of NTSC which is due to phase error by reversing the phase information of one of the chrominance signals during alternate line period, that is, during scanning of successive lines, the phase information is reversed. The technique involved in the reversal process is that the subcarrier to one of the colour difference signal is switched ±90° at every line. The subcarrier is a line- locked subcarrier at 4.43 MHz. This subcarrier is quadrature amplitude modulated (QAM) by the two colour difference signals B-Y and R-Y in the system.
To avoid over modulation of the channel carrier frequency, the (B-Y) and (R-Y) colour difference signals are scaled down by some value. These scaled down chrominance values are called U and V PAL signals. The scaled down values are
given as U=0.489(B-Y) and V = 0.877(R-Y) but the chrominance signal whose information is reversed during every alternate line is the V signal. That is, the phase of V is inverted every second line. This phase inversion is achieved by an electronic switch called the PAL switch.

9.3.2 PAL ENCODER The foregoing mathematical explanations are likened to what happens in the encoder section of the PAL TV transmitter. The PAL encoder encodes the input signals R, G and B to produce PAL composite colour video signal. The block diagram is shown in figure 9.5.
[Figure 9.5:The block diagram of PAL encoder]
From the figure, the R,G and B signals are combined by resistive network of the encoder to form luminance (Y) signal. The U and V are generated by other resistive network. The subcarrier generator output is given to the U modulator. It is also given to block circuit to produce ±90° phase shift. The phase shifted carrier is given to V modulator. The phase shift is decided by pulse from the sync pulse generator. The sync generator takes trigger from colour subcarrier generator. The modulated colour difference signals are combined by phaser addition to produce the chrominance signals. The final adder adds luminance, chrominance and vertical-horizontal sync pulses to produce PAL composite colour video signal. This signal is shown in figure9.5.A delay line is inserted for luminance signal to compensate for delay of the processing of chrominance signal.

9.3.3 CANCELLATION OF PHASE ERROR IN PAL

The inverting of the phase of the V carrier every second line allows cancellation of phase rotations by adding the V signal from two consecutive lines by means of a 64𝜇s delay line. This alternation of the signal tends to cancel out the error due to phase. This happens so because, if for example the Blue colour is too blue on one line, it will not be blue enough on the other line due to the phase reversal. In this way, if a phase error is present during the scanning of one line, a compensating error (of equal amount but in the opposite direction) will be introduced in the next line. Therefore, on the average, the resulting phase information (picture) presented by the two successive lines taken together, will be free from such phase error, hence from hue error.
The process can be illustrated with figure 9.6(a). The phase of V signal is reversed on every alternate line. The alternation tends to cancel out the error due to phase. Let us consider that an orange colour is being transmitted. U and V will take on their values according to this colour and chrominance signal ‘O’ will form for orange colour. This is shown in figure 9.6(b).
[Figure 9.6(a): Orange colour signal formation for Nth line with no phase error Figure 9.6(b): chrominance signal for Nth line with “∅” degree phase shift]
On the next line (N+1)th line phase of carrier for V, it will change to -90° with respect to carrier of U . Therefore, signal V will be reversed. And let us assumed that the chrominance signal formed undergoes the shift of ‘∅’ degrees. Figure 9.6 (b) shows the chrominance signal again for Nth line with ‘∅’ degree phase shift. Figure 9.6 (c) shows the chrominance signal for (N+1)th line the same degree phase shift. The difference is that phaser ‘V’ is now reversed.
[Figure 9.6 (c):chrominance signal for (N+1)th line the same degree phase shift as figure 9.6 b]
During reproduction at the receiver, the phaser On ͞ϴ as shown in figure 9.7(a) will be changed to its mirror image [(N+1)th line] as shown in figure 9.7(b) because phaser Vo in figure 9.6(c) will be inverted at the receiver. This is shown in figure 9.7(b). Figure 9.7 (a) shows phaser O’ϴ at the receiver. Phaser O’ϴ will produce yellow colour on Nth line whereas phaser On ͞ϴ will produce red colour on (N+1)th line. Mixing of the two colours will take place when they are perceived by an eye. The averaging effect at the eye perceives intermediate colour that is orange. This is depicted in figure 9.7 (c). Thus, the errors in the colour due to phase change are cancelled in PAL system.
Figure 9.7(a): Phasor O’ ∅ corresponding to Nth line at receiver. It represents yellow colour because of the phase shift of “∅” Figure 9.7(b): Phasor O” ∅ corresponding to (N+1)th line at receiver. It represents red colour because of the phase shift of ∅
[Figure 9.7(c): Yellow colour is produced in Nth line and Red colour is produced on (N+1)th line. Averaging effect of the eye sees average of the two colours, i.e orange]
9.3.4 LIMITATION OF PAL SYSTEM One major disadvantage of the PAL system is the deterioration in the detected output signal in the form of reduced saturation. This occurs because two lines are thus required to depict the corrected hue information, and the vertical detail of the hue information is correspondingly lessened. This produces no serious degradation of the picture when the phase errors are not too great because, human eye does not require fine detail in the hues of colour reproduction and the mind of the observer averages out the two compensating errors. If the phase errors are more than about 20°, however, visible degradation does occur. This effect can be corrected by introducing into the receiver, a delay line electronic switch.

9.3.5 VARIANTS OF PAL TV SYSTEM

PAL has many variants which include PAL-B/G, PAL-I, PAL-M, PAL-N and PAL60. PAL-I is the version used in the United Kingdom. PAL-M is a hybrid of NTSC and PAL with 525 lines /60 Hz used in Brazil. PAL-N is a variant of PAL with narrow bandwidth which is used in Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay. Other European countries use PAL-B/G. PAL60 uses 59.94 fields per second like NTSC. It is used mainly for displaying NTSC video or DVD on a PAL TV set.
9.4 SECAM TV SYSTEM No table of contents entries found.
SECAM TV system was introduced in France in 1967, where it is still used; it has also been adopted in many former French colonies, as well as parts of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. It is an analog television system that uses frequency modulation to encode chrominance information.
The system was developed to correct the phase error suffered by NTSC system which occurs because of sub-carrier that carries both chrominance signals (R-Y and B-Y) simultaneously. Using the system, luminance information is transmitted in the usual manner, and the chrominance signal is interleaved with it. However, the two types of chrominance content or information (hue and saturation) which result as phasor combination of the two chrominance signals (R-Y and B-Y) required to encompass
the colour values for transmission does not occur concurrently. The good effect is that the errors associated with simultaneous amplitude and phase modulation of the resulting combined chrominance signal as it is the case with NTSC does not occur. Instead, the R-Y and B-Y are transmitted in alternate lines in sequence leading to the chrominance signal being only frequency modulated unlike the NTSC system where the chrominance signal is both amplitude and phase modulated. The alternate line transmission of the chrominance signals means that only one chrominance signal, R- Y or B-Y, is transmitted on one line. During this transmission process, alternate line scans carry information on luminance and red colour signal, while the intervening line scans contain luminance and blue. Since individual line scans carry only half the colour information, this reduces the colour detail (measured in the vertical dimension) by half. Consequently, half of the colour information is not used on each line, leading to a slight loss in vertical colour resolution (definition), though this effect is not detected by an eye since the eye is not sensitive to the hue and saturation of small details. The implication is that the vertical colour resolution is halved relative to picture definition we get in PAL and NTSC system.

9.4.1 SECAMENCODER

Figure 9.8: Block diagram of SECAM encoder system Figure 9.8 shows the block diagram of the encoder in the SECAM system. The chrominance signals are band limited to 1.5 MHz by passing them through filters. These signals are then applied to FM modulator through commutator switch. The modulator takes switching signal colour sub-carrier generator. The commutator switches to its inputs on every alternate line. Thus the colour subcarrier is modulated alternately by two chrominance signals from successive lines. The modulated subcarrier from FM modulator is then combined with luminance signal, sync pulse, blanking and switching burst, to form composite video signal. The burst or switching pulse is transmitted on every alternate line. Thus burst or switching pulse is used at the receiver for correct switching of the commutator. The composite video signal and the sound signal are then imposed on a carrier wave of specific allocated frequency and transmitted over the air or over a cable network. After passing through a receiving antenna or cable input at the television receiver, the SECAM TV signals are shifted back to their original frequencies through demodulation process and applied to the receiver’s picture tube display and loudspeaker as the signal output.

9.4.2 SECAM TV RECEIVER

The SECAM TV receiver employs FM detectors to demodulate the chrominance signal since frequency modulation is used on the chrominance sub-carrier at the transmitter. In the receiver, both chrominance signals are needed together to produce a complete colour picture. But for the fact that these signals are not coming to the receiver combinable, there is therefore the need for the receiver to store or memorize one colour signal for the duration of the line until the alternate chrominance component is available, this is the reason the system is named “sequential color with memory” which in French translates as “Sequential Couleur avec Memoire”, hence the name SECAM.
The green information is derived within the receiver by subtracting the red and blue information from the luminance signal. To subtract the red and blue information from the luminance information and obtain the green information, the red and blue signals must be available in the receiver simultaneously. This is not the case with the SECAM receiver, since the chrominance signals are transmitted one after the other, in time sequence. However, this requirement for simultaneity is met in the receiver by holding the signal content of each line scan in storage (or “memorizing” it – hence the French name of the system “electronic colour system with memory”), that is, the receiver stores or memorizes one colour signal for the duration of the line until an alternate
chrominance component is present. The storage device that does this function is known as a delay line. The delay line holds the information of each line scan for 64𝜇sec, the time required to complete the next line scan. To match successive pairs of lines, another device called electronic switch is also needed.
Since SECAM system reproduces the colour information with a minimum of error, it has been argued that SECAM receivers do not have manual controls for hue and saturation. Such adjustments, however, are usually provided in order to permit the viewer to adjust the picture to individual taste and to correct for signals that have broadcast errors due to such factors as faulty use of cameras, lighting, and networking. SECAM system has other three variants that are in use in different regions of the Europe. These variants are French SECAM, MESECAM and D-SECAM.French SECAM is used in France and its former colonies. MESECAM is used in the Middle East, while D-SECAM is used in the Commonwealth of Independent States and Eastern Europe.

9.6 OTHER TYPES OF TV SYSTEM

In addition to the other types of the television system discussed so far, emerging trends and innovations in TV industries have seen to the development of other TV systems which include digital TV, cable TV and satellite TV

9.6.1 DIGITAL TV

Digital TV (DTV), also known as high-definition TV (HDTV), was designed to re- place the National Television Standards Committee (NTSC) system. The HDTV system is an extremely complex collection of digital, communication, and computer techniques. The goal of HDTV is to greatly improve the picture and sound quality. The first HDTV stations began transmission in the 10 largest U.S. cities on September 1, 1998. The DTV standard is based on the standard recommendations by the Advanced Tele- vision System Committee (ATSC). This standard provides for the transmission of television programs in the HDTV screen format, 16 X 9. It also provides for the transmission of a standard definition television (SDTV) format that provides a digital picture with comparable resolution to analog NTSC formats. The new standard also provides the capability for broadcasters to transmit multiple SDTV programs over a single television channel. HDTV is still relatively new.

9.6.1.1 HDTV Standards

HDTV uses die scanning concept to paint a picture on the CRT. So you can continue to think of the HDTV screen in terms of scan lines, as you would think of the standard NTSC analog screen. The screen format is 16 X 9 and it uses progressive scanning techniques.
HDTV Screen
You should also view the HDTV screen as being made up of thousands of tiny dots of light called pixels. Each pixel can be any of 256 colors. These pixels can be used to
create any image. The greater the number of pixels on the screen, the greater the resolution and the finer the detail that can be represented. Each horizontal scan line is divided up into hundreds of pixels. The format of a HDTV screen is described in terms of the numbers of pixels per horizontal line by the number of vertical pixels (which is the same as the number of horizontal scan lines).

9.6.1.2 HDTV Transmission of video and audio signal

In HDTV both the video and the audio signals must be digitized by A/D converters and transmitted serially to the receiver. Because of the very high frequency of video signals, special techniques must be used to transmit the video signal over a standard 6- MHz bandwidth TV channel. And because both video and audio must be transmitted over the same channel, multiplexing techniques must be used. The FCC's requirement is that all of this information be transmitted reliably over the standard 6-MHz TV channels now defined for
Video signal The format typically used to convert the analog video to a digital format is the ITU-R 601 4:2:2 formats. This is an international standard for digitizing component video. The base sampling frequency for the ITU-R 601 standard is 3.375 MHz. The 4:2:2 represents the sample rate for the following elements of a component video signal.
The audio signal The digital compression technique specified for digital television, as defined by ATSC document A/52, details the digital audio compression (AC-3) standard. This system provides five full-bandwidth audio channels (3 Hz to 20 kHz). The five channels are for the left, center, right, and left-right surround-sound channels. The standard also provides one low-frequency enhancement channel, which has a reduced bandwidth (3 Hz to 120 Hz), The new audio system is commercially called the 5.1 Channel Input. The standard provides for various sample rates and input word lengths (up to 24 bits) for compatibility to the many available digital audio encoding formats. The six audio outputs are multiplexed together, which results in a 5.184-Mbps data stream. This data stream is then compressed to a 384-kbps data stream.

9.6.1.3 Difference Between NTSC Analogue TV and HDTV

One major difference between conventional NTSC analog' TV and HDTV is that HDTV can use progressive line scanning rather than interlaced scanning. In progressive scanning each line is scanned one at a time from top to bottom. Since this format is compatible with computer video monitors, it is possible to display HDTV on computer screens. Interlaced scanning can be used on one of the HDTV formats. The 720p format uses a larger aspect ratio of 16:9 (a 4:3 format is optional at this resolution also). This format is better for showing movies. This format obviously gives the best resolution. The HDTV set should be able to detect and receive any available format.

9.6.2 CABLE TV

Cable TV, sometimes called CATV, is a system of delivering the TV signal to home receivers by way of a coaxial cable rather than over the air by radio wave propagation. A cable TV company collects all the available signals and programs and frequency multiplexes them on a single coaxial cable that is fed to the homes of subscribers. A special cable decoder box is used to receive the cable signals, select the desired channel, and feed a signal to the TV set. Today, most TV reception is by way of a cable con- nection instead of an antenna.

9.6.2.1 Signal Processing in Cable TV

The TV signals to be redistributed by the cable company usually undergo some kind of processing before they are put on the cable to the TV set. Amplification and impedance matching are the main processes involved in sending the signal to remote locations over what is sometimes many miles of coaxial cable.
