text:
10.1 Introduction 10.2 The Telephone set 10.3 The Telephone mode 10.4 The local loop 10.5 The public Telephone 10.1 INTRODUCTION                                     Network 10.6 Set-up of a Telephone In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell developed               exchange a system that could transmit the entire               10.7 Telephone comm call set-up 10.8 Telephone signaling voice signal which formed the basis for               10.9 Telephone Network voice communication.                                  10.10 Digital Telephone handset The telephone system is an analog system originally designed for full-duplex communication                          of voice signals. Although at present, it involves digital techniques.         It    further represents a worldwide grid of connection that enables point to point communication between subscribers. The modern telephone network being developed to provide full-duplex real-time transmission of voice signals implies that a simultaneous transmission of signals in both directions is achieved. This may be achieved by simply providing two separate circuits, one for each direction, resulting in an uneconomic duplication of facilities, but duplex as applied to telephone systems involves the simultaneous transmission over the same channel. Hence, a telephone system must be able to transmit in both direction and must also provide a means of signaling from each terminal to the other.
The word telephone is derived from a combination of two Greek words “tele” which means “far off” and “phone” which means “sound”. Telephony generally, is the transmission of speech current over wires, enabling two or more persons to converse over any distance, while Telephone is the combination of apparatus for converting speech energy into electrical waves, transmitting the electrical energy to any distant point and then reconverting the electrical energy to audible sound. Hence, the term telephone involves the conversion of sound signal at the transmitting end into electrical signal which can be transmitted over a distance and reconverted to sound upon reception at the receive end. It is the main focus of telephone system to establish good quality voice communication between customers at distant location, maintaining the nominal bandwidth of 4KHz across a sequence of transmission and switching facilities, since all telephone networks operate on the basis of circuit switching. The telephone system is either owned on a private or public basis. Private telephone systems are employed for internal communication, in a building or premises and may provide access to the public telephone system. Private telephone systems are of two types namely; key system and PBX systems (Private Branch Exchange) key system: These are small telephone systems designed to serve between 2 to 50 user telephones within an organization.
PBX systems (private branch exchange): This telephone system is designed to take 50 or more user telephones within an organization. Large organizations such as Shell Petroleum Development Company, (SPDC) Railway Corporations,Enugu Electricity Development Company (EEDC) etc, use the private telephone systems. In public telephone services, the switching necessary to connect any given subscriber to another in the same locality is carried out at a telephone exchange which also provides circuits and apparatus whereby signaling to and from the exchange can be carried out. The switching process may be done manually by an operator or automatically by a group of electronic switch gears at an automatic exchange. For long distant calls more than one exchange is involved. The term junction applies to relatively short lines, whereas the term toll or trunk is applied to lines of greater length, such as the ones that links between states. For public telephone service, usually the country is divided into areas or zones (states). Each zone is subdivided into smaller areas known as groups. The geographical extent of any group area depends on the telephone traffic, which relates to the number and average duration of calls made within a specified period. Where the traffic is high, the group area is relatively small while in rural districts where the telephone density is
relatively small the group area is larger. In each group area, there may be three types of exchange, namely; i.    The main exchange: This is contained in the group called group centres, where interconnections are made between subscribers. ii.    The minor exchange: This is provided with direct circuits to the group centre exchange. Usually long distant calls from or to a minor exchange, are then routed through the group centres. iii.    The dependent exchange: A dependent exchange on the other hand has no direct circuits to a group centre. (except a special case when it is located geographically adjacent to a group centre.) Therefore, long-distance calls which originate at a dependent exchange normally first passes through a minor exchange and then on to the group centre. Long-distance calls proceed from a group centre to a zone centre which is an exchange in the zone handling all long-distance traffic for, or from the zone. Inter-zone communication then takes place between zone centres.
10.2 THE TELEPHONE SET The telephone set or basic telephone is simply an analog baseband transceiver. In its simplest form, it consists of i.   A microphone and earpiece, which is normally combined into a single handheld unit otherwise known as transceiver (A combination of transmitter and receiver). ii. A means of signaling the exchange when a call is to be made. iii. A means of sending the “address” (subscriber’s identity) information of the called subscriber to the exchange iv. An incoming call alarm, provided by a ringer v. A means of signaling the exchange that the call has been answered. In this regard, the requirement of (ii) and (v) are met by completing a d. c loop. When the handset is removed from its rest position the d. c path is set up through a carbon transmitter, providing the necessary polarizing current for the transmitter. The diagram of the basic telephone is shown in figure 10.1 (see page 322)
[Figure 10.1 (a): The Basic telephone set Figure 10.1(b) The carbon granule microphone]
The carbon microphone developed for the telephone provides an adequately good frequency response for speech at high sensitivity avoiding the need for amplification less sensitive microphones with amplifiers are now more common, having longer life and avoiding the problem of granules breaking down and causing noise which will likely distort the entire intelligence signal. A bell supplied from the local exchange provides the incoming call alarm. This is being replaced by an audible tone from a small loudspeaker. A choice of tone is available in some equipment, to allow a number of phones in a restricted area to be identified. This is referred to as “caller tone” The subscriber identity or address is represented by a series of digits. The first group in the server provides the routing information to the local exchange, while the second group provides the subscribers identity number, in the exchange. As a result of the prevalence of the automatic exchanges, the series of digits has been provided by a dial which produces an impulse sequence, breaking the d. c path. The impulses in the train are; i.   33⅓ ms(Depicts ‘ON’ State) ii.   66⅔ ms (Depicts ‘OFF’ State)
It provides an impulse rate of 10 impulses per second (10ips).
The speed restriction is imposed by the switching rate of the mechanical selectors and not by the transmission path. Hence the introduction of electronic switching has made possible a much faster switching rate and reduced the time required to set up a call. Press button switches have therefore replaced dials on modern telephones. When used in areas still served by mechanically switched exchanges, the keypad is quicker and more convenient to use, but has to store the number and send it to line as 10ips signal hence the actual time required to set up the call is not substantially reduced. When operated into a digital exchange, however multi-frequency coding is employed, each digit being represented by two audio tones. Dual tone multi frequency (DTMF) signaling allows 10 digits in addition to * and # symbol to be coded as shown in figure 10.2
[Figure 10.2: Dual tone multi frequency (DTMF) signaling]
At present, telephones will produce either type of signal with a simple change-over to enable them operate with either type of exchange.

10.3 THE TELEPHONE MODE

A telephone set when used for communication operates in two modes; transmit mode and receive mode. Each of these modes has some functions it provides.
10.3.1 THE TRANSMIT MODE The transmit mode provides the following functions
a) It triggers an indication to the telephone system that a call is to be made when the calling subscribers lifts the handset from the cradle. b) It indicates that the telephone system is ready to be used by generating a signal, called the dial tone. c) It is a way of transmitting the telephone number to be called, to the telephone system. d) It is a Reception indication that the call is being made by receiving a ringing tone. e) It is a means of receiving a special tone indicating that the called line is busy. f) It is a means of signaling the telephone system that the call is complete.
10.3.2 THE RECEIVE MODE The Receive mode provides the following functions; a) It serves as an incoming signal that rings a bell or produces an audio tone, indicating that a call is being received. b) It sends a signal to the telephone system indicating that the signal has been received. c) It provides Transducers that convert voice into electrical signals and electrical signals into voice.
10.4 THE LOCAL LOOP (SUBSCRIBER’S LOOP) This refers to the two-wire twisted pair connection between the telephone and the central office. The circuits in the telephone and at the central office, when connected form a complete electric circuit or loop. The d. c power for operating the telephone is generated at the central office and supplied to each telephone over the local loop. The a. c voice signals are transmitted along with the d. c power. Despite the fact that only two wires are involved, simultaneous send and receive is possible, following a full- duplex operation. Furthermore, all dialing and signaling operations are also carried out on this single twisted pair.
10.5 THE PUBLIC TELEPHONE NETWORK AND LOCAL EXCHANGE
Telephone instruments are installed at private subscriber’s premises, or made available to the general public at call offices. Every of these stations are connected by
a pair of wires called the subscribers loop to a local exchange which serves up to 10,000 lines. Each local exchange provides a means of connecting any of the subscriber’s lines to each other. The local exchange is also connected to other similar exchanges in the same area (or the same town) by further lines (pairs of wire) called junctions. For calls routed outside this area the junction lines are linked to the trunk exchanges, which provide the means of connecting calls over long distance routes (trunk lines) to subscribers in other areas anywhere in the world. These long distance circuits may use cables (lines) or they may use radio for transmission between the exchanges. Various ranks of exchanges of different statue are provided to make for each call to have its own route to its desired destination. In the UK, three ranks of trunks exchanges exist which are; the primary centre, the secondary centre and tertiary centre. In the United State of America, up to four ranks are used, the fourth one being quartenary centre.
10.6 SET-UP OF A TELEPHONE EXCHANGE The initial building and later growth of a telecommunication system, comprising of a network of switching centres and transmission links, involves the setting up of plans for; i. Routing ii. Numbering iii. Signaling iv. Transmission v. Charging or billing system vi. Network Control and Network Administration etc. These plans are affected by the predicted growth rate of the telecommunication systems. 10.6.1 ROUTING PLAN These comprise; i. Mesh network ii. Star network iii. Mixed routing iv. Alternative routing v. Trunk networks vi. International routing

10.6.1.1 The Mesh Network

When there are only a few number of switching centres a simple routing arrangement is done with the provision of direct routes, inter connecting all centres as is evident in figure 10.3 above. It shows a mesh of trunk routes for four centres where there is a total of six routes.
10.6.1.2 Star Network The star network is an alternative to the mesh arrangement, where one centre acts as a trunk centre to all the others. In this regard, every telephone must have its own separate line to every other telephone. This would require millions of wires to be connected to each instrument, which makes it obviously impossible to achieve.
[Figure 10.4: Star routing network connection]
The figure above shows a representation of a star network with four centres. In this arrangement, each route carries a total of 6 Erlangs of traffic and only three routes are involved. In a local telephone systems based on analog technology covering a town, it is the fixed cost which usually predominates. This indicates that the total number of circuits is the significant factor and suggests that MESH is preferable to star connection. But for long distance networks, the fixed cost is less significant and greater economy is obtained by bringing together circuits into fewer routes. In these cases STAR networks are usually preferable. The impact on the switching centre design must also be considered. A mesh connection requires more trunk terminations on every switching centre. With the star arrangement, the outer centre requires fewer terminations but the trunk center has a greatly increased number of terminations. In the star connection, more through traffic has to be switched. Therefore the star arrangement reduces the design requirements on all but one of the switching centres but introduces the need for a longer more powerful trunk centre. Since only one larger centre is required. The net effect on switching cost is often to make the star arrangement preferable.
10.6.1.3 Mixed Routing In practice, a network is hardly pure star or pure mesh, rather, mixed. Mixed routing is therefore a combination of star and mesh networks.
[Figure 10.5: Mixed routing network connection]
For a medium-sized town the mixed routing system can be used. Here there are a number of direct routes if the traffic justifies it otherwise the connections are via a trunk centre. In very large towns such a Kano and Abuja, there are several trunk centres serving many local centres. Such local trunk centres that serves many local centres in metropolitan areas are referred to as TANDEM centres, or exchanges. There may be several suburban tandem centres and one large central tandem serving all the centres in a large town like Abuja.
[Figure 10.6: Illustration of tandem network]
10.6.1.4 Alternative Routing For particular ranges of cost ratio, it is more economical to route a stream or parcel of traffic via a TANDEM centre rather than to route it directly between local centres. Sometimes certain routes can be busy necessitating the use of alternative routes. Choice of Alternative Routing There are usually many possible alternative routings between two local centres. The figure below shows the possible paths between two centres A and B, where each centre has a direct route and routes to three other centres.
[Figure 10.7: Choice of alternative routes]
When the direct route AB is busy, a route may be attempted via C,D, or E. now E has a direct route to B, but other routes exist such as EDB or ECB or even ECDB. It is normally a design requirement of a switching centre that the choice of routes should depend upon only the destination. That is the choice should be independent of the origin and of the route already taken. With this requirement some care has to be taken with choice of alternative routes. For instance, D could be programmed to choose a route to E if the direct route to B is busy and E could be programmed to choose a route to D if route EB is busy. These choices can lead to problem if routes DB and EB are both completely busy. In this case, a call to B, arriving at D will be routed to E. E finds EB busy, so it routes the call back to D, which then routes it back to E and so on. This process leads to a problem in the network, called ring around the rosie problem. This problem can be avoided if the signaling system between the centres can convey information about the route already taken. Provision for this kind of information transfer is made in modern international signaling systems where the additional cost of switching and signaling equipment is justified because of the resulting increased efficiency of use of the international trunks. A more straightforward technique for avoiding ring around the Rosie problem is to limit the choice of alternative routes at each centre. This is done by what is known as the far-to-near strategy. When there are alternative intermediate centres, the first choice is the centre nearest to the destination centre. The final choice is the centre furthest from the destination centre, but never the less nearer than the centre making the choice. When this strategy is applied to the network above, the first choice is the direct route AB. If this route is busy the first alternative is via the centre nearest to B which in this case is E. E, has a direct route to B. If this is busy the call will be blocked since routing via D or C are not allowed, they are further from B than E. if route AE is busy. The second alternative choice from A is AD. Now D can choose the direct route DB or next DE and so on. If this strategy is applied, the valid routes between A and B in order of choice are; AB ACB AEB ACEB ADB
ACDB ADEB ACDEB There are three special types of route in this situation. i.   A fully-provided route: This refers to the only route between two centres. Eg. EB ii.   A high-usage route: This refers to the first choice route between two centres. iii.   A final or back-bone route: This refers to the last choice route between two centres.
10.6.1.5 Trunk Networks Long distance telecommunication is usually carried by separate networks from that of the local network, called trunk lines. One reason is that different types of transmission and multiplexing equipment are used for long distance communication and the function of the switching centres, are somewhat different. Trunk networks are arranged with a hierarchy of switching centres. Primary and secondary centres are such that they have to be grouped together and parented by a tertiary trunk centre. In North America, quartenary centres are also required. At each level of the hierarchy, the main routes are supplemented by large numbers of direct routes. The figure below shows some examples of possible routes.
[Figure 10.8: Principle of alternative routing in a hierarchal network.]
It is evident from the picture above, that a local centre could be connected directly to any of the trunk centres if this were justified by the volume of traffic. Alternative Routing In Hierarchical Network When alternative routing is applied to hierarchical networks, an additional rule is required to avoid ring around the rosie problem. The rule is used if no direct route is available between a particular centre and a destination centre. This particular centre should first test (in far-to near order) any possible routes via centres in the next hierarchical level above that of the destination. There is no need to test all possible routes but those that are tested must be in the order discussed. The figure above shows how alternative routing is applied to a three-level trunk network in providing a route between two primary centres PC1 and PC2. Each primary centre is parented on a different secondary centre. The secondary centres SC1 and SC2 are parented on tertiary centres TC1 and TC2 respectively. TC1 and TC2 are directly by a trunk route. Each centre has a list of alternative routes based on the rules described. a. PC1: The first choice is a direct route PC1-PC2 if it is provided and free. The next choices must be selected from the secondary centres. In this example, there are only two and they are selected in far-to-near order, that is SC2, then SC1. There may be direct routes from tertiary centres for terminating traffic but these are not normally used for originating traffic because they usually have high cost ratios. So in this example, the final route from PC1 is that to SC1. b. SC1: By similar reasoning, the choices from SC1 are PC1 SC2 TC2 and (final choice) TC1. c. TC1: This has three choices; PC1, SC2 and (final choice) TC2. d. TC2: This has two choices; direct to PC2 or (final choice) SC2 e. SC2: This has only the final choice (fully provided) route to PC2. Strict adherence to these rules prevents the ring around the rosie problem. In the hierarchical arrangement just considered, the backbone routing between two primary centres consists of the routes: PC1 – SC1 –TC1 – TC2 –SC2 – PC2.
Advantagaes of Hierarchical Network Routing i.   The traffic dispersal is near the economic optimum. ii.   No Ring around the rosie problem iii.   Routing decisions are made at each trunk exchange independently of the origin of the call or its routing so far. iv.   It provides an upper limit to the number of links connected end-to-end.

Evidently, interchange systems are not restricted in speed as are the subscriber’s signaling systems because of the slow-moving dial, and they are not required to produce the tones, which the local exchanges must produce to keep the subscriber informed of the program of the call in details. At present, setting up of call also requires that the computers controlling the switches communicate with each other to exchange the signaling information. Modern and separate communication lines are introduced to interconnect these computers. This

10.8 TELEPHONE SIGNALLING

[Figure 10.12: Call set-up]
To establish a telephone call, a series of signaling messages must be exchanged. There are two basic types of signal exchanges: firstly, the one between the user and the network (Out-of-band signaling) and secondly the one within the network (In-band signaling). Both types of signaling must work together to establish the call.
[Figure 10.13: various types of signalling]
In general, the signaling messages generate control signals that determine the configuration of switches; that is, the messages direct a switch to a state in which a given input is connected to the desired output. As shown in figure 10.14, a traditional
network signaling information would arrive in telephone lines and be routed to the control system. Initially, hard-wired electromechanical or electronic logic was used to process these signaling messages. The class of stored-program control (SPC) switches emerged when computers were introduced to control the switching process.
[Figure 10.14: Stored-program control]
Through the intervention of the stored-program control computer, a request for call would come in, and a check would be made to see whether the destination was available, and if so, the appropriate connection would be made. The use of a program to control the switch provides great flexibility in modifying the control and introducing new features. Consider the operation of the signaling network. Its purpose is to implement connectivity between the computers that control the switches in the telephone network by providing for the exchange of messages.
10.8.1 FUNCTION OF TELEPHONE SIGNALLING The process of signaling in telephone system has at least three functions from the telephone communication call set-up. These are;
1. It indicates the state of the call to each subscriber by; a. Dial tone b. Ring tone and ring current c. Busy tone or number-unobtainable tone. 2. Tells the system what to do next e.g. by indicating the path for the call 3. Initiating a billing procedure, usually by tripping the calling subscribers meter at the correct charging rate.
10.8.2 TYPES OF TELEPHONE SIGNALING SYSTEM The types of signaling that are commonly used in telephone system are; i.   Loop disconnect signaling
ii.   Multi-frequency signaling iii.   Voice frequency signaling iv.    Common channel signaling
10.8.2.1 Loop Disconnect Signaling The loop disconnects signaling is also referred to as the Rotary signaling. The basis of this signaling system is to interrupt the d.c path of the subscriber’s loop for a specific number of short periods to indicate the number dialed. This dial operates at about ten impulses per second (10ips), with a break of about 66⅔ ms (OFF state) and a make of about 33⅓ms (ON state). It is further necessary to indicate the end of a pulse train so that a decoding circuit can know where one digit ends, and where the next one begins. This is achieved by the mechanical design of the dial, which ensures a minimum make period between any two consecutive digits. This period is called the inter digit pause (idp) and it is typically of 200ms minimum. The clear signal is produced when the user replaces his handset, breaking the d. c path. This break is distinguished from the break produced by dialing, by its duration. Any break that lasts more than a few hundred milliseconds is taken as a clear signal. In this context, when the rotary dial is rotated, the finger hole which corresponds to the required digit is pulled round to the finger guard, and then the dial is released. A governor inside the dial causes it to rotate back automatically at a fixed speed, causing series of pulses to be sent down the subscriber’s line. After the dial has returned to its rest position, the next digit is dialed. The time between the last of the pulses for one
digit and the first pulse of the next is called the inter digit pause. It is the pause that allows the exchange to recognize the end of the digit.
[Figure 10.15 : ideal output from telephone dial]
10.8.1.2 Multi Frequency Signaling At present modern exchange equipment respond directly to the multi frequency signals and the calls associated, can be set up very quickly. This is chiefly because modern subscriber’s handsets are fitted with key-pads instead of dials; generally, the key pads send out two sets of frequencies instead of pulses, to represent a digit. Whether or not the much increased speed of multi frequency signaling can be realized, depends on the local exchange. A multi frequency key-phone working into a strowger- typed exchange, gives no overall improvement rather it changes the position in the process at which the caller must wait. When a dial is used, there is a long inter-digit pause and short post-dial delay whereas in a multi frequency system, there is little inter-digit pause because the numbers can be keyed in very quickly but since the exchange equipment operates at 10 impulses per second, the multi frequency signal must be converted into normal digits producing a lengthy post-dial delay.
10.8.1.3 Voice Frequency Signaling Over long transmission lines the use of dc signaling is limited by several factors such as the variation of equipment performance, and the effect of the characteristics of the lines used to transmit between exchanges, degrade of the pulse shape of the dialed digits to such an extent that errors can be caused. In addition, the receiving equipment requires a higher voltage than would be necessary if the system used alternating
current signals. Apart from these considerations multi-channel working makes dc signaling inappropriate. The normal telephone channel occupies a bandwidth of 300-3400 Hz, from the range of 0-4000 Hz which it is allocated. If ac signaling is to be used it must operate at frequencies within this range, and it is therefore known as voice-frequency signaling. The frequencies used can be either inside the normal speech band (in-band signaling) or outside that band and within the 0-4000 Hz range (out-of -band signaling). As the frequencies used for voice frequency signaling are the same as those used in speech, special care must be taken to ensure that the two functions do not interfere. In understanding the characteristics of speech it is possible to specify signaling systems that will not be operated erroneously by speech frequencies. Since signaling is done by tones within the baseband of the telephone channel it is possible to use voice frequency signaling when the channels are multiplexed on to a common carrier, either a line or radio. 10.8.1.4 Common-Channel Signaling (CCS) In this context, the signaling information is separated from groups of voice trunks and sent in serial binary form over a single path dedicated only to signaling. The common-channel signaling (CCS) information must contain address data identifying the voice channel to which it relates, the CCS is only possible between exchanges using processor control so that the correct association between signal and relevant voice channel can be re-established at the receiving exchange. The physical route taken by the CCS channel can differ from that of the traffic circuits so that the signaling network may be economically optimized. The common-signal channel can also be advantageously used to carry non-traffic-related signals required for operational or maintenance purposes.
[Figure 10.16: Common-Channel Signaling (CCS)]

10.9 TELEPHONE NETWORK

[Figure 10.17 : Telephone network]
Figure 10.17 shows the telephone network as consisting of two parts: a signaling network that carries the information to control connections and a transport network that carries the user information. Communications from the user are split into two streams at the Service Switching Point (SSP). The signaling information is directed toward the signaling network where it is routed and processed as required. The signaling system then issues commands to the switches to establish the desired connection. The signaling network functions much like the ‘nervous system’ of the telephone network, directing the switches and communication lines in the network to be configured to handle the various connection requests. The second stream in the SSP consists of the user information that is directed to the transport network where it flows from one user to the other. Note that the signaling network does not extend to the user because of security concerns. Separate user-to-network signaling procedures are in place. The function of the signaling network in the telephone network is to provide communications between the computers that control the switches. The computers communicate through the exchange of discrete messages. The best way of implementing such a network is through a packet-switching network that transfers information in the form of packets between network elements. The introduction of a packet-switching signaling network in digital telephony is important, since it is at this point that the evolution of the signaling network for telephony converges with the evolution of computer networks.
10.9.1 ANALOG SIGNALING SYSTEM Analog telephone signaling system comprises the magneto system and central battery signaling system.
10.9.1.1 The Magneto System The magneto system is one of the earliest switching systems used in manual telephony. It uses a low frequency subscriber’s voltage for the purpose of signaling. The signaling voltage is produced by manually operated generators, both at the exchange and at the subscriber’s telephone. When an exchange is handling a large volume of traffic, the use of manually operated generators at each position reduces the overall operating efficiency. It is usual therefore at large magneto exchanges to install a machine driven alternator and for the operator to connect the signaling voltage to a circuit by means of a key.
10.9.1.2 Central Battery Signaling (CBS) Systems In the central battery signaling, (C.B.S) system, a direct current is used for signaling, when subscribers call the exchange. The source of e. m. f for signaling is obtained from a battery situate at the exchange. The local battery provides the source of current for energizing the transmitter The processes of calling and clearing signals in this context are automatically controlled by the removal and replacement of the subscriber’s receiver. Two supervisory relays are provided on each pair of cords, one on the answering side and one on the calling side, these relays operate the supervisory signals when a call is in progress. The central battery located at the exchange is used for all general signaling purposes and a battery of 2 cells for speaking purposes, is associated with each telephone at the subscribers’ stations.
10.9.1.3 Comparing Magneto System and CBS In the magneto system, and the central battery signaling system, the calling device on the switch board consists of an electromagnetic flap indicator, but in some cases, the
magneto switchboards have had the indicators replaced by lamps. The CBS has advantages it offers over the magneto system, but it equally has some disadvantages. Advantages of CBS over Magneto System The advantages of the CBS systems are: 1.    Existence of Automatic signaling between the subscriber and the exchange 2.    Existence of Automatic signaling over junction circuits 3.    The external plant is necessarily maintained in the high condition of efficiency which the system demands for satisfactory working. 4.    No generator is required at the subscriber’s station.
Disadvantages of CBS The disadvantages of the systems are: 1.    Relatively large batteries required at small exchanges. 2.    Complexity of the exchange apparatus and of that at subscribers’ premises when extension circuits are necessary. 3.    Complexity of junction circuits.
10.9.2 HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE OF TELEPHONE SWITCHING SYSTEM Telephone switching system simply refers to a central system which comprises switches and other communication equipment, used to establish connection between two or more telephone or telecommunication devices.
[Figure 10.18: classification of switching systems]
Electronic switching system (ESS) is a telephone switching system that uses digital electronics, and computerized control to interconnect telephone circuits for the purpose of establishing telephone calls. Manual switching Prior to the advent of automatic switching, all telephone connections were made by hand at the manual switchboard. In this regard, the calling subscriber rings up an operator at a switch office who interconnects the calling subscriber to the called subscriber in other to initiate a communication contact between them. Plug-and-cord switching A plug and cord switchboard consist of one jack per subscriber, a calling indicator per subscriber and as many cord circuits as the number of calls, so require. In order to connect two subscribers, one cord of a pair is inserted in the calling subscribers jack. The basic switching plan is shown in figure 10.18 below. The jack and calling indicator are usually arranged in a numerical order on the vertical face of the switchboard forming a “Jackfield” while the cord circuits are equipped on the horizontal key shelf.
Each cord consists of three conductors connected to the three contract points of the plugs which are i. The Tip ii. The Ring and iii. The Sleeve The number of line which can be accommodated on a switch board is limited both by size, of the jacks and indicators and by the size of the jackfield. Disadvantages abound in relation to their labor intensity, and complexity of connecting calls across multiple switches.
[Figure 10.19 : plug-and-cord switching mechanism]
Step-By-Step (Strowger) Switch The step-by-step (SXS) or Strowger switching system was the first automatic telephone switching system in the word introduced by Almond.B.Strowger. This system uses selectors for switching. The selectors used in strowger switches are majorly of two types, namely: (i). The uniselector (ii). The two-motion selector
[Figure 10.20: The Strowger ( s x s) switch]
The step by step switches are electromechanical switches which consist of a large number of line finders to which group of individual subscribers are assigned for dial tone. The transmitting party dials a series of numbers which causes the making and breaking of an electric circuit; as shown above. These electrical pulses cause successive mechanical line selectors to click across contacts that set conversation path as the complete number is dialed. This set of switches major disadvantages are: (i). low speed (ii). High cost. (iii). Bulky size (iv) Limitation in terms of capacity (v). High cost of maintenance, etc. The (SXS) Step-by-step system houses both the control path and the speech path, integrated into the same unit. As each digit is dialed the connection is made to one further stage until the final selection when two digits are required in the final selector. The uniseletor and the two motion selectors belong to the same types of switches referred to as rotary switches. Uniselector The uniselector is so called because the rotary motion of the switch is one direction in other words the wiper assembly moves only in one direction hence the prefix, “uni” it consists of moving parts called wipers which are used to make electrical connections with any one of several contact geared forwards through the arc around it. The arc in most cases consists of ten steps. The wiper assembly is divided into three sets of wipers so that the switch has to turn through only one-third (1/3) of a full circle, when separated. These wipers are operated by an electromagnet called Pawl magnet with the help of a ratchet and pawl mechanism. When current flows through the
windings of the driving magnet, it is energized and attracts the armature, as the pawl slips over one tooth of the ratchet wheel. The ratchet is prevented form movement in the reverse direction by a decent. When the current stops through the winding of the driving magnet, it is de-energized and the armature carries it back to its rest position. During the reverse back movement of the armature and hence that of the pawl, the ratchet wheel stops ahead in the clock wise direction by one tooth, and the wipers to the next contact. The uniselector rotates as many steps as the electromagnet is energized and de energized.
[Figure 10.21: Uniselector, comprising Pawl and Ratchet mechanism]
The Two-motion selector (Rectangular motion selector0 The two- motion selector is a type of rotary switch in which the motion of the wiper assembly is in two directions, thus; (i). Vertical direction (ii). Horizontal direction In the vertical direction, the wipers move upward to the desired level and make no connections with the bank contacts, while in the horizontal direction the wipers make connection with the bank contacts. The two motion selector has (10) ten levels; each of the ten levels, also have 10 (ten) contacts hence 10x10 = 100 accessible contacts. Each contact in the two-motion selector represents the terminals of one switch of the higher stage or of one telephone line in the case of final selector. The dialing pulses cause the wiper assembly to step up or down to the desired level. Considering a final selector where up to 100 lines can be connected, the vertical and horizontal stepping of the selector are controlled by the digits dialed by the subscriber, when the first digit is dialed, the dialing pulses energize and de-energizes the vertical magnet. The vertical magnet with the help of ratchet and Pawl mechanism step up the wiper assembly, corresponding to the digit dialed, - This is called vertical stepping. As the second digit is dialed the dialing pulses are diverted to another magnet called horizontal magnet, with the help of the relay. These pulses energize and de-energize the horizontal magnet with the help of ratchet and pawl which causes the wiper assembly to rotate to the proper contact, corresponding to the second digit dialed. This is called the horizontal stepping. Thus, the wiper assembly makes connection with the required number dialed by the subscriber. Upon completion of the call, the wiper assembly comes back to the home position. For this purpose, the rotary magnet is operated by the current and thus the wiper assembly moves through the remaining contacts of the level. A spring forces the wiper assembly to drop vertically and then to return horizontally to its normal position. Thus the two-motion selector does not require an additional magnet for its homing process.
[Figure 10.22: two motion uniselector]
Line Hunter A line hunter is a switch which has its wipers connected to the calling circuit and which when self-driving, searches for a free outlet. This is called hunting because, just as with a human hunter, there will be some occasion when its search is unsuccessful. This happens when all the selectors to which it has access are already in use by other subscribers. The subscriber’s line uniselectors are being used as hunters to concentrate traffic from a large number of subscribers to a few number of outlet.
Line Finder A line finder is a switch which has its wipers connected to called circuit and the calling circuits are connected to the bank contacts so that when self-driving, it searches for the circuit on which the calling signal originated. Since the switch self-drives in this way, only when there is such a calling signal, it is always possible for it to find the calling circuit. Two-motion selectors are economically used as line-finders.
[Figure 10.23: Constructional feature of the line hunter and line finder mechanism]
Crossbar switching The crossbar switch is a matrix switch used to establish a speech path between subscribers. In a crossbar switch, a request for dial tone is recognized by a marker which directs a sender to the dialed digits. To this end, an electrical contact is established by actuating a horizontal and vertical relay.
[Figure 10.24: (a) 4 x 4 crossbar switching (b) 3 x 3 crossbar switching]
Common Control Switching
[Figure 10.25: common control switch mechanism]
In line with the step-by-step switch system, all control equipment are provided on a per-cell basis. However, with the common control system there exist an integration of computer technology with the telephone system where the conversation is digitized and switches over high speed digital circuit with all processes accomplished through programmed logic. This system is microprocessor based, as it offers advantages of increased intelligence, greater speed in relation to call set up call processing and reduced component size, alongside lower cost of maintenance, ability to be monitored and managed from a remote location, greater capacity and better efficiency as well as room for expansion and upgrade of the system. Additional feature such as data, Video, etc. are also incorporated. Types of signal to be switched: A two wire circuit carries signals in both directions at the same time in pairs. In order to provide a means of connecting this type of circuit to other local lines or trunks each switch in the local switching system must be capable of connecting at least two wires to two other wires and must be capable of transmitting signals in both directions. It would be possible to have only one speech wire to be switched within the switching centre, however the signal will be converted from a balanced to an unbalanced form by means of a transformer as shown below.
However, the use of unbalanced signals within the switching centre can lead to interference being picked up by other unbalanced transmission paths within the centre, thus increasing the background noise and possibly allowing conversations to be overheard by other users. (This is called crosstalk). In general, the use of unbalanced switches is only practicable in very small switching centres where the physical length of the unbalanced path is sufficiently small to avoid significant pick-up. This is shown in figure 10.26.
Figure 10.26 (a) Use of balance-to-unbalance transformer to provide single-wire transmission within a switching machine Figure 10.26 (b) Use of two-to-four wire converter (hybrid) in trunk transmission sysytem
Within a switching system it is often more economical to transmit the control signals along a separate path from the information. So each switch may have to switch more than two wires. The trunks used in long distance telephone networks are usually provided by multiplexed transmission system. It is necessary to split the two directions of speech to produce what is called a four-wire circuit. Before the circuit can be switched at the other end of the trunk it often has to be reconverted to a two- wire circuit. There is in fact a considerable advantage to the overall transmission system if the intermediate
trunk switching centres can switch the four-wire circuit directly. The switches in such systems must switch at least four wires, but they need only pass signals in one direction. In video systems, the high bandwidth involved makes it impracticable to construct two-to-four wire converters and therefore it is not normally practicable to use a cable for bi-directional transmission of video signals. As a result, all video switching must be four-wire if two-way communication is needed. Data signals in analogue form can be switched by analogue switches. However, in switching systems designed for data signals, the signal is first converted to digital form. This means that the switch elements themselves may be digital and use conventional logic gates.
10.9.3 TELEPHONE SWITCHES AND SWITCHING MECHANISM There are three classes of switch based on the division of information in space, time and frequency. The difference can be shown by considering the simple example of figure 10.25 in which three inlets has to be connected to any of three outlets.
[Figure 10.27 (a) Requirement for switching in space, time, and frequency]
[Figure 10.27 (b) Space divided switches]
10.9.3.1 Space division switches A space divided switch is one which provides a fixed physical path for the duration of a connection. This could be constructed by (three) 3-way switches as shown in figure 10.28 in which, for a particular set of connections, inlet 1 is connected to outlet 2, inlet 2 is connected to outlet 3 and inlet 3 is connected to outlet 1. The advantage of space division is its simplicity and the fact that the bandwidth of the signal is not unduly limited by the switch mechanism. It is of course limited by crosstalk considerations and by the characteristics of the switch itself. The disadvantage of space division is that the switches can be relatively slow to operate, it can be bulky and can involve a large amount of wiring because each connection needs its own set of wires. The switches used in space division (space division switches) are of various types which include, conventional relays, reed relays and uniselectors. Conventional relays used in space division switches These are simple devices which, when used for switching, connects one inlet to one outlet via a set of contacts In order to build a switching network, relays have to be arranged into matrices as shown in figure 10.28. Each relay is known as cross point. A space switch must remain operated (or latched) for the duration of a call. Magnetic latching can be achieved by the use of combinations of hard and soft magnetic materials in the magnetic circuit. A pulse of current operates the relay and it is released by a pulse of current of the opposite polarity. Mechanical latching relays are also sometimes used; These require two solenoids, one to operate and the other to release the contact.
[Figure 10.28 Matrices of relay and Principle of electrical latching]
Reed relays used in space division switches One common electro-mechanical switch used in modern switching equipment is the reed relay. This consists of a pair of contacts made of a soft magnetic material and enclosed in an evacuated or rarefied. A number of these contacts may be placed inside a single coil. When the coil is energized the contacts are attracted to each other and a connection is made. The advantage of this type of switch is that it is fast operating (about 2-10ms), it has a potentially long and reliable life and it is cheap to construct and handle by automatic means. In switching centres, reed relays are usually arranged in matrices and need to be electrically latched. An alternative to electrical latching is a magnetic latching reed relay called a ferreed. There is one permanent magnet and one magnet whose direction of magnetization can be reversed by means of a current pulse through its winding. When the magnets are both magnetized in the same direction, the contacts operate. The main disadvantage of this system is the large currents needed to operate the coils and the associated back e. m. f. A more recent development is the remanent reed, which relies on the magnetic properties of the reed contacts themselves to provide the magnetic latching.
Uniselectors used in space division switches These are an extension of the principle of the relay in that they can connect one inlet to one of a number of outlets, instead of just one. There are many forms of these devices, the simplest of which uses an electromagnetically operated ratchet to step a number of wiper arms around a bank of contacts. Another version uses a motor with an electromagnetic clutch to stop the wipers at a particular position. A large number may be driven by a heavy-duty common motor with individual selectors operated by means of electromagnetic clutches. The number of outlets that can be provided on a uniselector depends on the speed with which the wiper can be rotated across all the contacts. A motor uniselector can go as fast as 200 steps per second. In most switching machines it is necessary to position the selector within a short time.
10.9.3.2 Time division switches An alternative to providing a separate physical path for each connection is to connect all the inlets and outlets to a common transmission medium via high speed switches. These switches connect the required inlet and outlet onto the same path for a short time, followed by another inlet and outlet, as shown in figure 10.29. Each input is in effect ‘sampled’ by the operation of its switch. This process is repeated periodically. The connection pattern can be changed by altering the time at which the outlets are switched. This technique may only be used where the signal is not affected by the
sampling process. For example, it may be used for digital information which has already been sampled, or for analogue signals which have been band limited before sampling. In the latter case a reconstruction filter (usually an amplifier) is needed in the outlets. The major advantage of the time division is that it can be fast and compact, but it is usually of practical value only when the signal is already in a digital form. Time division switching of analogue signals has only limited application.
[Figure 10.29 Time divided switch]
10.9.3.3 Frequency division switches A second alternative to space division involves the use of a common transmission path, as in time-division switching, but in this case each signal is modulated onto a different carrier frequency. See figure 10.30. Switching is achieved if each outlet is provided with a demodulator which can have its carrier frequency changed. Until recently, there was no practical application involving frequency division switching, apart from that, which is implicit in radio communication. This is because a space-divided switch is needed to change the demodulator frequencies and so no savings are obtained. However, frequency division switching is now finding application in demand-assigned satellite communication links.
[Figure 10.28 Frequency divided switch]

10.9.4 Switched Network Configurations

10.9.4.1 Message switching system Message switching is more familiar to the business or military user. The terminals of message switched systems are usually teleprinters, but unlike the telex network they are not interconnected directly. Instead, when a terminal user types a message destined for some other terminal, the system stores the message and delivers it to the required terminal at some later time. The reason for the delay is that the system is designed to maximize the utilization of transmission links by queuing messages awaiting the use of a link. In order to set up a direct connection over many links connected end-to-end it is necessary for each link to be simultaneously free. This implies that the average utilization of the links must be low if the probability of a direct connection being available on demand is to be high enough to satisfy most users. However, in a message switched system, where messages are queued for each link, much higher link utilization is achieved. Another name for this type of system is store-and-forward switching. 10.9.4.2 General purpose packet switching systems More recently, general purpose packet switching systems have been developed which takes data from a terminal of a computer and transmit it as short packets of information to the required destination. The interchange of packets may be made so rapid that a terminal appears to provide a ‘conversational’ connection while at the same time high transmission link utilizations are obtained through queuing.
10.9.4.3 Transmission link systems In this context, a simple way of structuring a switched network is to arrange that each terminal has a direct transmission link to every other terminal, as shown in figure 10.31. Each terminal needs a switch to connect it to the required link and a switch to make connection to a link in order to receive an incoming call. For N terminals this arrangement needs a total of 12N(N − 1)links.
[Figure 10.31:Full interconnection for five terminals link system]
It is very clear that some form of switching is needed within each terminal to connect it to the appropriate link, for the full interconnection of the system. An alternative approach which needs only N links is to provide one link per terminal and to arrange that all other terminals have access to it as shown in figure 10.30. This simplifies the terminal equipment because it removes the need to connect a terminal to a link for an incoming call. This is a practical arrangement for systems such as house telephone or intercoms where there is relatively small number of terminals close together. For instance, it is possible to provide a twelve-terminal system with each terminal having eleven buttons and twelve pairs of wires going around to each instrument. However, when the number of terminals increases, or their geographical separation increases, the cost of cabling makes this arrangement uneconomic. Another example of the technique illustrated above, is a radio telephone network in which each terminal is given its own frequency. An originator can set up call by tuning his transmitter to the frequency of the called terminal.
[Figure 10.32: Interconnection of N channels with N Links.]
Each terminal is permanently connected to one channel and all other terminals may access a particular terminal by operating a switch which connects it to the appropriate channel.
[Figure 10.33 : Interconnection of N channels with less than N Links.]
It is possible to use an arrangement similar to that just described but with fewer than N links, as shown in figure 10.33. With this arrangement it is necessary for the calling terminal to select a free link and for the called terminal to be connected to the same link. One technique used extensively for radio telephones involves a common channel
to which all free terminals are connected. A calling signal (which may be coded or verbal) is sent along this link and is received by the terminals. The calling signal informs the called terminal (or its user) of an incoming call and indicates the link to which the terminal should be switched in order to receive the call. The recognition of the calling signal and the switching operations may be performed automatically in a system using coded signals. In simpler systems the users may be required to listen out for and act upon verbal calling signals. At present, the ‘distributed’ switching technique is applied only to small telephone systems and to some radio telephone networks. One of the possibilities ahead is what is called a ‘digital ring main’ in which a high speed binary digital link is connected to a large number of terminals. Similar techniques to that described above may then be used. For example, a terminal could connect itself to a free time slot within the digital bit stream in order to set up a communication path to the called terminal.
10.9.4.4 Centralized switching system In most practical switched networks it is usually more economic to provide a link between each terminal and a central location and to perform all switching operations there, as illustrated in figure 10.34. This arrangement significantly reduces the total transmission costs in the network. However, the switching centre must be operated by remote control from the terminal and this tends to increase the total switching costs.
Figure10.32: The use of centralized switching machines (a) single machine which reduces average length of transmission link (b) use of additional switching machine to reduce transmission cost
The total transmission costs may be reduced even further if a number of local switching centres are used instead of one national centre because this reduces the average length of the connection between a terminal and its nearest switching centre. The local centres must be interconnected by transmission links which are usually called trunks. These trunks are shared by all the terminals connected to a local centre and can be very much smaller than the number of terminals. The use of multiplexing techniques for long distance transmission makes cost per unit distance for a trunk less than the cost per unit distance for the link between a terminal and its local switching centre. Therefore, increasing the number of switching centres, lowers the total transmission cost. However, as the number of centres is increased the total switching costs tend to increase for two reasons. First, the local centres become more complex because they must be able to decide on a suitable routing to another point, and because the centres involved in a call must be able to exchange information. Secondly, economy of scale is lost with an increased number of local centres because two half sized centres, plus their buildings and power supplies, cost more than one full sized centre. In general, there are optimum number of local centres for minimum total cost of transmission and switching. This optimum number of local centres depends upon the relative costs of switching equipment and transmission equipment and the geographical distribution of terminals. If certain assumptions are made about the geographical distribution of terminals, their traffic characteristics, and the costs of switching and transmission, it is possible to make mathematical analyses of the minimum cost for a total system. However, these analyses have limited value because the practical details of a given situation invalidate the generalized assumptions. For instance, in the telephone field, detailed costing of possible network plans are needed in order to decide how many switching centres should be installed to cover a particular area, or more usually, to decide whether it is better to install a new switching centre in the suburbs of a growing town, or to extend the main centre. These costing are simplified by using detailed computer models of the area under consideration to facilitate rapid estimation of the costs of alternative arrangements.
10.9.4.5 Hierarchical systems As the number of separate switching centres increases the number of different trunk routes between them increases. Above about ten centres the number of trunk routes becomes very large and routes tend to contain too few circuits to make the network economic. The same argument that led to centralized local switching now applies to the trunk routes, so trunk switching centres are introduced to switch between trunks. Figure 10.35 shows how the trunk centres reduce the total length of trunk circuits. However, this arrangement introduces the additional cost of trunk switching centres and also necessitates at least three switching points (rather than one or two) on some connections.
Figure10.35: Mesh of trunk routes
The process of centralizing switching centres can occur at several levels leading to what is called a hierarchical network. This is best explained by reference to the public telephone network. In a country there are a number of local switching centres, each serving anything from 20 to 10,000 terminals (or even up to 100,000 in other cases). These local centres are gathered into groups and each group is served by a trunk centre which can connect calls between local centres within the group. For calls between terminals of one group of local centres, and those of another, the trunk centres themselves have to be interconnected by ‘super’ trunk centres each covering an area consisting of many local groups. Usually there are a number of these wider areas and these too will be interconnected by higher level trunk centres. This principle is extended to the level where the number of trunk centres at that level is small enough for it to be practical to interconnect them fully with a mesh of trunk routes. The result is as shown in figure 10.36. Figure 10.36(a) is the Hierarchical network of switching centres and figure 10.36(b) is conventional representations.

10.10 DIGITAL TELEPHONE HANDSET

Digital telephone handset is an electronic gadget which avails the user, some features and facilities provided by digital exchanges.
10.10.1 FEATURES OF DIGITAL TELEPHONE HANDSET Some unique features exist of digital telephone handsets, which are but are not limited to following: Chats, Video calls, Caller identity, Multi-party call, Hot-line dialing, Abbreviated dialing, Alarm service, Call waiting, Call blocking, and Call diversion,etc. 10.10.1.1 Chats This feature enables users to transmit or share information as well as pictures. It could also be done, on group basis.
10.10.1.2 Video calls This feature enables both the caller and the called to transmit videos even while call is in progress.

10.10.1.3 Caller identity

This feature enables the called subscriber to know the identity of the subscriber that calls him. Some digital telephone handsets that have this facility can store up to a thousand outgoing or incoming calls which can be recalled on request.

10.10.1.4 Multi-party call

This feature allows a subscriber to add a third party to an existing call link. All participants can talk and listen to each other simultaneously without any restriction. The subscriber can keep both calls private or open for a general discussion. At least one of the party callers must be a subscriber with this facility. It is popularly called conference call.

10.10.1.5 Hot-line dialing

Some subscribers call a certain number often. The subscribers may find it useful to get the number required without repeated dials. The digital telephone handset has a feature which enables the calling subscriber to program the required number. Once it is activated in the system, the subscriber can call the other party without necessarily dialing the entire number.

10.10.1.6 Abbreviated dialing

This feature helps in saving time and for security reasons. Here the telephone number can be replaced by a digit code and be dialed instead of the number. The code is also displayed on the set whenever the number it represents is dialed. This prevents the exposure of very special numbers.

10.10.1.7 Alarm service

A subscriber who uses the digital telephone handset can set up an alarm system to remind him or her of a time. The execution of an alarm order is the responsibility of the exchange. Executing the order the subscriber requests through his digital handset, the telephone exchange initiates the alarm call. Here, the hours (times) are entered using the standards (GMT) 24hours clock. The subscribers can specify the desired time of the alarm call. It will be executed automatically at about the specified time. The telephone will ring for some seconds. If unanswered or the line is engaged, the alarm call repeats after 5 minutes.

10.10.1.8 Call waiting

Call waiting feature allows a subscriber to be informed about a call attempt by a third person while the subscriber is talking to another subscriber. This feature allows the user to answer all calls without missing any call. The notice of incoming call is subtle. You hear a beep (attention signal) in every three seconds which the person you are talking with does not hear. You can choose to accept or ignore the waiting call. The subscriber called may control this feature by digit or by hook flash.
Control of call waiting feature by digits require the subscriber called to hook flash and on reception of dial tone to enter a specific digit to control the call. A digit ‘0’cancels the call waiting attempt and inhibits further attempts for this call. A digit ‘1’ switches to subscriber B. A digit ‘2’ switches to subscriber ‘C’ which is on hold and sets subscriber B on hold. The control of the features by hook flashes enables subscriber A to alternate between subscriber B and C.

10.10.1.9 Call blocking

For fear of abuse, many subscribers block their telephones such that either outgoing calls or in-coming calls cannot be made from that number.

10.10.1.10 Call diversion

This feature enables the user to divert or re-route calls to another number. This feature is first activated in the system before it could be performed at the subscribers end. It is this code that is activated and recognized by the system before it can be performed by the digital telephone handset. If a subscriber of line A activates a call diversion to line B, then all calls to line A are routed to line B.

10.11 TELEPHONE TRAFFIC THEORY

Telephone traffic refers to the aggregate of all user requests being serviced by the network with regards to number of calls and duration of calls. In this regard, service requests arrive randomly and it usually requires unpredictable service times because, a subscriber could make call at any time, yet the resources to make such call is shared by all subscribers and capacity fixed, following the design.
10.11.1 TELEPHONE TRAFFIC ENGINEERING ANALYSIS This provides the basis for analysis and design of the telecommunication network as desired. It is further used to provide the method for determining the cost effectiveness particular of various sizes and configuration of the network.
Traffic engineering analysis, provides means to determine the quantum of common equipment required to provide a particular level of service for a given traffic pattern and volume. It is also used to determine the ability of a telecommunication network to carry a given traffic at a particular loss probability.
10.11.2 TECHNIQUES FOR TELEPHONE TRAFFIC ANALYSIS Loss system: In this system overload traffic is rejected without being serviced Delay system: In this system overload traffic is held in a queue until the facility for use become available to initiate the call.
10.11.3 PROBABILITY OF CALL BLOCKING Two theories are used to estimate the probability of the occurrence of call blocking They are; Traffic theory and Queuing theory As a result of the random nature of the network, traffic fundamental of probability theory is applied. The unpredictable nature of traffic arrives as a result of
(i). Call Arrivals and (ii). Holding time In either case, the traffic load depends on frequency of arrival and average holding time for each arrival.
10.11.4 TRAFFIC MEASUREMENT Measurement of traffic within a network allows a network analyst (manager) to make both day to day decision about operation and plan for long term developments giving rise to the provision of more reliable and efficient telephone service. These measurements are conducted on a continuous basis and the result compiled into report for further network management with intent to resolve potential sources of
network congestion. Traffic measurements are used in many fundamental activities such as; (i)      Calculating traffic intensity in specific circuit or group (ii)     Identification of traffic pattern and trends monitoring services (iii)    Forecast of future network demands Etc. Calls are lost during congestion problem, giving rise to customers dissatisfaction and hence loss of revenue to the network provider.

10.12 TELEPHONE NETWORK OVERLOAD

Telephone network overload is a phenomenon which occurs in a network when it experiences congestion as a result of various influences on the network.
10.12.1 TYPES OF TELEPHONE NETWORK OVERLOAD Some general classes of overload exist in telephone network, namely; General overload, local overload, focused overload and overload occasion by vandals,etc. 10.12.1.1 General Overload This kind of overload, generally affects a whole network and it is caused by increased activity on a holiday or particularly busy days e.g. Christmas, salah, or other festive periods. In this context, subscribers come in from various locations hence, the seemingly less densely populated areas suddenly become overpopulated, thereby overloading the network within that period, under review.
10.12.1.2 Local Overload This is caused by local problems such as major equipment failure. The difficulty here is to prevent the effect of the congestion from spreading into the rest of the network.
10.12.1.3 Focused Overload This is generally caused by local disasters such as Floods, Snowstorms, Widespread fires, Earthquakes, Hurricanes, Typhoons, or airplane crashes, etc, where the calling rate from the rest of the network into and out of theaffected area becomes abnormally high.
10.12.1.4 Overload Occasioned By Vandals, or Terrorist Groups and Militants This is experienced more, in the oil rich Niger Delta region of Nigeria, where militants blow up communication equipment with ease, as well as areas under siege by other terrorist groups such as Boko haram, ISIS, etc.
10.12.2 CAUSES OF OVER LOAD IN TELEPHONE NETWORK Overload could be caused in a telephone network, following a lot of factors amongst which are:
i.   Too many subscribers above the carriage capacity of the equipment provided. ii.   Too many requests on the network. iii.   Low bandwidth iv.    Use of outdated hardware and equipment v.    Wrong configuration management. vi.    Rogues interference. eg.     One who taps through another’s Wifi connection,etc.

10.12.3 CONTROLLING OVERLOAD IN A TELEPHONE NETWORK

All the classes of overload discussed so far have effects on switching centres and trunk networks. Therefore, controls must be introduced to limit the traffic at source, to prevent calls with high probability of being abandoned, from entering the system. Such calls may occupy resources for a significant time before being abandoned. Overload within a switching machine is most easily detected by monitoring the number of calls which are waiting for a register. This is found to be a stable and sensitive indicator, since the queues build up quickly, once the machine’s maximum capacity is approached. One of the advantages of this indicator is that it is independent of the number of registers in service. When the number of calls waiting exceeds some preset limit, the machine is assumed to be in a state of near congestion, and some form of traffic limitation is introduced. Furthermore, for machine congestion caused by locally originated calls, the simple technique for traffic restriction is to disconnect temporarily, the calling side of all but predetermined priority subscribers like police and medical emergency units. A more sophisticated method is to split the non-priority subscribers into a number of groups, and withhold calling detection from all but one group for several minutes. If the accepting group is rotated, the effective calling rate is reduced, assuming that all subscribers are discouraged from making the calls except the persistent ones.
10.12.3.1 Directionalization in Telephone Network Directionalization is one of the techniques used in improving the effective traffic capacity of a network and controlling over load. When a machine recognizes the onset of trunk congestion, it switches some of its both-way trunks to the higher order centres
to incoming calls only. This provides a preference for terminating, rather than originating traffics, therefore calls which have already passed through several links are given a greater probability of success, compared with new calls, which have so far used fewer resources. 10.12.3.2 Supplementary routing to utilize time difference between international exchange At certain times of the day there will be little traffic between the two time zones and the circuits will be under used. So their use for this purpose increases their efficiency. Similar routing are used in North American, where early morning traffic between East coast centres are sometimes routed via the West coast. Another case where supplementary routing is desirable is when one of the links is already carried by a satellite circuit. The hierarchical system is not generally applicable to the military switching systems because the military system requires a more dispersed type of routing to minimize the effect of the loss of a trunk route or a switching centre. This leads to a routing plan based on hexagonal grids, which can provide a wide range of alternative routes.

10.13 NUMBERING SCHEMES IN TELEPHONE NETWORK SYSTEM

In modern systems, the numbering scheme used by a telephone administration to allocate subscribers’ numbers has an underlying plan, and there are a few constraints on the development of the plan that must be taken into account: i.   It must provide each subscriber with a unique number within the national network. ii.   The allocation to areas must be able to meet forecast growth for several decades. iii.   The number of digits should not exceed that recommended by CCITT
In principle, (i) is easy to satisfy if (ii) and (iii) have been met. The length of the number recommended by CCITT is 11 – n where n is the country code (see figure 10.39 below). If, for example, n is 2, then the national number should not exceed nine digits in length. These digits are used to denote the subscriber’s number on the local exchange, the exchange within a given area, and the area within the national numbering scheme. In many local exchanges there is a maximum capacity of 10 000
(0000 - 9999) lines, thus the last four digits of the national number are allocated to the subscriber’s number in the exchange of the remaining five digits in our example, the first two would denote the area and the remaining three the exchange within the area. Thus the number has the form shown in figure 10.38
[Figure 10.38: National telephone number]
The division of digits between area exchange and subscriber’s code may not be the same as that shown, but all three components exist in every number. For automatic long distance dialing a prefix is necessary to indicate to the exchange equipment that a trunk call is being made. In many countries a “0” is used, but any other digit would do. In calculating the length of the national number the prefix is not included.

10.13.1 NUMBERING PLANS

Today, person-to-person calls could be made very easily via individual instruments and satellite links. For such availability of connections to be possible each subscriber in the world must have a unique number. To achieve that, some agreement between countries is essential; each country must be identified by a number different from that of all other countries. That is achieved by agreement through CCITT {Comite’ Consultatif International de Telegraphie et Te’le’phonie or International Committee on Telegraphy and Telephony – In English Language} on the way in which these codes, called country codes are allocated. The first digit of the country code is the zone code; the world is divided up into nine zones and each country belongs to a zone. The relationship between zone number and geographical area is shown in the table below. In all but two of the zones, one or two digits are added to the zone number to produce the country code. For example, Nigeria has a zone number of 2 and an additional country code of 34 to give its country code 234.Brazil has a zone number 5 and an additional country code digit 5 to give its country code 55.
The two exceptions are zones 1 (North America and the Caribbean) and 7 (USSR). Throughout each of these zones there is a linked numbering scheme that means, for example, that no subscriber in Canada has the same national number as a subscriber in the USA. In many countries local calls use a shorter code. For calls within the same area, the area code is omitted, and for small single exchange areas no exchange code is used for own-exchange calls. Coupled with this, the last arrangement will be a very short code for calls to adjacent exchanges. These arrangements are particularly well suited to rural areas. The major disadvantage of short codes is that they change with the location of the calling subscriber, and therefore a short code directory must be available in each exchange area.
