10.13.3.1 Components of telephone number

So it is usual in public telephone network to have three lengths of number; Subscriber or customer number, National number and International number. Subscriber or customer number This refers to a shortened version of numbers, for local use only. It is the number to be dialed to reach a subscriber in the same local network or numbering area. It consists of two parts namely; the exchange code and the terminal number. The fusion of both the exchange code and the terminal number is generally of about eight digits or less, e.g. 200053. The terminal number is usually between 2 to 5 digits where an individual switching Centre could have between 100 to 100,000 subscribers. National number This refers to a standard length of numbers, used within the country. It is the numbers that ought to be dialed within the same country but at different areas (states). National number comprises a combination of Trunk Code and Subscriber’s Number e.g. 084200053. (0 84 20 0053) International number This refers to a full version of numbers, for international use. An international number consists of an international prefix (used to gain access to appropriate equipment) followed by country code, and then the national number. For instance, if we have 084200053 {+ 2 34 84 20 0053}, we can break it down to different components that make up the overall phone number.
+ depicts International prefix 2 depicts Continent or zone code, in this case, Africa 34 depicts the remainder of the Country code (Nigeria) 84 depicts State code, in this regard, Rivers State 20 depicts Area code (of the River State), Ahoada (LGA) Area code 0053 is the subscriber’s number

10.14 BILLING SYSTEM

In a telephone network it is necessary to charge users for the calls they make. Three major types of billing systems exists, namely; i.        Flat rate rentals ii.       Itemized billing and iii.      Bulk billing 10.14.1 FLAT RATE RENTALS Flat rate rental is the simplest type of billing system, as it saves the cost of collecting any call data. This method is about the oldest billing method. It is effective for local (short distance) calls; but for long distance calls they are charged on time and distance basis. So the information regarding the location and time of the day is of essence. The basic information required for charging are; i.            The destination ii.           Duration of call and iii.          Identity of the calling subscriber.
10.14.2 ITEMIZED BILLING In this type of billing system, call information is collected, regarding call distance, duration of call, etc. These information are used to generate the call cost to the customer as they vary in costs following the characteristics.
10.14.3 BULK BILLING Bulk billing system applies to individuals or corporate organizations that are attached to post billing system where it applies to the entire workforces who are using the telephone provider’s lines. In this regard, the aggregate call bill for the period under review is issued on a periodic basis, in most cases, monthly periodic basis.

10.15 NETWORK MANAGEMENT AND ADMINISTRATION

It is of great importance to ensure thata telephone network is always used in the most effective manner. It implies that the network must therefore cope with unexpected peaks of demand and occasional failures of trunk routes and switching centres. The network design must ensure that effects on the remainder of a system of local overload or failure sre minimized. This is achieved by incorporating controls in individual centres and by provoding network management centres which collect and process information from switching centres and transmission facilities in a geographical araea. This information allows network controllers to detect the onset of overload or failures and issues command to contain the problem.

10.16 OVERVIEW OF THE TELEPHONE NETWORK

In recent years, the telephone network has developed dramatically so that it is now possible to make calls automatically between subscribers separated by thousands of miles. Long distance calls pass through several stages of switching and several possible transmission links before reaching their destinations, and to make such calls possible many facets of telecommunications must be integrated and reasonable compromises made by systems designers. In practice, there are very few occasions when a telecommunication administrator has the opportunity to design a network from the beginning till absolute completion. Usually some sort of network exists already and there is a demand for increased service, more lines, better performance, more facilities, more comprehensive direct dialing etc. the demand has to be satisfied by grafting on to the existing system, new switching and transmission equipment that may be totally different in types, and in its principles of operation.
[Figure 10.39: Hierarchical routing system]
Recent years have seen two revolutionary developments: The integrated circuits leading to cheap, reliable, small and very powerful digital systems, and the optical fibre, which is much better in many respects than conventional transmission media. These two have led to an entirely new approach, and enormously enhanced facilities for future systems. One of the major planning problems is how to graft such new systems on to existing equipment. Although the structure of telephone networks has developed considerably as demand has increased, it still has some identifiable form. The passage of a call through a national network can be represented by the multi-level diagram shown in figure 10.39. Several levels of switching that combine to form the complete network, exists as contained in figure 10.39. It is usual to think of the systems in two parts. The first is the junction network, serving the subscriber and consisting of the link from subscriber

10.17 MULTIPLEXING IN TELEPHONE NETWORK

This involves the sharing of expensive network resources by several connections or information flows. The network resource in this context is the bandwidth measured in Hz for analog systems and bits per second for digital transmission systems. Two types of multiplexing techniques as used in telephone network, are frequency division multiplexing and time division multiplexing. In addition to using multiplexing in telephone network, another system called channelization is also in use.

10.17.1 FREQUENCY DIVISION MULTIPLEXING (FDM)

In the diagram of figure 10.40, each user has W Hz bandwidth and the channel that is available is greater than 3W Hz. In FDM, the bandwidth is divided into a number of frequency slots, each of which can accommodate the signal of an individual
connection. The multiplexer assigns a frequency slots to each connection and uses modulation to place the signal of the connection in the appropriate slot. This process results in an overall combined signal that carries all the connections as shown above. The combined signal is transmitted and demultiplexer used to recover the signals corresponding to each correction thereby reducing the number of wires that need to be used and hence an overall cost reduction of the system.
[Figure 10.40: Combined signals fits into channel bandwidth.]
FDM was introduced in the telephone network in the 1930’s the basic analog multiplexer combines 12 voice channels in one line. Each voice signal occupies 4KHz of bandwidth. The multiplexer modulates each voice signal so that it occupies a 4KHz slot in the band between 60 and 108 KHz. The combined signal is called a group. A hierarchy of analog multiplexer has been defined thus; 1 GROUP carries 12 voice channels. 1 SUPER GROUP is an equivalentof 5 GROUPS, which carries 60 voice channels. Formed by the multiplexing of 5 groups each of bandwidth, 48KHz, into the frequency band from 312 to 552KHz. 10 super groups gives 1master group. (10 multiplexed super group=1master group)
which contains 600 voice signals that occupies the band 564 to 3084KHz. various combinations of master groups have also been defined. For the purpose of multiplexing, each group is treated as an individual signal. Examples of FDM are broadcast radio, television and cable television where each station has assigned frequency band. Station in AM, FM and television are assigned frequency bands of 10kHz, 200kHz and 6MHz respectively. FDM is also used in cellular telephones. In cellular telephone 25-30KHz each are shared by the users within a geographic cell each user is assigned a frequency slot for each direction.FDM allows the simultaneous transmission of several independent message signals over a single common channel without mutual interference.

10.17.2 TIME DIVISION MULTIPLEXING

[Figure 10.41: Transmission of Time Division Multiplexed signals]
In time-division multiplexing, the transmission between the multiplexers is provided by a single high speed digital transmission line. Each connection produces a digital information flow that is then inserted into the high speed line. In the figure 10.41, each connection generates a signal that produces one unit of information every 3T seconds in bits, bytes, or fixed size block of bits.The transmission line is organized into frames that in turn are divided into equal sized slots. It is evident that from
figure10.41(a) that the transmission line can send one unit of information, every T seconds, and the combined signal in figure 10.41b, has a frame structure that consists of three slots one for each user. During connection set-up, each connection is assigned a slot that can accommodate the information produced by the connection.

10.17.3 CHANNELIZATION

Channelization involves the assignment of circuits to channels and the arrangement of those channels into separate groups and supergroups. These could be achieved by the use of various multiple access techniques for transmission of signals which is any of the following techniques; i.      Frequency Division Multiple Access ii.     Time Division Multiple Access iii.    Code Division Multiple Access. 10.17. 3. 1 Frequency Division Multiple Access (FDMA) In this regard, each station transmits its information continuously on an assigned band. With guard bands to reduce co-channel interference as shown in figure 10.42 .It is used for cellular telephone transmission and reception where each cell uses a forward and reverse channel to communicate to and from a base station.
[Figure 10.42: Frequency Division Multiple Access]
10.17.3.2 Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) In TDMA system, stations take turns making use of the entire transmission channel. Guard bands are required to ensure that transmissions from different stations do not overlap. TDMA systems are more flexible than FDMA systems. They are used in two ways to connect to a base station or a base controller. These are as Frequency Division Duplex (FDD) or Time Division Duplex (TDD)
Frequency Division Duplex In this regard, two separate frequency bands are used one for ‘forward’ direction communication from base station to other stations, while the second is used in the ‘reverse’ from stations to the base station, it is called Frequency Division Duplex transmission. Time Division Duplex In this context, base stations and other stations take turns transmitting over the same shared channel. TDMA is used with FDD in several digital cellular systems and with TDD in cordless telephone systems for in-building communications.
[Figure 10.43: Time Division Multiple Access]
10.17.3.3 Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) In CDMA the transmission from different stations occupy the entire frequency band at the same time. The transmissions are separated by the fact that different codes are used to produce the signals that are transmitted by the different stations. The receivers use these codes to recover the signal from the desired station.
[Figure 10.44: Conceptual view of CDMA]

10.18 GSM COMMUNICATION

GSM communication involves the transmission and reception of information over long distance without a physical link system. In this type of communication, the digital telephone handset is the telephone used for the communication. Other electronic devices for communication are also in use.

10.18.1 TRENDS IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF GSM COMMUNICATION

In line with the sequence of development of GSM to the present time, the global system for mobile communication has passed through series of advancement processes to get to its present stage. These trends are discussed as follows;

10.18.1.1 The First Generation (IG)

The first generation technology (IG) system is an analog system, which is continuous in Amplitude and time. It was used in the early 1980’s with a speed range of 4800- 9600bps (bits per second). The Advanced mobile phone system (AMPS) being first launched by the United States of America and spread to other parts of the world. It involved analog systems which transmitted only analog signals and therefore the transmission was only over short distances since it could only transmit analog voice signals which do not have capacity to travel in analog form, over long distance. The first generation systems is based on frequency division multiple access system (FDMA). It allows users to make voice calls in one country, hence, could not handle international calls. The first generation technology is characterized by; i.     Analog communication only ii.     No roaming iii.      Poor voice quality iv.      Large phone size v.      Zero security vi.      Frequent call drops vii.      Limited capacity viii.      Poor hands off reliability ix.      Poor battery life. 10.18.1.2 The second Generation (2G) Technology
The second generation systems use global systems for mobile communication (GSM). The 2G system was first used in Europe in the 1990’s. The 2G system provides voice and limited data services and uses digital modulation for improved audio quality. It involves a digital technology with a data speed rate of 9.6 kbps. It could be propagated over a long distance as it involves analog to digital conversion before transmission, and then a reconversion upon reception. The 2G Technology was first developed in 1991 in Finland with an initial data speed rate of 9.6 kbps. The second generation system is associated with
i.   GSM ii.   CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) iii.   D-AMPS (Digital Advanced mobile phone system) iv.    PDC (Personal digital communication) 2G can be divided into two standards, thus; i.   TDMA – Originally from Europe but used in the whole world. ii.   CDMA – Used in USA, and parts of Asia. The second generation also involves the 2.5G and 2.75G attached. The 2.5G This contains the GPRS [General Packet Radio Service] with a higher speed than the 2G System. The speed is up to 144kb/s. The 2.75G This contains EDGE- Enhanced data rates for GSM Evolution with a higher speed and increased data rate of 170kbps. Hence the second generation also involves the 2.5G and 2.75G attached. The shortcomings of the 2G Technology i. Low transmission quality ii. Spotty coverage iii. Inability to support complex data such as video iv. Low system capacity v. Limited coverage area of cell towers vi. Abrupt dropped calls. Etc.

The third generation technology has the capability of transferring voice, data and non- voice data music, E-mails, instant messages video and video calling, over the same network simultaneously. 10.19 FACSIMILE

Facsimile, Telefax or Fax for short is an electronic system for transmitting graphic information or radio. It involves the telephonic transmission of scanned printed materials, containing either or all of graphics, texts and picture information to a telephone number, connected to a printer or other output devices. The original document is scanned with a fax machine or a Telecopier, which processes the contents as a single fixed graphic image, converting it into a bitmap, and then transmitting it through the telephone system in the form of audio frequency tones. The receiving fax machine interprets the tones and reconstructs the image, and prints a paper copy of it.
